column4: Comparative Reasoning: Making an Audio Language Model Better at Comparing Emotions
column6: Large audio-language models (LALMs) can reason about audio, yet it remains unclear whether they can perform comparative judgments between two speech signals along emotional, environmental, linguistic, prosodic, and interpersonal dimensions. We study this question in the context of speech emotion recognition (SER), where the model determines which utterance exhibits higher arousal, valence, or dominance. We introduce a reasoning-guided ordinal SER framework that conditions an LALM on paired speech inputs. The model is trained using reasoning traces generated from both semantic audio descriptions and acoustic evidence derived from GeMAPS features, enabling interpretable comparative decisions. Beyond direct supervision, we also employ direct preference optimization to encourage stronger separation for emotional differences. Experiments show that the proposed framework improves preference prediction while requiring only 5% of the training data used by conventional ordinal SER systems.
column7: Abinay Reddy Naini(Carnegie Mellon University; The University of Texas at Dallas); Jaeyeon Kim(Carnegie Mellon University); Chao-Han Huck Yang(NVIDIA); Shinji Watanabe(Carnegie Mellon University); Carlos Busso(Carnegie Mellon University)

column4: Exploring the effect of the visual channel in vocal expression of affect in an Irish (Gaelic) synthetic voice
column6: This paper explores the effects of the visual context on the perception of emotion in synthesised speech. Vocal stimuli targeting the affects angry, happy, sad, bored and relaxed were created through voice source modifications to a synthetic utterance. These were combined with facial expressions targeting the same affects with the addition of interested. A perception test was conducted with the following combinations: (i) voice only (no visuals), (ii) congruent (matching vocal and visual affect) and (iii) incongruent (opposing vocal and visual affect). The initial hypothesis that the addition of congruent visual context would enhance the perception of the targeted affect received little support. While this points to a dominance of the vocal channel, the results for the incongruent stimuli underline the importance of the visual channel. A second hypothesis that the visual information would allow for better discrimination among high- (or low-) activation states was largely borne out.
column7: Anna Maria Giovannini(Trinity College Dublin); Zihan Wang(Trinity College Dublin); Ailbhe Ní Chasaide(Trinity College Dublin); Christer Gobl(Trinity College Dublin)

column4: ParaSpeechCLAP: A Dual-Encoder Speech-Text Model for Rich Stylistic Language-Audio Pretraining
column6: We introduce ParaSpeechCLAP, a family of dual-encoder models that map speech and text style captions into a shared embedding space, supporting rich intrinsic (speaker-level) and situational (utterance-level) descriptors, such as pitch, texture, and emotion, beyond the narrow set handled by existing models. We train separate Intrinsic and Situational models alongside a unified Combined model, finding that specialized models are stronger on individual style dimensions while the unified model excels on compositional evaluation. We further show that ParaSpeechCLAP-Intrinsic benefits from an additional classification loss and class-balanced training. We demonstrate performance on style caption retrieval, speech attribute classification, and usability as inference-time reward models for style-prompted TTS. ParaSpeechCLAP models outperform baselines on most metrics across all three applications. Our models and code are released at https://github.com/ajd12342/paraspeechclap.
column7: Anuj Diwan(The University of Texas at Austin); Eunsol Choi(New York University); David Harwath(The University of Texas at Austin)

column4: Daily Affect Inference from Longitudinal Speech-based Journals: A Comparison of Acoustic and Linguistic Models
column6: Speech-based journaling provides both acoustic cues and semantically rich content, offering strong potential for mental health monitoring. But how well do current models infer indicators such as mood and stress from naturalistic data? We introduce a longitudinal corpus of 61 speakers and 769 daily recordings, labeled with the Multidimensional Mood Questionnaire and Perceived Stress Scale, to compare eGeMAPS and wav2vec2 models with GBERT-large and zero-shot Mistral-7B-Instruct. We reveal that linguistic models clearly dominate at the population-level: GBERT reaches .122 concordance for arousal, and Mistral .466 for valence and .360 for stress, whereas acoustic results are near zero. Mistral, however, is geared towards inferring trait-like differences rather than daily speaker variations. The acoustics indicate a relation between pause variations and valence at the speaker-level. We conclude that our models are limited in their ability to monitor individuals and require personalization.
column7: Michelle D Schlicher(TUM University Hospital); Andreas Triantafyllopoulos(TUM University Hospital); Nadine N Schmitt(University of Tübingen; FA-University of Erlangen-Nuremberg); Johanna Löchner(FA-University of Erlangen-Nuremberg); Björn W Schuller(TUM University Hospital; Imperial College London)

column4: Enhancing Visual Paralinguistics: Motion-Guided Spatial Denoising for Non-Verbal Interaction Analysis
column6: In Human-Computer Interaction, non-verbal cues like micro-gestures are essential for understanding human intent alongside speech. However, extracting these subtle movements in unconstrained environments is difficult due to severe visual clutter and spatial ambiguity. We propose a signal processing-inspired framework centered on a Motion-Guided Spatial Refinement Module (MG-SRM). Rather than relying solely on heavy spatial encoders, MG-SRM utilizes multi-order temporal differences to explicitly filter out static background artifacts in pose heatmaps. In addition, we introduce a Class-Learnable Fusion (CLF) strategy that adapts modality weights based on action semantics, prioritizing input streams according to the target micro-gesture. Experiments on the challenging MA-52 dataset show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance by directly improving the signal-to-noise ratio of micro-movements. Our proposed framework is highly accurate and computationally efficient, providing a robust visual frontend for multimodal conversational systems.
column7: Junjie Wan(Harbin Inst. of Tech.)

column4: Modality Importance is Not Static: Temporal Dynamics via Gating in Multimodal Emotion Recognition
column6: Multimodal emotion recognition is inherently dynamic, as the importance of text, speech, and visual signals changes across time. However, most existing systems rely on static fusion, implicitly assuming time-invariant modality contribution and ignoring temporal variation. We present a temporal fusion framework that models modality importance as a time-varying, class-conditional distribution. A GRU-based module applies emotion-query gating to adapt modality weights over dialogue context. Under 6-class IEMOCAP LOSO evaluation, temporal modeling improves over static fusion (+9.01 in mean(F1, UA)), and gating further improves over temporal modeling without gating (+1.63), while outperforming Transformer-based fusion with fewer parameters. Perturbation-based occlusion and Area Over the Perturbation Curve(AOPC) provide evidence that modality importance is non-stationary across time, suggesting multimodal emotion recognition as a dynamic decision process rather than a static fusion problem.
column7: Jiyeon Ryu(GIST); SeongHun Noh(Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST)); Jin-Hyuk Hong(Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST)); Woojin Kang(Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST))

column4: ReDimNet2: Scaling Speaker Verification via Time-Pooled Dimension Reshaping
column6: We present ReDimNet2, an improved neural network architecture for extracting utterance-level speaker representations that builds upon the ReDimNet dimension-reshaping framework. The key modification in ReDimNet2 is the introduction of pooling over the time dimension within the 1D processing pathway. This operation preserves the nature of the 1D feature space, since 1D features remain a reshaped version of 2D features regardless of temporal resolution, while enabling significantly more aggressive scaling of the channel dimension without proportional compute increase. We introduce a family of seven model configurations (B0-B6) ranging from 1.1M to 12.3M parameters and 0.33 to 13 GMACs. Experimental results on VoxCeleb1 benchmarks demonstrate that ReDimNet2 improves the Pareto front of computational cost versus accuracy at every scale point compared to ReDimNet, achieving 0.287% EER on Vox1-O with 12.3M parameters and 13 GMACs.
column7: Ivan Yakovlev(Palabra AI); Anton Okhotnikov(Palabra AI)

column4: Text-Independent Speaker Verification Using Discrete Audio Tokens
column6: Neural audio codecs (NACs) enable efficient audio compression and have achieved success in downstream tasks such as speech synthesis. However, their discrete representations consistently underperform traditional spectral features in automatic speaker verification (ASV). We empirically demonstrate that speaker cues are implicitly preserved in discrete tokens but remain underutilized by conventional ASV training paradigms. To address this, we propose a Cross-Feature Knowledge Distillation (CFKD) framework. By guiding the codec-based student to mimic the embedding space of a strong Fbank-based teacher, CFKD provides structured supervision for effective utilization of speaker information in tokens. Experiments on the VoxCeleb benchmarks show that CFKD substantially improves the ASV performance of codec-based systems, allowing them to approach the accuracy of Fbank-based teacher models and highlighting the potential of discrete audio tokens for diverse speech tasks.
column7: Zheng Liang(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Junjie Li(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Kong Aik Lee(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University)

column4: Temporal Ensembling Threshold and Neighbor-Aware Label Mixup for Speaker Verification with Open-Set Noisy Labels
column6: During large-scale speaker dataset collection, noisy labels are unavoidable and seriously affect model training. Existing methods mainly alleviate noisy label effects via sample selection or label correction, but for open-set noisy samples, corrected labels remain inaccurate. This paper proposes a Temporal Ensembling Threshold and Neighbor-Aware Label Mixup (TET-LM) method. This method models the embedding similarity with a two-component GMM in each epoch and calculates the ensemble threshold using exponential moving average to distinguish clean labels from noisy labels. In addition, we generate mixed labels through the neighbor-aware mechanism to effectively mitigate the correction bias of open-set noisy samples. We further design a multi-stage training strategy. Experiments on VoxCeleb show TET-LM improves system robustness under various noisy label conditions, with EER and minDCF reduced by 54% and 42% over standard methods (52% and 40% vs. the best baseline).
column7: Zhihua Fang(Xinjiang University; AGIBOT); Shumei Tao(Xinjiang University); Liang He(Xinjiang University; Tsinghua University)

column4: Mixture Consistency Learning for Robust Speaker Verification in Noisy Environments
column6: Speaker verification (SV) systems often experience performance degradation in real-world environments due to diverse noise. A common solution is to add a speech enhancement (SE) frontend; however, most SE modules are trained to reconstruct predefined "clean" reference signals that still contain remaining noise and channel variability. This can lead the SE module to restore non-discriminative factors as well, thereby degrading SV performance. To address this limitation, we propose a Mixture Consistency Learning-based Speaker Verification (MCL-SV) system. Instead of relying on reference signals, MCL-SV enforces that the sum of the separated speaker and background representations matches the original input mixture, so that the enhanced signal is aligned with the input itself in a self-supervised manner. Experiments on multiple datasets show that MCL-SV consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves state-of-the-art results among recent noise-robust SV systems.
column7: Seung-bin Kim(University of Seoul); Chan-yeong Lim(University of Seoul); Jungwoo Heo(University of Seoul); Hyun-seo Shin(University of Seoul); Kyo-Won Koo(University of Seoul); Jisoo Son(University of Seoul); Kyung-Wha Kim(Supreme Prosecutor's Office); Ha-Jin Yu(University of Seoul)

column4: Adapting Audio Large Language Models for Speaker Verification
column6: This paper investigates adapting Audio Large Language Models (ALLMs) for speaker verification (SV). We reformulate SV as an audio question answering task and conduct zero-shot evaluations on public benchmarks, showing that current ALLMs have limited zero-shot SV capability and struggle in diverse acoustic conditions. To address this challenge, we perform supervised fine-tuning on SV data. A rule-based hard pair sampling strategy is proposed to construct more challenging training pairs. Lightweight fine-tuning substantially improves performance, though a gap remains between ALLMs and conventional models. We then extend the approach to text-dependent SV by jointly querying ALLMs to verify speaker identity and spoken content, yielding results competitive with cascaded ASR—SV systems. Our findings demonstrate that, with proper adaptation, ALLMs have strong potential as a unified framework for robust SV systems while maintaining general audio understanding capabilities.
column7: Yiming Ren(Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory); Xuenan Xu(Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory); Shuai Wang(Nanjing University); Chao Zhang(Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; Tsinghua University); Baoxiang Li(Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory)

column4: Speaker Verification with Speech-Aware LLMs: Evaluation and Augmentation
column6: Speech-aware large language models (LLMs) can accept speech inputs, yet their training objectives largely emphasize linguistic content or specific fields such as emotions or the speaker's gender, leaving it unclear whether they encode speaker identity. First, we propose a model-agnostic scoring protocol that produces continuous verification scores for both API-only and open-weight models, using confidence scores or log-likelihood ratios from the Yes/No token probabilities. Using this protocol, we benchmark recent speech-aware LLMs and observe weak speaker discrimination (EERs above 20% on VoxCeleb1). Second, we introduce a lightweight augmentation that equips an LLM with ASV capability by injecting frozen ECAPA-TDNN speaker embeddings through a learned projection and training only LoRA adapters. On TinyLLaMA-1.1B, the resulting ECAPA-LLM achieves 1.03% EER on VoxCeleb1-E, approaching a dedicated speaker verification system while preserving a natural-language interface.
column7: Thomas Thebaud(Johns Hopkins University); Yuzhe Wang(Johns Hopkins University); Laureano Moro-Velazquez(Johns Hopkins University); Jesus Villalba-Lopez(Johns Hopkins University); Najim Dehak(Johns Hopkins University)

column4: CAQA-Net: Continual Audio Quality Assessment Across Speech and Music Domains
column6: With the rapid advances of audio generation models and audio processing techniques, new types of distortions and audio domains are introduced, posing challenges to static audio quality assessment (AQA) models. Traditional AQA models cannot keep pace with the dynamic and diverse nature of real-world audio data. To address this issue, we propose CAQA-Net, a systematic continual learning framework for AQA, in which the model continuously acquires new knowledge from a sequence of tasks while retaining previously learned knowledge. The framework adopts a dual-branch and multi-head architecture that combines a trainable waveform encoder with a spectrogram-based semantic anchor. A knowledge-distillation regularizer preserves old knowledge, while a prototype-based gating mechanism supports task-agnostic inference. Results demonstrate that the proposed method successfully balances plasticity and stability, achieving performance within 0.036 SRCC (4.6%) of the joint-learning upper bound.
column7: Naiyuan Li(Ningbo University); Xiaoxun Wu(Ningbo University); Yuheng Huang(Ningbo University); Diqun Yan(Ningbo University; Ningbo University of Finance and Economics)

column4: The First Environmental Sound Deepfake Detection Challenge: Benchmarking Robustness, Evaluation, and Insights
column6: Recent progress in audio generation has made it increasingly easy to create highly realistic environmental soundscapes, which can be misused to produce deceptive content, such as fake alarms, gunshots, and crowd sounds, raising concerns for public safety and trust. While deepfake detection for speech and singing voice has been extensively studied, environmental sound deepfake detection (ESDD) remains underexplored. To advance ESDD, the first edition of the ESDD challenge was launched, attracting 97 registered teams and receiving 1,748 valid submissions. This paper presents the task formulation, dataset construction, evaluation protocols, baseline systems, and key insights from the challenge results. Furthermore, we analyze common architectural choices and training strategies among top-performing systems. Finally, we discuss potential future research directions for ESDD, outlining key opportunities and open problems to guide subsequent studies in this field.
column7: Han Yin(KAIST); Yang Xiao(University of Melbourne); Rohan Kumar Das(Fortemedia); Jisheng Bai(Xi’an University of Posts & Telecommunications; Xi’an Lianfeng Acoustic Technologies Co., Ltd.); Ting Dang(University of Melbourne)

column4: Benchmarking Language Modeling for Lossless Compression of Full-Fidelity Audio
column6: Autoregressive "language" models (LMs) trained on raw waveforms can be repurposed for lossless audio compression, but prior work is limited to 8-bit audio, leaving open whether such approaches work for practical settings (16/24-bit) and can compete with existing codecs. We benchmark LM-based compression on full-fidelity audio across diverse domains (music, speech, bioacoustics), sampling rates (16kHz-48kHz), and bit depths (8, 16, 24-bit). Standard sample-level tokenization becomes intractable at higher bit depths due to vocabulary size (65K for 16-bit; 16.7M for 24-bit). We propose Trilobyte, a byte-level tokenization schema for full resolution audio, improving vocabulary scaling from O(2b) to O(1) and enabling the first tractable 24-bit LM-based lossless compression. While LMs consistently outperform FLAC and yield state-of-the-art compression at 8-bit and 16-bit, we observe that compression gains become more modest as bit depth increases beyond 8-bit.
column7: Phillip Long(University of California); Zachary Novack(vUniversity of California); Chris Donahue(Carnegie Mellon University)

column4: Probing Spatial Structure in Pretrained Audio Representations
column6: Pretrained spatial audio encoders are increasingly used as general-purpose representations for perceptual tasks, yet their spatial encoding capabilities remain poorly understood. We introduce the Spatial Audio Representation Learning (SARL) benchmark, a controlled framework for evaluating spatial information in pretrained audio models. SARL probes source-level factors (azimuth, elevation, distance, class) and room-level factors (RT60, volume, shape). Experiments across diverse encoders reveal three patterns: input configuration and training paradigm shape spatial encoding; source factors are consistently easier to decode than room factors; and sensitivity analysis under controlled perturbations shows heterogeneous responses to source and room variation. These results reveal systematic biases in current pretrained audio representations. SARL is released as an open-source benchmark for reproducible evaluation of spatial audio representations.
column7: Chuyang Chen(New York University); Sivan Ding(New York University); Adrian S. Roman(New York University); Juan P. Bello(New York University)

column4: Interpretable Audio Editing Evaluation via Chain-of-Thought Difference-Commonality Reasoning with Multimodal LLMs
column6: Automatic mean opinion score (MOS) prediction serves as a principled alternative to both subjective listening tests and objective metrics, providing scalable and consistent audio evaluation. Inspired by the LLM-as-Judge paradigm, recent multimodal large language models offer strong perceptual modeling and reasoning capabilities, enabling audio quality assessment. In this work, we address the challenging problem of audio editing evaluation and propose the first natural language-based automated evaluation framework built upon Qwen2-Audio. Two caption-based fine-tuning tasks are introduced to enhance multi-audio understanding, together with a designed Chain-of-Thought prompting strategy to encourage structured, step-by-step reasoning. Experiments show that our framework produces interpretable and logically consistent text-based evaluations, aligning closely with human judgments while outperforming existing baselines. Code and tools will be released.
column7: Yuhang Jia(Nankai University); Xu Zhang(Nankai University); Yang Chen(Nankai University); Hui Wang(Nankai University); Enzhi Wang(Nankai University); Yong Qin(Nankai University)

column4: DASM: Detecting AI-Synthetic Music via Authentic Manifold Deviation Modeling
column6: Current music deepfake detectors rely on a discriminative paradigm that fits decision boundaries to known fake distributions. As generative algorithms evolve, these methods suffer from structural vulnerability due to non-stationary distribution shifts. We propose DASM, a framework that models the stable distribution of authentic audio rather than tracking evolving forgeries. A learnable memory bank is trained exclusively on authentic samples via reconstruction loss to represent a compressed manifold prior. A dual-branch classifier utilizes both original features and memory-reconstructed features as complementary inputs, identifying forgeries as manifold-space divergence from the authentic distribution. Furthermore, a lightweight prompt tuning strategy adapts a frozen MERT encoder to the detection task with minimal parameters. Experiments on the SONICS dataset demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and robust resistance to acoustic degradations.
column7: Xinya Zhu(North China University of Technology); Mengyu Qiao(North China University of Technology); Wenqiang Li(North China University of Technology); Zhihui Yang(North China University of Technology)

column1: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 6 - Oral 5 - Neural Audio Codec Architectures

column4: MSR-Codec: A Low-Bitrate Multi-Stream Residual Codec for High-Fidelity Speech Generation with Information Disentanglement
column6: Audio codecs are a critical component of modern speech generation systems. This paper introduces a low-bitrate, multi-scale residual codec that encodes speech into four distinct streams: semantic, timbre, prosody, and residual. This architecture achieves high-fidelity speech reconstruction at competitive low bitrates while demonstrating an inherent ability for information disentanglement. We construct a two-stage language model for text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis using this codec, which, despite its lightweight design and minimal data requirements, achieves a lower Word Error Rate (WER) and superior speaker similarity compared to several larger models. Furthermore, the codec's design proves highly effective for voice conversion, enabling independent manipulation of speaker timbre and prosody. Our inference code, pre-trained models, and audio samples are available at https://github.com/herbertLJY/MSRCodec.
column7: Jingyu Li(LIGHTSPEED); Guangyan Zhang(LIGHTSPEED); Zhen Ye(The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology); Yiwen Guo(Independent Researcher)

column4: OmniCodec: Low Frame Rate Universal Audio Codec with Semantic–Acoustic Disentanglement
column6: Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced audio generation through discrete representation learning. However, most existing neural codecs focus on speech and emphasize reconstruction fidelity, overlooking unified low frame rate modeling across diverse audio domains, including speech, music, and general sound. Moreover, high reconstruction quality does not necessarily yield semantically informative representations, limiting effectiveness in downstream generation tasks. We propose OmniCodec, a universal neural audio codec tailored for low frame rate. It adopts a hierarchical multi-codebook design with semantic-acoustic decoupling by leveraging the audio encoder of the pre-trained understanding model, along with a self-guidance strategy to improve codebook utilization and reconstruction. Compared with the Mimi, experiments show that OmniCodec achieves outstanding performance at the same bitrate, delivering superior reconstruction quality while also providing more semantically informative representations that benefit downstream generation tasks. Our model and code will be open-sourced. Our demo page is available.
column7: Jingbin Hu(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Haoyu Zhang(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Dake Guo(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Qirui Zhan(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Wenhao Li(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Huakang Chen(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Guobin Ma(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Hanke Xie(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Chengyou Wang(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Pengyuan Xie(Shanghai Lingguang Zhaxian Technology); Chuan Xie(Shanghai Lingguang Zhaxian Technology); Qiang Zhang(Shanghai Lingguang Zhaxian Technology); Lei Xie(Northwestern Polytechnical University)

column4: U-Codec: Neural Speech Codec under Extreme Temporal Compression for Fast High-Fidelity Speech Generation
column6: We propose U-Codec, an Ultra low frame-rate neural speech Codec that achieves high-fidelity reconstruction and fast speech generation at a frame-rate of 5Hz (5 frames per second). Extreme temporal compression typically leads to severe intelligibility and spectral detail loss. We overcome this by introducing a Transformer-based inter-frame long-term dependency module and systematically exploring residual vector quantization (RVQ) depth and codebook size to identify optimal configurations. Moreover, we apply U-Codec to a large language model (LLM)-based auto-regressive TTS model, which leverages global and local hierarchical architecture to effectively capture dependencies across multi-layer tokens. Experiments demonstrate that U-Codec improves LLM-based TTS inference speed by 3x over high-frame-rate codecs while maintaining similarity and naturalness. These results validate the feasibility of using 5Hz discrete tokens for fast and high-fidelity speech synthesis.
column7: Xusheng Yang(Peking University); Long Zhou(Tencent Hunyuan); Wenfu Wang(Tencent AI Lab); Kai Hu(Tencent Hunyuan); Zixiang Wan(Peking University); Yushen Chen(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Shulin Feng(Tencent Hunyuan); Chenxing Li(Tencent AI Lab); Meng Yu(Tencent AI Lab); Dong Yu(Tencent AI Lab); Yuexian Zou(Peking University)

column4: Elastic Time: Dynamic Frame Rate Bottlenecks for Neural Audio Coding
column6: Neural audio autoencoders have become a core component of compression, feature extraction, and generation. However, while existing systems support variable bitrate, the vast majority of models still operate at a fixed latent frame-rate, allocating equal temporal budget to regions with very different information density, which can result in unnecessarily long sequences. We introduce Elastic Time, a dynamic frame-rate bottleneck that converts fixed-frame-rate autoencoders to dynamic ones. Our method learns a lightweight latent predictor used to decide which frames can be skipped and later reconstructed, enabling efficient greedy boundary selection at inference. Experiments show our method enables deployment-time rate control while improving efficiency-quality tradeoffs relative to baselines. Overall, we provide a flexible mechanism for adjusting temporal resolution in audio autoencoders, potentially facilitating more efficient downstream modeling for generation and long-context tasks.
column7: Dimitrios Bralios(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Paris Smaragdis(Massachusetts Institute of Technology); Minje Kim(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)

column4: SDP-Codec: A Speaker-Decoupled Speech Codec with Pitch Injection for Low-Bitrate Coding and Zero-Shot Voice Conversion
column6: Speaker-decoupled speech codecs can reduce bitrate by separating global speaker attributes from local content and prosody, while supporting voice conversion. Existing speaker-decoupled codecs face a trade-off: methods that explicitly suppress speaker leakage often rely on multi-stage or auxiliary training, whereas simpler designs can leave residual speaker information in local tokens. We propose SDP-Codec, a speaker-decoupled, pitch-injected codec trained with a single-stage optimization pipeline. SDP-Codec derives local tokens from continuous pre-quantization features of a pretrained self-supervised encoder and injects normalized F0 via a pitch encoder-decoder with global-conditioned denormalization and soft-label pitch reconstruction objective. Across 16 kHz and 24 kHz settings, SDP-Codec achieves competitive reconstruction and strong zero-shot voice conversion at comparable bitrates, with the lowest speaker-probing accuracy among compared systems, suggesting reduced speaker leakage. 1
column7: Hounsu Kim(KAIST); Juhan Nam(KAIST)

column4: A Dual-Stream Discrete Neural Codec with Fixed-Length Global Speaker Tokens and Dynamic Frame Rates for Low-Bitrate Speech Tokenization
column6: Discrete speech tokens are an effective interface for speech language models (SLMs), yet many codecs are inefficient due to high token rates and mix speaker characteristics with content-related variation, increasing the modeling burden for downstream SLMs. We propose a low-bitrate dual-stream discrete codec comprising (i) a time-varying token stream from a single codebook and (ii) a small set of fixed-length global speaker tokens. To reduce redundancy, we introduce similarity-based dynamic frame aggregation that merges consecutive frames and enables controllable token rates at inference via a single threshold. An adaptive deaggregation module restores the sequence to the base frame rate for waveform reconstruction. Experiments demonstrate strong intelligibility and audio quality at low bitrates, with improved bitrate-quality trade-offs over fixed-rate baselines while maintaining speaker similarity.
column7: Boyang Zhang(Zhejiang University; StepFun); Yechang Huang(StepFun); Xuerui Yang(StepFun); Ziyue Jiang(Zhejiang University)

column1: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 7 - Oral 9 - Speech Synthesis: Speech Features, Codec and Representations

column4: Semantic-VAE: Semantic-Alignment Latent Representation for Better Speech Synthesis
column6: Mel-spectrograms have been widely used in zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS); their inherent redundancy leads to inefficiency in text-speech alignment. Compact VAE-based latent representations have emerged as a stronger alternative but exhibit an optimization dilemma: higher-dimensional latents improve reconstruction quality and speaker similarity but degrade intelligibility, while lower-dimensional latents improve intelligibility at the cost of reconstruction fidelity. To overcome this dilemma, we propose Semantic-VAE, which uses semantic alignment regularization in the latent space. This design alleviates the reconstruction-generation trade-off by capturing semantic structure in high-dimensional latent representations. When integrated into F5-TTS, our method achieves 2.10% WER and 0.64 speaker similarity on LibriSpeech-PC, outperforming mel-based systems and vanilla acoustic VAE baselines with improved training efficiency. Demo and codes: https://zhikangniu.github.io/semantic-vae/
column7: Zhikang Niu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute); Shujie Hu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Jeongsoo Choi(KAIST); Yushen Chen(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute); Peining Chen(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Pengcheng Zhu(Geely); Yunting Yang(Geely); Bowen Zhang(Geely); Jian Zhao(Geely); Chunhui Wang(Geely); Xie Chen(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute)

column4: One-Step Token-to-Waveform Generation with MeanFlow in Latent Space
column6: Neural audio codecs are central to modern LLM-based Text-to-Speech (TTS) and multimodal systems. As low-bitrate semantic codecs gain prominence, the Token-to-Waveform (Token2Wav) decoder becomes a bottleneck determining both perceptual quality and system efficiency. Conventional multi-step flow-matching decoders offer superior quality but suffer from high inference latency due to iterative sampling, creating a severe quality-speed trade-off. In this paper, we propose a novel Token2Wav architecture that overcomes this limitation by applying MeanFlow in a highly compressed latent space. By modeling the average velocity rather than the instantaneous velocity field, MeanFlow enables true one-step generation. Operating in the latent domain mitigates the memory and stability issues of waveform-level flows, yielding up to a 17× improvement in Real-Time Factor (RTF) compared to multi-step baselines with negligible quality degradation. Furthermore, we introduce refinement strategies that mitigate latent mismatch, including decoder-only fine-tuning with the MeanFlow generator frozen and end-to-end joint fine-tuning, improving fidelity without increasing inference-time cost. Code and demo are publicly available.
column7: Zheqi Dai(CUHK); Guangyan Zhang(Tencent); Zhen Ye(HKUST); Jingyu Li(Tencent); Haolin He(CUHK); Chunyat Wu(CUHK); Yiwen Guo(Independent Researcher); Qiuqiang Kong(CUHK)

column4: CycleCodec: Distillation-Free Factorized Neural Speech Codec via Cycle-Consistent Speaker Swapping
column6: Factorized neural speech codecs often rely on distillation from pretrained self-supervised learning (SSL) encoders or automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems to disentangle content and speaker information. However, this dependency limits their applicability to low-resource languages where reliable teacher models are unavailable. In this paper, we propose CycleCodec, a distillation-free factorized codec trained from scratch. CycleCodec introduces cycle-consistent speaker swapping, a codec-internal self-supervision signal that reduces cross-stream leakage during speaker-conditioned generation. To facilitate speaker-content disentanglement, CycleCodec also limits temporal capacity and improves speaker modeling with a query-based Transformer aggregator and a speaker contrastive loss. Experiments on in-domain (English) and unseen languages (Mandarin and Vietnamese) show that CycleCodec outperforms distillation-free baselines and achieves more robust speaker-content disentanglement.
column7: Rui-Chen Zheng(USTC; University of Edinburgh); Nicholas Sanders(University of Edinburgh); Jinzuomu Zhong(University of Edinburgh); Yang Ai(USTC); Zhen-Hua Ling(USTC); Korin Richmond(University of Edinburgh)

column4: Low-Framerate Speech Tokenization via Two-Stage Latent Patch Modeling
column6: Recent advances in neural speech tokenizers rely on low-framerate, semantically rich latent representations that facilitate downstream generative modeling tasks such as text-to-speech. However, achieving high perceptual quality at low bitrate and framerate remains computationally demanding, as it typically requires joint compression, adversarial training, and semantic supervision, resulting in expensive training. In this work, we introduce Z-CODEC, a two-stage latent speech codec. In the first stage, we train a high-framerate variational autoencoder (VAE) with adversarial objectives to capture fine-grained acoustic details and absorb the complexity of adversarial training. In the second stage, we perform final compression within the latent space of the first stage using flow matching and incorporate semantic supervision, enabling high-quality low-framerate tokenization. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction quality for both low-bitrate discrete tokenizers and continuous settings, outperforming or matching strong baselines. Importantly, the staged design of Z-CODEC makes training tractable on a single RTX 4070 GPU, enabling high-quality, low-framerate speech tokenizer reproducible on consumer-grade hardware.
column7: Théodor Lemerle(Sorbonne Université); Diego Torres(Sorbonne Université); Téo Guichoux(Sorbonne Université); Nicolas Obin(Sorbonne Université); Axel Roebel(Sorbonne Université)

column4: Transcript-Free Flow-Matching Text-to-Speech via Speech Feature Conditioning
column6: Recent flow-matching text-to-speech (TTS) models, such as F5-TTS, rely on a reference transcript at inference time, obtained from an external ASR system. This dependency makes zero-shot TTS brittle for accented or dysarthric speakers, precisely the scenarios where it is most needed. Moreover, we find that text-based reference conditioning can propagate atypical acoustic patterns from atypical speech into synthesis, even when ground-truth transcripts are available. To address this, we propose RTFree-F5, which replaces the reference transcript with continuous self-supervised speech representations mapped into F5-TTS's text-conditioning space via a lightweight adapter, while reusing the pretrained checkpoint. On dysarthric speech, RTFree-F5 reduces WER from 24.6% to 10.4%, surpassing even the ground-truth reference transcript baselines, while improving naturalness and remaining competitive on standard benchmarks without requiring any reference transcript.
column7: SooHwan Eom(KAIST); Hee Suk Yoon(KAIST); Eunseop Yoon(KAIST); Mark Hasegawa-Johnson(UIUC); Chang D. Yoo(KAIST)

column4: Unified Prosody Restoration Using Diffusion Models for Controllable Text-to-Speech Synthesis
column6: Controllable text-to-speech systems that use explicit prosodic features enable fine-grained control, which is particularly useful for emotional speech synthesis. However, specifying frame-level details often imposes a heavy burden on users. To alleviate this burden, we formulate prosody restoration as a unified problem of recovering frame-level prosody from simplified and easy-to-specify prosodic inputs. By expanding two prior tasks with three novel ones, we address a total of five tasks. Together, they support practical user workflows by enabling restoration from prosody that is partial, coarse, or both. We also propose two diffusion-based prosody restorers: a supervised model trained to reverse simulated degradations, and an unsupervised model leveraging samplers for linear inverse problems. Experiments across all five tasks show that our methods restore prosody more accurately than non-diffusion baselines, preserving linguistically valid prosodic structures.
column7: Yuki Ito(Sony Group Corporation); Junki Ohmura(Sony Group Corporation); Hayato Futami(Sony Group Corporation); Toshiyuki Sekiya(Sony Group Corporation); Toshiyuki Kumakura(Sony Group Corporation)

column1: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 8 - Oral 6 - Self-supervised Speech Representation Learning

column4: Causal Redundancy in Speech Representations: The Hydra Effect and Limits of Sparse Disentanglement in WavLM
column6: Self-supervised speech models learn rich acoustic representations, yet how low-level properties are internally encoded remains opaque. We investigate this using linear probing, Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), and Iterative Null-space Projection (INLP). While probing confirms early-layer localization of acoustic features, raw neurons exhibit severe polysemanticity. We apply JumpReLU SAEs to disentangle these activations, but latent ablation reveals a Hydra effect: discrete removal fails to suppress acoustic features due to massive representational redundancy. To overcome this, we employ INLP to erase entire acoustic linear subspaces. Subspace erasure achieves targeted suppression, selectively removing features such as pitch while preserving other acoustic probes. Evaluated on RAVDESS, CREMA-D, and TIMIT, our results demonstrate that acoustic features in SSL speech models occupy separable yet distributed subspaces, requiring subspace-level rather than neuron-level intervention.
column7: Patalee Narasinghe(University of Moratuwa); Kasindu Bandara(University of Moratuwa); Vilash Nawagamuwa(University of Moratuwa); Janak Senevirathne(University of Moratuwa); Uthayasanker Thayasivam(University of Moratuwa)

column4: Prosody-Aware Speech Representations for Emotion Recognition under Pragmatic Ambiguity
column6: Speech emotion recognition (SER) systems often rely on semantic or spectral representations learned by speech encoders, while prosodic cues conveying emotional intent are not explicitly modeled. In real-world conversations, emotional meaning is conveyed through prosody when linguistic cues alone are insufficient, especially in pragmatically ambiguous utterances. We propose a prosody-aware speech representation for emotion recognition and downstream applications by injecting pitch and energy into shared hidden representations of a pretrained Whisper encoder. We evaluate the approach using a 59-class emotion classification task and a Pragmatic Ambiguity Resolution (PAR) evaluation task. Experiments show improvements up to 13.93%p in emotion classification and 11.6%p in PAR compared to the same Whisper model without prosody. The proposed model also outperforms text-based LLM inference (GPT-4o mini) on PAR, highlighting the importance of prosody-aware representations for emotion systems.
column7: Yeonwoo Park(Hanyang University ERICA); Chioh Lee(Pusan National University)

column4: DysfluentNet: Joint Stuttering Event Detection and Dysfluency-Aware Transcription via Hierarchical Self-Supervised Learning
column6: Stuttering affects approximately 70 million people worldwide, yet automatic speech recognition systems perform poorly on stuttered speech, and dedicated detection systems rarely integrate transcription. We present DysfluentNet, a hierarchical multi-task framework that jointly performs fine-grained stuttering event detection and dysfluency-aware transcription from raw waveforms. Our model couples a frozen WavLM-Large encoder with a lightweight dysfluency-conditioned decoder trained under a novel stuttering-aware connectionist temporal classification (SA-CTC) objective. We further introduce a curriculum learning schedule that progressively exposes the model to harder disfluency patterns, and an annotator-agreement-based difficulty partitioning of SEP-28k. Evaluated on SEP-28k and FluencyBank, DysfluentNet achieves a macro F1 of 72.4 on stuttering event detection and a dysfluency-inclusive word error rate (DI-WER) of 18.3 on FluencyBank transcription, outperforming the best published baselines by 6.8 and 4.1 points respectively. Code and reproducibility scripts are released publicly.
column7: Mohankumar Muthu(SRMIST, Chennai, India); Sasikala E(SRMIST, Chennai, India); Girirajan S(SRMIST, Chennai, India)

column4: Adaptive Federated Fine-Tuning of Self-Supervised Speech Representations
column6: Integrating Federated Learning (FL) with self-supervised learning (SSL) enables privacy-preserving fine-tuning for speech tasks. However, federated environments exhibit significant heterogeneity: clients differ in computational capacity, causing straggler effects under unified fine-tuning, while diverse downstream tasks require different representation depths, making full-model updates inefficient. To address these challenges, we propose an adaptive federated fine-tuning framework with early exits. Lightweight prediction heads are inserted at intermediate layers of the SSL backbone, allowing clients to terminate computation based on local constraints and task requirements. We further introduce a layer-wise, depth-aware partial aggregation strategy to better utilize representations from different network depths. Experiments show that the framework reduces edge overhead, supports heterogeneous hardware, and maintains competitive performance in resource-constrained federated environments.
column7: Xin Guo(Wuhan University); Chunrui Zhao(Wuhan University); Hong Jia(University of Auckland); Ting Dang(University of Melbourne); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University); Xianrui Zheng(University of Cambridge); Yan Gao(University of Cambridge; Flower Labs)

column4: Leveraging Soft Distributions of SSL-Derived Discrete Speech Tokens for Downstream Inference
column6: Discrete speech tokens obtained from self-supervised learning (SSL) models provide efficient data compression while maintaining strong performance, and have been widely used as intermediate representations in various tasks. However, discretization inevitably causes information loss, leading to degraded performance compared with continuous SSL features. In this work, we propose to apply soft token assignment only during downstream inference. This approach preserves the efficiency of hard discretization during training while enhancing the expressiveness of the tokens at inference. The proposed method outperforms conventional hard assignment on both ASR and speech synthesis tasks, and exhibits particularly strong generalizability to out-of-domain data. For ASR of non-native speech, it even surpasses models using continuous SSL features. Moreover, analysis of the resulting representations shows they align more accurately with phonemes compared with conventional hard assignment.
column7: Kentaro Onda(The University of Tokyo; AIST); Satoru Fukayama(AIST); Daisuke Saito(The University of Tokyo); Nobuaki Minematsu(The University of Tokyo)

column4: Gumbel-BEARD: Automatic Layer Selection for Self-Supervised Adaptation of Whisper in Low-Resource Domains
column6: Speech foundation models often struggle in low-resource domains due to domain mismatch and data scarcity. We propose Gumbel-BEARD, a domain adaptation framework that automates Whisper encoder layer selection via an end-to-end trainable hard Gumbel-Softmax selector. It enables self-supervised adaptation with a BEST-RQ objective that dynamically adapts to target acoustic characteristics without manual tuning. Experiments on the MyST child speech corpus demonstrate efficiency and scalability: with 10 h of labeled data for fine-tuning, our method matches a fully supervised baseline trained on the complete 133 h labeled set. We establish new state-of-the-art word error rates (WERs) of 8.21% using Whisper-medium on MyST and 11.06% using Whisper-small on the OGI Spontaneous dataset. Evaluation on CORAAL further confirms robustness to adult dialectal domain shifts, with up to 6% relative WER reduction, highlighting the generalizability of our approach to diverse low-resource conditions.
column7: Zilai Wang(UCLA); Natarajan Balaji Shankar(UCLA); Mohan Shi(UCLA); Kaiyuan Zhang(UCLA); Abeer Alwan(UCLA)

column1: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 11 - Oral 3 - Entrainment and Dialogue Coordination

column4: Articulatory Entrainment and Coordination Complexity in Spontaneous Autistic and Non-autistic Dialogue
column6: Articulatory entrainment, the adaptation of vocal tract coordination to facilitate interaction remains underexplored in spontaneous dialogue, particularly among autistic speakers. Many prior studies have utilized task-based, phoneme-level analyses with invasive measurement techniques. Here, we introduce a speaker-independent framework to quantify articulatory entrainment in spontaneous dyadic conversations among autistic and non-autistic adults using acoustic-to-articulatory inversion and coordination complexity metrics. We examine temporal changes in articulatory coordination across interaction. Non-autistic dyads exhibit increasing coordination complexity and stronger entrainment over time, autistic dyads show moderate effects, and mixed dyads demonstrate the least alignment. Greater articulatory entrainment correlates with higher self-reported conversational success, indicating increase in coordination complexity as a marker of effective social interaction.
column7: Thanushi Withanage(University of Maryland); Carol Espy-Wilson(University of Maryland); Elizabeth Redcay(University of Maryland); Desi Jones(University of Maryland); Noah Sasson(The University of Texas at Dallas)

column4: On Entrainment in Semi-Spontaneous Multilingual Parliamentary Speech
column6: Entrainment has predominantly been studied in monolingual instances of either spontaneous or task-oriented speech, leaving open questions of how speakers adapt to their interlocutors in mixed-spontaneity settings where dialogue can also span multiple languages. Our work studies entrainment in the semi-spontaneous context of the Hansard French-English parliamentary proceedings. We examine previously unexplored acoustic-prosodic features of Hansard's spoken exchanges alongside their semantic aspects at multiple levels of temporal granularity, finding that speakers adapt across inter-related dimensions of entrainment and cross-lingual language settings in accordance with primacy and recency effects. Our findings give rise to novel insights into potential planning and priming mechanisms in an understudied context, motivating further work on the entrainment dynamics of linguistically diverse speech settings.
column7: Jennifer Jane Ries(Columbia University); Debasmita Bhattacharya(Columbia University); Julia Hirschberg(Columbia University)

column4: Speak or Stay Silent: Context-Aware Turn-Taking in Multi-Party Dialogue
column6: Existing voice AI assistants treat every detected pause as an invitation to speak. This works in dyadic dialogue, but in multi-party settings, where an AI assistant participates alongside multiple speakers, pauses are abundant and ambiguous. An assistant that speaks on every pause becomes disruptive rather than useful. In this work, we formulate context-aware turn-taking: at every detected pause, given the full conversation context, our method decides whether the assistant should speak or stay silent. We introduce a benchmark of over 120K labeled conversations spanning three multi-party corpora. Evaluating eight recent large language models, we find that they consistently fail at context-aware turn-taking under zero-shot prompting. We then propose a supervised fine-tuning approach with reasoning traces, improving balanced accuracy by up to 23 percentage points. Our findings suggest that context-aware turn-taking is not an emergent capability; it must be explicitly trained.
column7: Kratika Bhagtani(Purdue University); Mrinal Anand(Ishiki Labs Inc.); Yu Chen Xu(Ishiki Labs Inc.); Amit Kumar Singh Yadav(Ishiki Labs Inc.)

column4: Speech Entrainment in Multi-Party Conversations with a Digital Agent
column6: It has been widely observed that individuals engaged in conversation tend to adapt their speaking style to more closely match the other interlocutors. However, most prior work has focused on dyadic interactions among humans. In this paper, we investigate entrainment effects in a novel setting: a multi-party interaction between groups of humans and a digital agent. This scenario offers important insights into how the participation of non-human actors modulates both short-time and temporally resolved conversational dynamics. To address these questions, we collect and analyze a unique dataset that consists of both adult and family (parent/children) sessions, enabling us to examine how entrainment manifests differently across these cohorts. We consider a range of knowledge-driven and model-based entrainment features and find that, while individuals locally entrain with other humans, global entrainment, and entrainment with the agent remains limited and cohort-dependent.
column7: Nicholas Mehlman(University of Southern California); Kaitlin Zareno(University of Southern California); Kleanthis Avramidis(University of Southern California); Anfeng Xu(University of Southern California); Shrikanth Narayanan(University of Southern California)

column4: What happens when we speak together? Multidimensional convergence in face-to-face interaction
column6: Convergence is a pervasive phenomenon in human communication, in which speakers adapt their behaviour to their interlocutor. It is assumed to reflect both automatic and socially motivated processes. However, existing research has predominantly examined individual parameters in isolation, leading to a fragmented understanding. Moreover, the interplay between patterns of convergence and modulations related to prosodic structure remains largely unexplored. This study addresses these issues by investigating convergence as a multidimensional and multimodal phenomenon, with particular attention to its relationship with prosodic prominence. Drawing on an information-structurally controlled dataset of interactive speech from 15 dyads, we analyse several acoustic-prosodic, articulatory, and co-speech kinematic parameters, providing a more comprehensive account of convergence.
column7: Lena Pagel(University of Cologne); Doris Mücke(University of Cologne); Simon Roessig(University of Cologne)

column4: When “yeah” means “not quite”: Multimodal detection of backchannels expressing incomplete understanding
column6: Multimodal backchannels are fundamental to conversational grounding and understanding. However, backchannels do not always transparently reflect the interlocutor's actual cognitive state. "Incongruent backchannels", where the observable feedback implies understanding although there is no genuine understanding, are a potential source of ambiguity in any interaction. Using acoustic, head movement, and discourse-related data from 45 naturalistic dyadic interactions, we investigate whether incongruent and congruent backchannels show systematically different properties using a classification task. Results show that these backchannels are indeed separable based on multimodal features. Incongruent backchannels are typically characterised by more neutral head movement configurations and lower acoustic dynamism, while discursive cues strongly influence the classification. Overall, the findings suggest a relatively reduced effort in the signalling of incongruent backchannels.
column7: Olcay Türk(Bielefeld University); Stefan Lazarov(Paderborn University); Yu Wang(Bielefeld University); Angela Grimminger(Paderborn University); Hendrik Buschmeier(Bielefeld University); Petra Wagner(Bielefeld University)

column4: From Signals to Patterns: Non-Invasive Tuberculosis Detection from Cough Audio using Bandit Weighted Hyperbolic Prototypes
column6: In this study, we focus on cough-based tuberculosis screening (CBTS) and hypothesize that fusing speech/audio foundation representations with spectral descriptors will yield stronger screening performance. We expect this fusion to reveal complementary strengths: spectral features preserve fine-grained short-time acoustic detail in cough signals, while foundation embeddings capture higher-level temporal and event-level patterns learned from large-scale pretraining. To this end, we propose COBALT, a novel fusion framework based on codebook-aligned hyperbolic prototypes and bandit-style reliability weighting to integrate heterogeneous representations effectively. Using the CODA TB DREAM Challenge benchmark, COBALT consistently outperforms individual representations and a concatenation baseline, achieving the best overall performance when fusing MFCC with PaSST thereby establishing a new state-of-the-art on the benchmark.
column7: Mohd Mujtaba Akhtar(Ulster University); Girish(Ulster University); Sanjam Wadhwa(Thapar Institute of Engineering and Technology); Muskaan Singh(Ulster University); Ning Ma(University of Sheffield)

column4: Towards Paradigm-General Suicide Risk Detection via Speech LLM
column6: Suicide risk among adolescents remains a critical public health concern, and speech provides a non-invasive and scalable approach for its detection. Speech-based suicide risk assessment commonly relies on carefully designed speech elicitation paradigms (e.g., verbal fluency, reading, or question answering) to probe cognitive and affective states. Existing approaches, however, typically focus on one single paradigm at a time. This paper, for the first time, investigates cross-paradigm approaches that unify diverse speech elicitation paradigms within a single model. Specifically, we use a speech LLM as backbone with a mixture of DoRA experts (MoDE) to capture complementary cues across assessments dynamically, tested on 1,223 participants across ten speech elicitation paradigms. Results show that MoDE outperforms both paradigm-specific and conventional joint-learning models. Moreover, it can generalise to unseen paradigms and provide better confidence calibration.
column7: Jialun Li(Tsinghua University); Weitao Jiang(Tsinghua University); Ziyun Cui(Tsinghua University); Yinan Duan(Tsinghua University); Diyang Qu(Tsinghua University); Chao Zhang(Tsinghua University, Shanghai AI Lab); Runsen Chen(Tsinghua University); Chang Lei(Tsinghua University); Wen Wu(Shanghai AI Lab)

column4: FedMPA: A Novel Privacy-Performance Optimization Approach for Multimodal Speech-Based Depression Detection
column6: Speech-based automatic depression detection (ADD) enables scalable, non-invasive mental health assessment but raises privacy concerns due to sensitive speech data. However, jointly ensuring privacy and performance remains challenging, and quantifying this balance is underexplored. We propose FedMPA, a Federated Multimodal Prototype Alignment framework that improves performance, privacy, and multimodal consistency for decentralized speech-based ADD. FedMPA employs modality-specific prototypes, an Exponential Moving Average-stabilized global prototype bank, prototype-guided losses, and softmax-prototype hybrid inference. We introduce a task-specific Privacy-Performance Score (PPS) to quantify this trade-off, representing the first framework to optimize and measure privacy-performance balance in depression detection. Experiments on E-DAIC show that FedMPA outperforms FedAvg, FedProx, FedProto, and FedGPD, achieving a PPS of 0.92 with strong classification performance.
column7: Dushanthi Madhushika Manamalage(DeepNet Discovery Network, The University of Auckland); Frederick Sundram(DeepNet Discovery Network, The University of Auckland); Partha S. Roop(DeepNet Discovery Network, The University of Auckland); Seyed Reza Shahamiri(DeepNet Discovery Network, The University of Auckland)

column4: Can deep learning based voice editing enhance voice quality perception skills in speech therapy students?
column6: The perceptual assessment of voice quality remains a challenging task, especially concerning reliability and accuracy. With novel deep learning technologies, new possibilities have emerged for editing voice quality. In our study, we used artificially generated speech as a tool to explain voice characteristics to speech therapy students. Twenty participants rated 16 voices along three voice characteristics (creaky, breathy, and rough) before and after an explanation. A control group listened to natural anchor voices during the explanation, while the other group received synthesized samples. The synthesis-based explanation increased perceptual sensitivity and agreement with the gold standard, whereas no such effect was observed for the control group. The sensitivity for 'rough' improved from below-chance to above-chance only in the synthesis condition. These results suggest that deep learning based voice editing adds a valuable contribution to perception training in applied settings.
column7: Jana Wiechmann(Bielefeld University); Frederik Rautenberg(Paderborn University); Reinhold Haeb-Umbach(Paderborn University); Petra Wagner(Bielefeld University)

column4: S-DiverSe: Spanish Diverse Speech
column6: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has advanced remarkably for standard speech, yet speech affected by neurological conditions remains a challenge. We present S-DiverSe (Spanish Diverse Speech), a corpus of 3.2 hours of in-the-wild Spanish speech from 22 speakers with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, and stroke. The dataset contains 444 manually transcribed audio segments with metadata on speaker sex, disease type, and intelligibility. S-DiverSe is designed to support ASR evaluation and development for neurologically affected Spanish speech. We describe the dataset, analyze its composition, and report baseline ASR results alongside initial adaptation experiments. Our findings reveal that heuristic text post-processing is more robust than fine-tuning for out-of-domain neurological Spanish speech. This underscores the need for dedicated in-the-wild Spanish benchmarks.
column7: Fernando López(Telefónica Innovación Digital; Universidad Autónoma de Madrid); Fernando Ibañez(Universidad Autónoma de Madrid); Ana Martínez(Universidad Autónoma de Madrid); Iván Alonso(Universidad Autónoma de Madrid); Pablo Gómez(Telefónica Innovación Digital); Santosh Kesiraju(Brno University of Technology); Jordi Luque(Telefónica Innovación Digital)

column4: GADVOX: The German Anxiety and Depression Voice Examination Dataset
column6: We present GADVOX, the first openly accessible German-language speech dataset designed for the automated detection and severity estimation of depression and anxiety. Recordings from 1,004 adults were collected via a crowdsourcing platform using ten structured free-speech prompts presented in randomised order, yielding an average of 18.4 minutes of spontaneous speech per participant. Each session is annotated with validated PHQ-9 and GAD-7 severity scores (Cronbach's α = .85 and .86, respectively), enabling regression-based modelling beyond binary classification. A multi-stage quality assurance pipeline comprising attention checks, automated voice activity detection, and human annotation ensured data integrity from an initial pool of 1,420 candidates (29.3% exclusion rate). Metadata including demographics, psychosocial context items, and per-session speech quality estimates (ITU-T P.SAMD / P.566) are released openly; full audio is available upon reasonable request.
column7: Robert P. Spang(Bauhaus-Universität Weimar; Technische Universität Berlin); Wafaa Wardah(Technische Universität Berlin; German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence); Hritik Sauw(Technische Universität Berlin); Ole Möller-Nilsson(Senseven Health GmbH); Etleva Gjoni(Senseven Health GmbH); Stefan Brandenburg(University of Technology Chemnitz); Maria Kreußlein(University of Technology Chemnitz); Lana Mohr(University of Technology Chemnitz); Sebastian Möller(Technische Universität Berlin; German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence)

column4: Beyond Text-to-Music: Control, Agency, and Evaluation in Generative Audio
column6: Generative audio has rapidly expanded from speech synthesis to music, singing, environmental sound, instrument synthesis, and audio production. This talk surveys this landscape for the speech community, connecting music and audio generation to familiar problems such as TTS, voice conversion, enhancement, source separation, prosody modeling, and neural vocoding. We will review audio language models built on neural codecs, diffusion and flow-matching methods, Transformer generators, and differentiable DSP methods. The central theme is control. Text prompts are accessible but musically ambiguous; creators also need interpretable and editable representations such as MIDI, lyrics, stems, reference audio clips, and synthesizer knobs. We will examine tasks including text-to-music, singing synthesis, Foley, continuation, inpainting, stem-conditioned generation, symbolic modeling, and generative enhancement. We conclude with evaluation: why perceptual quality and Fréchet distances are insufficient, and how conditioning adherence, musical coherence, and creative agency can guide future interactive music tools.

column4: Negation in Audio Generation Models
column6: What happens when a text-to-audio (T2A) model is asked to generate silence or exclude a specific sound? Existing models often generate the very events they are instructed to omit. Negation comprehension is critical for faithful audio generation, yet no benchmark has systematically measured it. We introduce Audio Negation Benchmark, comprising one million negated prompts spanning four negation types and three negation scopes, derived from AudioCaps captions. Human annotation of a representative subset confirms that the intended negation is correctly introduced in 99.6% of prompts. To evaluate negation understanding at scale, we propose an Audio Question Answering (AQA) protocol that probes the presence or absence of negated events using multiple-choice questions, scored against the ground-truth absence label. Evaluating three state-of-the-art models, AudioGen, AudioLDM2, and TangoFlux, we find that AQA recall for negated audio falls below 0.05 across all negation types and all models: negated and affirmative prompts produce acoustically near-identical outputs. Re-captioning the generated audio independently confirms that negative prompts consistently default to affirmative soundscapes. These results establish negation handling as a fundamental open problem in multimodal generative AI and motivate negation-aware training objectives for semantically faithful audio generation.
column7: Arjun Arora(Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur); Anshul Jain(Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur); Gubbala Mohith Nukesh(Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur); Bikash Dutta(Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur); Richa Singh(Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur); Mayank Vatsa(Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur)

column4: DiffRhythm 2: Efficient and High Fidelity Song Generation via Block Flow Matching
column6: Generating full-length, high-quality songs requires lyric–music consistency and coherent musical structure. Existing non-autoregressive (NAR) methods are efficient but often struggle with temporal alignment between lyrics and singing vocals. Meanwhile, reinforcement learning from human feedback across multiple preferences often relies on merging separately optimized models, causing performance degradation. We introduce DiffRhythm 2, an end-to-end framework for controllable song generation. It uses semi-autoregressive block flow matching to achieve faithful lyric–vocal alignment without duration labels or explicit constraints, while preserving NAR quality and efficiency. A 5 Hz music variational autoencoder enables long-sequence modeling with high-fidelity reconstruction. For multi-preference optimization, we propose cross-pair preference optimization, which jointly learns preference pairs across reward dimensions in one model and avoids merging-induced degradation. We further introduce stochastic block representation alignment loss to improve musicality and structural coherence. DiffRhythm 2 generates songs up to 210 seconds, outperforms open-source models in subjective and objective evaluations, and remains efficient. Code and weights are availble at: https://github.com/xiaomi-research/diffrhythm2.
column7: Yuepeng Jiang(ASLP Lab); Huakang Chen(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Ziqian Ning(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Jixun Yao(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Zerui han(Xiaomi Inc.); Di Wu(Xiaomi Inc.); Meng Meng(Xiaomi Inc.); Jian Luan(Xiaomi Inc.); Zhonghua Fu(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Lei Xie(Northwestern Polytechnical University)

column4: Scaling Properties of Continuous Diffusion Spoken Language Models
column6: Speech-only spoken language models (SLMs) lag behind text and text-speech models in performance, with recent discrete autoregressive (AR) SLMs indicating significant computational and data demands to match text models. Since discretizing continuous speech for AR creates bottlenecks, we explore whether continuous diffusion (CD) SLM is more viable. To quantify the SLMs linguistic quality, we introduce the phoneme Jensen-Shannon divergence (pJSD) metric. Our analysis reveals CD SLMs, mirroring AR behavior, exhibit scaling laws for validation loss and pJSD, and show optimal token-to-parameter ratios decreasing as compute scales. However, for the latter, loss becomes insensitive to choice of data and model sizes, showing potential for fast inference. Scaling CD SLMs to 16B parameters with tens of millions of hours of conversational data enables generation of emotive, prosodic, multi-speaker, multilingual speech, though achieving long-form coherence remains a significant challenge.
column7: Jason Ramapuram(Apple); Eeshan Gunesh Dhekane(Apple); Amitis Shidani(Apple); Dan Busbridge(Apple); Bogdan Mazoure(Apple); Zijin Gu(Apple); Russ Webb(Apple); Tatiana Likhomanenko(Apple); Navdeep Jaitly(Apple)

column4: FoleyGenEx: Unified Video-to-Audio Generation with Multi-Modal Control, Temporal Alignment, and Semantic Precision
column6: We present FoleyGenEx, a unified video-to-audio (VTA) framework integrating multi-modal control, frame-level temporal alignment, and fine-grained semantics, enabling synchronized, versatile audio synthesis for diverse tasks. Existing VTA methods either have multi-modal control but weak temporal alignment or strong alignment but lack reference audio conditioning and semantic precision. FoleyGenEx fills this gap via three core innovations: a conditional injection mechanism for audio-controlled VTA and Foley extension, a multi-modal dynamic masking strategy preserving training synchronization, and an adverb-based data augmentation algorithm leveraging signal processing and large language models to enhance textual supervision with nuanced semantics. Experiments on AudioCaps, VGGSound, and Greatest Hits demonstrate its competitive controllable VTA performance against existing methods. Demo samples are available at https://foleygenex.github.io/FoleyGenEx.
column7: Shiyao Wang(Nankai University); Xijuan Zeng(Kuaishou Technology); Hui Wang(Nankai University); Shiwan Zhao(Nankai University); Feng Deng(Kuaishou Technology); Chen Zhang(Kuaishou Technology); Yong Qin(Nankai University)

column4: Something from Nothing: Data Augmentation for Robust Severity Level Estimation of Dysarthric Speech
column6: Dysarthric speech quality assessment (DSQA) is critical for clinical diagnostics and inclusive speech technologies. However, subjective evaluation is costly and difficult to scale, and the scarcity of labeled data limits robust objective modeling. To address this, we propose a three-stage framework that leverages unlabeled dysarthric speech and large-scale typical speech datasets to scale training. A teacher model first generates pseudo-labels for unlabeled samples, followed by weakly supervised pretraining using a label-aware contrastive learning strategy that exposes the model to diverse speakers and acoustic conditions. The pretrained model is then fine-tuned for the downstream DSQA task. Experiments on five unseen datasets spanning multiple etiologies and languages demonstrate the robustness of our approach. Our Whisper-based baseline significantly outperforms SOTA DSQA predictors such as SpICE, and the full framework achieves an average SRCC of 0.761 across unseen test datasets.
column7: Jaesung Bae(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Xiuwen Zheng(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Minje Kim(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Chang D. Yoo(Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology (KAIST)); Mark Hasegawa-Johnson(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)

column4: Phy-VC: Physics-Informed Voice Conversion for Privacy-Preserving Pathological Speech
column6: Speech anonymisation aims to conceal the speaker's identity while retaining task-relevant information. Existing methods struggle with acoustic patterns rarely seen during training, such as dysfluencies in pathological speech. This fragility arises from purely data-driven spectral envelope estimation without physical constraints. We introduce Phy-VC, a voice conversion method that enforces articulatory-acoustic coupling as an inductive bias through a differentiable vocal tract resonance model. Trained on standard speech, Phy-VC improves intelligibility, prosody, and naturalness over state-of-the-art baselines on diverse speech patterns, including stuttering, dementia, elderly, and emotion datasets, while achieving effective anonymisation. Expert assessment confirms significant preservation of clinically relevant speech attributes. Further, the articulatory representation enables interpretable, systematic control of speaker variation.
column7: Suhita Ghosh(Otto-von-Guericke-University); Yamini Sinha(Otto-von-Guericke-University); Melanie Jouaiti(University of Birmingham); Tim Wansiedler(Otto-von-Guericke-University); Kim Hakenberg(Otto-von-Guericke-University); Julian Karcher(Otto-von-Guericke-University); Ingo Siegert(Otto von Guericke University; Department of Psychosomatic Medicine and Psychotherapy); Sebastian Stober(Otto-von-Guericke-University)

column4: Aligning Stuttered-Speech Research with End-User Needs: Scoping Review, Survey, and Guidelines
column6: Atypical speech is receiving greater attention in speech technology research, but much of this work unfolds with limited interdisciplinary dialogue. For stuttered speech in particular, it is widely recognised that current speech recognition systems fall short in practice, and current evaluation methods and research priorities are not systematically grounded in end-user experiences and needs. In this work, we analyse these gaps through 1) a scoping review of papers that deal with stuttered speech and 2) a survey of 70 stakeholders, including adults who stutter and speech-language pathologists. By analysing these two perspectives, we propose a taxonomy of stuttered-speech research, identify where current research directions diverge from the needs articulated by stakeholders, and conclude by outlining concrete guidelines and directions towards addressing the real needs of the stuttering community.
column7: Hawau Olamide Toyin(MBZUAI); Mutiah Apampa(); Toluwani Aremu(Mohamed Bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence); Humaid Alblooshi(MBZUAI); Ana Rita Valente(Speech Care;University of Aveiro); Gonçalo Leal(Speech Care); Zhengjun Yue(SLAI & CUHK (SZ)); Zeerak Talat(University of Edinburgh); Hanan Aldarmaki(Mohamed Bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence)

column4: BabAR: from phoneme recognition to developmental measures of young children's speech production
column6: Studying early speech development at scale requires automatic tools, yet automatic phoneme recognition, especially for young children, remains largely unsolved. Building on decades of data collection, we curate TinyVox, a corpus of more than half a million phonetically transcribed child vocalizations in English, French, Portuguese, German, and Spanish. We use TinyVox to train BabAR, a cross-linguistic phoneme recognition system for child speech. We find that pretraining the system on multilingual child-centered daylong recordings substantially outperforms alternatives, and that providing 20 seconds of surrounding audio context during fine-tuning further improves performance. Error analyses show that substitutions predominantly fall within the same broad phonetic categories, suggesting suitability for coarse-grained developmental analyses. We validate BabAR by showing that its automatic measures of speech maturity align with developmental estimates from the literature.
column7: Marvin Lavechin(Université Aix-Marseille); Elika Bergelson(Harvard University); Roger Levy(Massachusetts Institute of Technology)

column4: Making Room for Speech Diversity: A 50 Year Retrospective of Speech Science and Technology through a Neurodivergent Lens
column6: Interest in diversity and inclusion in speech science and technology has grown in recent years, reflected in an increasing number of Interspeech publications on "atypical" speech from disability communities. We take this momentum as an opportunity to examine how diversity has been framed in Interspeech's research discourse. Using neurodivergent speech as a case study, we conduct a scoping review of relevant Interspeech and ICASSP papers from 1976 to 2025. Our content and discourse analysis identifies three recurring issues: (1) medicalized and interventionist framings position neurodivergent traits as deficits to be corrected; (2) minimal inclusion of neurodivergent individuals in the research process, distancing stakeholders and limiting impact; and (3) ableist language that contributes to the marginalization in speech technology research. We conclude by proposing pathways through which Interspeech can achieve its stated goal of celebrating "all voices" in its research and practice.
column7: Rebecca Lietz(University of California Santa Cruz); Jingjin Li(AImpower.org); Peiyao Liu(University of California Santa Cruz); Jennifer Chien(Stanford University); Norman Makoto Su(University of California Santa Cruz); Shaomei Wu(AImpower.org)

column4: Breaking Shortcut Learning for Cross-Trial EEG-Guided Target Speech Extraction via Two-Stage Training
column6: Recent end-to-end models for EEG-guided target speech extraction report impressive results, underscoring potential for neuro-steered hearing technologies. However, our analysis reveals that high within-trial performance can be driven by trial-specific EEG structure that acts as shortcuts for target selection, leading to poor generalization on unseen trials. To overcome this gap, we propose TRUST-TSE, a two-stage framework to mitigate shortcut learning. By introducing contrastive pretraining with attended-speaker negative sampling, we encourage the EEG encoder to capture fine-grained EEG-speech alignment while suppressing trial-identity cues. We also employ a confidence-weighted extraction objective based on EEG-source similarity to guide extraction using the learned representations. Experiments on KUL and DTU datasets show that TRUST-TSE outperforms end-to-end baselines under strict cross-trial protocols, addressing a key reliability bottleneck of existing approaches.
column7: Wonchul Shin(Seoul National University); Inyong Choi(University of Iowa); Kyogu Lee(Seoul National University)
