column4: Assessing the effect of volitional and synthetic pitch raising in female speakers on automatic speaker recognition
column6: Volitional pitch raising is a form of voice disguise in forensic casework, yet its impact on automatic speaker recognition (ASR) remains unclear. This study examines ASR performance with raised pitch speech, focusing on between-speaker variability among females. Initially, three speakers were analysed using a spectral x-vector system, comparing default and raised pitch samples. Pitch raising reduced recognition accuracy, but effects varied across speakers. The worst-performing speaker had the highest median f0 in the raised pitch condition, the largest increase from default to raised pitch speech and limited f0 excursion. A pilot study using synthetic pitch manipulations with more speakers confirmed speaker-specific effects, though synthetic f0 raises did not fully capture volitional f0 raising strategies. Future work should use larger multi-speaker datasets of volitional pitch raising to clarify individual versus group effects on ASR.
column7: Chloe Patman(University of Cambridge); Linda Gerlach(Oxford Wave Research); Anil Alexander(Oxford Wave Research); Finnian Kelly(Oxford Wave Research); Kirsty McDougall(University of Cambridge)

column4: Intonation Perception in Real and Synthetic Speech across Varying Familiarity Levels: A Pilot Study of Equivalence Assessment
column6: Language training relies on a corpus constructed by a large number linguistic materials. AI-powered voice clones provide a way to construct the corpus with relatively low cost. Singing voice conversion (SVC) model is used to generate synthetic voices. This study compares participants' performances on natural and synthetic speech in two experiments, similarity perception and intonation recognition. In the accuracy of similarity perception task, a significant interaction between speech type and intonation is found, suggesting that question may serve as a cue for speaker identification but may be influenced by synthetic features. In the accuracy of intonation recognition task, a significant interaction between speech type and familiarity is observed, indicating that speech type affects how much familiarity contributes to voice processing.
column7: Hanrui Zhou(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Gaoyuan Zhang(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Yixiang Chen(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Yujie Xing(Capital Normal University); Feng Xu(Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences); Xurong Xie(Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences); Hui Chen(Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences)

column4: A barrier or a booster? Familiarity effects on Mandarin emotion prosody recognition using AI-powered voice cloning
column6: Emotion prosody perception requires simultaneous processing of acoustic cues and speaker identity. While listeners effortlessly decode natural speech, AI synthetic voices introduce cognitive complexities due to subtle acoustic atypicalities. It remains unclear how these synthetic features interact with a listener's prior social knowledge and memory of a familiar speaker. This study investigated how speech sources (human vs. AI) and speaker familiarity affect emotion recognition accuracy and cognitive load. A within-subject task with Mandarin-speaking adults evaluated behavioral (accuracy, reaction time) and physiological data (heart rate variability). Results showed that human voices yielded significantly higher accuracy and faster processing times than AI voices, while HRV did not significantly differentiate between conditions. These findings show that decoding synthetic speech is gated by top-down social cognition, highlighting limitations in current AI synthesis technologies.
column7: Feng Xu(Chinese Academy of Sciences; Macquarie University); Gaoyuan Zhang(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Shanshan Xue(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Yixiang Chen(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Hanrui Zhou(Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences); Xurong Xie(Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences); Hui Chen(Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences)

column4: Modulation of Phonetic Realizations in Cantonese Dialogue with Human and AI Interlocutors
column6: Speech patterns in human-AI interaction have received much attention recently. Prior research has focused on emotionally expressive systems in intonation languages. Less is known about how interlocutor identity (human vs. AI) shapes phonetic realizations in dialogue in tone languages. This study examined whether interacting with a human versus an AI interlocutor modulates phonetic properties in Cantonese. Scripted interactive dialogues in neutral and negative contexts with human and AI interlocutors in a Wizard-of-Oz setup were collected from 17 native Cantonese speakers. Word duration, F0 of the six tones and F1 and F2 of three corner vowels were measured. Results show evidence of phonetic modulation in AI interaction with shorter target word duration and specific tonal difference compared to human interaction. Emotional effect was marginal with a larger vowel space area in the negative context. The findings indicate more fine-grained interlocutor effects than previously reported.
column7: Xinyi Chen(Chinese University of Hong Kong); Grace Wenling Cao(University College Dublin); Yusheng Tian(Chinese University of Hong Kong); Manson Chun Man Wong(Chinese University of Hong Kong); Miko Hoi Tung Ng(Chinese University of Hong Kong); Tan Lee(Chinese University of Hong Kong; Chinese University of Hong Kong); Peggy Pik Ki Mok(Chinese University of Hong Kong)

column4: Perceptual and Acoustic Correlates of Racial Identity in Text-to-Speech Voices
column6: Voice-activated artificial intelligence (Voice-AI) systems are increasingly human-like in production, raising questions regarding how these synthetic voices are socially perceived. In this study, we show that listeners are generally capable of perceiving a sense of speaker race when hearing synthesized speech, and that they even engage in racial stereotyping. We do, however, see a bias towards rating voices as sounding 'White'. To explore this, we train a Gradient Boosted Decision Tree classifier on acoustic features to distinguish between voices rated as Black from White. Our model performs with an accuracy of 65%. From this analysis, we find that voices with lower Residual H1* and spectral tilt in the lower/higher frequencies are more regularly rated as Black. Noise measurements, as well as formants (F1, F2, and F4), also seem to vary reliably between race labels. These results have implications regarding the development, use, and efficacy of racially-marked AI.
column7: Noah Khaloo(University of California); Nicole Holliday(University of California); Sarah Creel(University of California)

column4: Multilingual Phonological Feature Recognition with Self-Supervised Speech Models
column6: Phonological features provide a language-general and linguistically grounded representation of speech. We present PhonoQ-2.0, a multilingual frame-level phonological feature recognizer built on self-supervised speech models. The system directly predicts a structured 22-dimensional feature vector per frame encoding manner, vowel quality, place, and voicing, instead of deriving features from phoneme outputs. To ensure phonologically coherent predictions, we introduce a manner-conditioned gating mechanism that activates valid feature groups. Evaluated across multiple languages and corpora, PhonoQ-2.0 achieves an average macro-F1 of 91.3% in-domain and 88.9% out-of-domain. Compared to a strong CTC phoneme baseline, it delivers consistent gains of +8.8 F1 in-domain and +8.6 out-of-domain on average. In unseen-language evaluation, PhonoQ-2.0 improves macro-F1 from 66.9% to 73.6% (+6.7 on average), with gains of up to +10.8 points.
column7: Abner Hernandez(Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg); Tomás Arias-Vergara(Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg; GITA Lab, Facultad de Ingeniería, Universidad de Antioquia UdeA); Daiqi Liu(Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg); Andreas Maier(Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg); Paula Andrea Pérez-Toro(Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg; GITA Lab, Facultad de Ingeniería, Universidad de Antioquia UdeA)

column4: Vocal Effort Modulation Strategies: A Cross-Corpus Taxonomy with Noise Robustness and ASR Implications
column6: Speakers adapt vocal output through diverse acoustic strategies, yet inter-speaker variability remains poorly characterized. We analyze 50 speakers from the AVID corpus at four effort levels, fitting linear slopes for F0, RMS energy, spectral tilt, and speaking rate, then applying K-means clustering. Three stable clusters emerge: High Modulators (broad F0/energy elevation), Spectro-Temporal speakers (spectral redistribution and rate reduction; female-leaning), and Conservative Modulators (minimal changes). ANOVA confirms significant differences (all p < 10⁻⁵, η² = 0.25-0.55); gender shows a directional but non-significant association with cluster membership within AVID (χ² = 4.37, p = 0.113). A corrected fold-wise LOSO classifier achieves 96-98% accuracy (macro-F1 = 0.97). Three validations confirm robustness: noise recoverability (SNR ≥ +10 dB, 12 noise types), French Lombard replication (cosine = 0.873), and systematic ASR WER differences in Whisper and Wav2Vec2.
column7: Lubos Marcinek(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Jonas Beskow(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Joakim Gustafson(KTH Royal Institute of Technology)

column4: Spatially-Augmented Sequence-to-Sequence Neural Diarization for Meetings
column6: This paper proposes a Spatially-Augmented Sequence-to-Sequence Neural Diarization (SA-S2SND) framework, which integrates direction-of-arrival (DOA) cues estimated by SRP-DNN into the S2SND backbone. A two-stage training strategy is adopted: the model is first trained with single-channel audio and DOA features, and then further optimized with multi-channel inputs under DOA guidance. In addition, a simulated DOA generation scheme is introduced to alleviate dependence on matched multi-channel corpora. On the AliMeeting dataset, SA-S2SND consistently outperforms the S2SND baseline, achieving a 7.4% relative DER reduction in the offline mode and over 19% improvement when combined with channel attention. These results demonstrate that spatial cues are highly complementary to cross-channel modeling, yielding good performance in both online and offline settings.
column7: Li Li(Whuan University; The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen); Ming Cheng(Whuan University); Juan Liu(Whuan University); Ming Li(Whuan University; The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen)

column4: Bidirectional Retention Network-based Segmentation Model for Speaker Diarization
column6: End-to-end neural diarization with vector clustering (EEND-VC) has emerged as a robust solution for real-world applications due to its ability to handle overlapped speech and an arbitrary number of speakers. Existing EEND-VC segmentation back ends typically employ recurrent neural networks (RNNs), attention-based architectures, or Mamba. In this paper, we propose a novel segmentation model that integrates a WavLM-based front end with a bidirectional Retention Network (BiRetNet) back end. RetNet provides dual parallel and recurrent formulations with favorable computational scaling with respect to sequence length, motivating its use as a promising segmentation back end for speaker diarization. We evaluate the potential of BiRetNet by benchmarking it against established RNN, attention, and Mamba-based variants. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms these baselines, achieving state-of-the-art performance on two widely used diarization datasets.
column7: Jian You(Cisco Systems); Xiangfeng Li(Cisco Systems); Tengfei Zhou(Cisco Systems); Erwan Zerhouni(Cisco Systems)

column4: Role-Aware Semi-Supervised Domain Adaptation for Teacher-Student Speaker Diarization
column6: Speaker diarization identifies anonymous speakers, yet educational settings require role-based segregation (teacher vs. student). Generic models struggle here due to data scarcity and domain shifts. We propose a Mean Teacher-based Role-Aware Semi-Supervised Domain Adaptation framework using our proposed TSSD, a semi-supervised dataset. By exploiting unlabeled target-domain data, our method aligns generic acoustic priors with classroom distributions. To drive this adaptation, we propose Role-Aware Union Loss that reformulates the task from identity distinction to role detection, enabling fine-grained separation via coarse supervision to resolve overlapping ambiguity without explicit IDs. we also adopt PIT-MSE consistency loss to enforce robust student-teacher model alignment invariant to speaker ordering. Experiments show our method disentangles complex acoustic scenes into distinct role-based streams, offering a scalable solution for "many-to-one" mapping in conversational analysis.
column7: Zhen Liao(Huazhong University of Science and Technology); Gaole Dai(Huazhong University of Science and Technology); Weiwei Jiang(Huazhong University of Science and Technology); Mengting Wang(Huazhong University of Science and Technology); Wei Xu(Huazhong University of Science and Technology)

column4: Leveraging Diarization Labels for Robust Score Calibration in Target Speaker Tagging via Gaussian Mixture Modeling
column6: Target speaker tagging (TST) diarizes multi-speaker audio and assigns enrolled speaker identities to the resulting segments. However, the short duration of many diarized segments leads to unreliable verification scores with high variance. While aggregating scores across co-labeled segments within a session offers a potential remedy, naive averaging is inherently fragile under erroneous diarization labels. We propose a calibration method based on a two-component Gaussian mixture model (GMM) fitted to the score distribution within each diarization cluster. One component captures correctly clustered segments and the other absorbs misclustered ones. Each segment is assigned the mean of its most probable component, enabling robust aggregation that is resilient to diarization errors. Experiments on TST-Bench and the ICSI Meeting Corpus demonstrate consistent improvements over uncalibrated scoring and conventional baselines across multiple operating points and embedding architectures.
column7: Hee-Soo Heo(NAVER Cloud Corporation); Minjae Lee(NAVER Cloud Corporation); Youngki Kwon(NAVER Cloud Corporation); Han-Gyu Kim(NAVER Cloud Corporation); Bong-Jin Lee(NAVER Cloud Corporation)

column4: SphereVBx: Spherical Variational Bayes Clustering for Simplified EEND-VC Diarization
column6: We propose SphereVBx, a Bayesian clustering framework for hyperspherical embeddings based on Toroidal Probabilistic Spherical Discriminant Analysis (T-PSDA). The method follows the variational Bayesian formulation of VBx while replacing the Gaussian Probabilistic Linear Discriminant Analysis (PLDA) backend with T-PSDA, resulting in variational inference in a mixture of von Mises-Fisher distributions. We apply SphereVBx to speaker diarization and in particular to the end-to-end neural diarization with vector clustering (EEND-VC) framework. A parameter-free variant, denoted SphereVBx-PF, corresponds to a spherical similarity model closely related to cosine scoring and does not require pretrained backend parameters. Experiments on multiple diarization benchmarks show that SphereVBx improves clustering accuracy in cascaded diarization pipelines and achieves comparable or better performance in the EEND-VC framework while significantly simplifying its clustering stage.
column7: Petr Pálka(Brno University of Technology); Jiangyu Han(Brno University of Technology); Prachi Singh(Brno University of Technology); Marc Delcroix(NTT, Inc.); Naohiro Tawara(NTT, Inc.); Lukáš Burget(Brno University of Technology)

column4: Indic DiarBench: A Multilingual Joint Diarization and ASR Benchmark for Indian Languages
column6: In this work, we introduce Indic DiarBench, a speaker diarization and ASR benchmark dataset spanning all 22 scheduled languages of India. This corpus comprises approximately 108 hours of natural multi-speaker audio from near-field meetings, far-field recordings, and in-the-wild audios. All annotations are human-corrected with time-aligned speaker attributed transcriptions. The dataset captures conversational nuance prevalent in Indian speech, such as English code-mixing, dialectal variation, and frequent speaker overlap. To establish a baseline for joint ASR and diarization capabilities we evaluate leading systems including commercial speech APIs and multimodal large language models. Indic DiarBench is released as an open-access resource to advance inclusive, multilingual speech technology research for Indian languages.
column7: Deovrat Mehendale(Sarvam AI); Aditya Mehndiratta(Sarvam AI); Dhruv Rathi(Sarvam AI); Kaushal Bhogale(IIT Madras); Mitesh M. Khapra(IIT Madras)

column4: Speaker Separation via Audio Language Modeling
column6: We propose LlaSep, an autoregressive approach for speaker separation. LlaSep uses discrete audio tokens with a causal language model to generatively separate mixed speech signals. Unlike existing methods that rely on continuous spectral representations and task-specific components our system operates entirely in the discrete token domain. LlaSep generates per-speaker codec token streams in a single decoding pass, conditioned on the tokenized mixture and semantic features from a pretrained speech encoder. LlaSep is trained via supervised fine-tuning on ground-truth speaker tokens from a large-scale synthetic multilingual conversation dataset spanning seven languages and 15k hours. Evaluation on LibriCSS and CallHome demonstrates competitive separation and diarization performance and substantially higher audio quality compared to previous baselines, demonstrating that token-level language modeling is a viable paradigm for multi-speaker speech processing.
column7: Luca Lanzendörfer(ETH Zurich); Constantin Pinkl(ETH Zurich); Florian Grötschla(ETH Zurich); Roger Wattenhofer(ETH Zurich)

column4: RT-ASDNet: Unified, Real-Time Active Speaker Detection
column6: Existing audio-visual active speaker detection methods often rely on multi-stage pipelines or computationally expensive temporal modeling, limiting their applicability in real-time scenarios. In this paper, we propose RT-ASDNet, a unified, end-to-end audio-visual architecture for real-time active speaker detection. Our approach jointly processes raw audio waveform and video frames through two specialized streams that are fused into an anchor-free detection head, simultaneously localizing faces and predicting speaking activity in a single forward pass. Unlike multi-stage approaches that require separate face detection, feature extraction, and classification steps, RT-ASDNet performs joint localization and classification within a unified framework, significantly reducing inference latency and pipeline complexity. Moreover, since inference is performed only once per frame, the computational cost remains constant regardless of the number of people in the scene. We evaluate our method on the AVA-ActiveSpeaker benchmark and set the baseline for joint detection and classification on active speaker detection task.
column7: Okan Köpüklü(Microsoft)

column4: Joint Learning Global-Local Speaker Classification to Enhance End-to-End Speaker Diarization and Recognition
column6: Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in end-to-end speaker diarization and recognition. However, their speaker discriminability remains limited due to the scarcity of large-scale conversational data and the absence of explicit speaker representation optimization. To address this, we propose GLSC-SDR, a paradigm that jointly trains speaker classification with diarization and recognition. We further introduce a Global-Local Speaker Classification strategy, which uses clustered speakers as global labels and re-encoded intra-cluster speakers as local labels. This hierarchical design enhances fine-grained speaker discrimination while preserving semantic transcription accuracy. Experiments on AliMeeting, AISHELL-4, and AMI-SDM demonstrate that GLSC-SDR achieves competitive or superior performance compared to simulation-based and multi-encoder approaches, without relying on large-scale real conversational data.
column7: Yuhang Dai(Northwestern Polytechnical University; Soul AI Lab); Haopeng Lin(Soul AI Lab); Jiale Qian(Soul AI Lab); Ruiqi Yan(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Hao Meng(Soul AI Lab); Hanke Xie(Northwestern Polytechnical University; Soul AI Lab); Hanlin Wen(Soul AI Lab); Shunshun Yin(Soul AI Lab); Ming Tao(Soul AI Lab); Xie Chen(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Lei Xie(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Xinsheng Wang(Soul AI Lab)

column4: POP-SED: Prototype Orthogonal Projection for Robust Few-shot Sound Event Detection
column6: Few-shot sound event detection (SED) must operate with limited examples that often contain overlapping background sounds, making robust detection challenging. We present prototype orthogonal projection for SED (POP-SED), a fine-tuning-free method that suppresses background influences by projecting the target-event prototype onto a subspace orthogonal to background vectors. Background vectors are obtained by fitting a von Mises-Fisher mixture model to features from background and query intervals, and then selecting a subset of mean vectors that maximizes a robustness-aware support-set criterion. On the DCASE2024 Task 5 validation set, POP-SED achieved an F-score of 62.35% without any fine-tuning, approaching the accuracy of top-performing systems that require both domain-level and support-set fine-tuning.
column7: Takehiko Kagoshima(Toshiba Corporation)

column4: CLEAR: Clinical LLM Embedding and Attention-based Reconstruction
column6: Clinical heart sound analysis is vital for cardiovascular diagnosis but is frequently disrupted by non-stationary noise. To overcome the limitations of traditional methods, we propose CLEAR: Clinical LLM Embedding and Attention-based Reconstruction. Given noisy audio, a pretrained Whisper encoder extracts high-dimensional semantic embeddings. A Graph Attention Network (GAT) models these as graph nodes to predict latent masks, isolating pure heart sounds. A Latent Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) then refines these representations to generate distortion-free signals. Evaluated under 10 dB SNR environmental noise, CLEAR demonstrated an exceptional peak restoration capability, achieving a maximum PESQ of 4.64 and SI-SDR of 64.35 dB from severely degraded inputs (PESQ 1.03, SI-SDR -29.37 dB). By delivering natural, artifact-free audio, CLEAR significantly enhances clinical auscultation and early disease detection.
column7: Eashita Wazed(Chonnam National University); Hieyong Jeong( Chonnam National University); Choonsung Shin(Chonnam National University); Shima Okada(Ritsumeikan University)

column4: Few-shot Class-variable Incremental Audio Classification via Prototype Adaptation and Pseudo Class-variable Training
column6: In the task of few-shot class-incremental audio classification, the number of classes is assumed to always increase without considering the possibility of decrease. However, the number of classes generally increases or decreases in practice. In this paper, we investigate a problem of Few-shot Class-variable Incremental Audio Classification (FCIAC), where the number of classes increases or decreases. We propose a FCIAC method using prototype adaptation and pseudo class-variable training. The model in our method consists of an encoder and a classifier. The classifier is initialized by a class-variable prototype adaptation network, whose structure dynamically changes with the change of classes. In addition, we design a pseudo class-variable training strategy to enhance the model’s adaptability to changing classes. Experiments on three public datasets show that our method exceeds previous methods in average accuracy. The code is at: https://github.com/cgq2971-afk/FCIAC.
column7: Yanxiong Li(South China University of Technology); Guoqing Chen(South China University of Technology); Qianqian Qianqian Li(South China University of Technology); Sen Huang(South China University of Technology)

column4: Quality Adaptive Angular Margin Learning for Respiratory Sound Classification
column6: We present a quality-adaptive angular-margin learning framework that improves feature generalization by enforcing intra-class compactness and inter-class separability. Our framework, titled QLung, introduces a no-reference audio quality margin derived from spectral entropy and root-mean-square energy, which adaptively scales angular margins based on recording quality. To this end, we propose a log-scaled angular margin that stabilizes training under severe class imbalance. We also use an angular classifier that normalizes features and class weights, ensuring margin penalties are applied consistently on the unit hypersphere. Our approach improves in-distribution performance on the ICBHI dataset by 2.46% over the cross-entropy baseline, and most significantly, achieves the strongest out-of-distribution performance on the SPRSound dataset compared to prior state-of-the-art methods. Code is available at https://github.com/RSC-Toolkit/QLung.
column7: Yoon Tae Kim(RSC LAB, MODULABS); Heejoon Koo(RSC LAB, MODULABS); Miika Toikkanen(RSC LAB, MODULABS); June-Woo Kim(Wonkwang University)

column4: Fair Cognitive Impairment Detection Through Unlearning
column6: Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is a medical condition characterized by a noticeable decline in memory, language, or thinking abilities. MCI detection from spontaneous speech is promising for scalable screening. However, learned models often exploit demographic cues correlated with labels, resulting in a large performance gap across subgroups. We present a multi-modal framework that combines (i) cross-model fusion between modalities (speech, text, and image), and (ii) unlearning using gradient reversal that discourages the shared embedding from encoding task-irrelevant demographic attributes. Evaluated on the multilingual benchmarks TAUKADIAL and PREPARE, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art multilingual and multi-modal baseline in MCI classification while substantially reducing the performance gap across patient subgroups (sex and language). We further analyze transfer across datasets, showing that demographic unlearning helps learn more robust representations for MCI detection.
column7: William Nguyen(University of Massachusetts Lowell); Jiali Cheng(University of Massachusetts Lowell); Hadi Amiri(University of Massachusetts Lowell)

column4: QuadVAD: Fine-Grained Speech Detection with a Compact Architecture
column6: Voice Activity Detection (VAD) is the foundational gatekeeper of the power-performance envelope in always-on edge devices and conversational AI systems. An ideal VAD must provide ultra-low algorithmic latency for barge-in and end-of-turn detection, maintain noise robustness, and minimize computation and footprint for edge deployment. We propose QuadVAD, a highly optimized, small-footprint neural VAD operating at a fine-grained 4 ms resolution. An efficient data synthesis and alignment pipeline leveraging Montreal Forced Aligner and fine-tuning on the TIMIT Acoustic-Phonetic Corpus ensures precise boundary detection. Experiments show improved onset detection with QuadVAD. The architecture combines convolutional blocks with an LSTM Cell, totaling 25 KB and achieves an RTF of 0.0014 on a 13th Gen Intel Core i7 laptop. QuadVAD effectively balances latency, robustness, size and compute, making it well suited for deployment in conversational AI systems and always-on speech interfaces.
column7: Ramakrishna Chaitanya Rachumallu(Meeami Technologies); Nivedita Chennupati(Meeami Technologies); Ankit Gupta(Meeami Technologies); Balaji Padmanaban(Meeami Technologies); ParvathiPriyanka Bolla(Meeami Technologies); Harish Rajamani(Meeami Technologies); Naveen Ambati(Meeami Technologies)

column4: Exploratory analysis of yellow mongoose vocalization: detection from in-the-wild recordings and call classification
column6: Understanding the vocal repertoire of social animals, such as the yellow mongoose (YM), is crucial for deciphering their social structure and evolutionary history. In this study, we present an exploratory analysis of YM vocalization detection and classification using both signal processing and machine learning approaches. The analysis uses two distinct datasets: (1) expert-annotated, clean pup vocalizations (n=940), and (2) noisy field recordings (n=29) captured with directional microphones. Our results indicate that handcrafted features, originally developed for human speech modeling to represent syllables, are effective for animal vocalization classification, suggesting potential shared acoustic structures. Although detecting YM vocalizations in wild recordings proved challenging, our objective is to aid annotators by flagging potential vocalization segments. The results presented in this work provide a foundation for scalable, semi-automated analysis of animal vocal repertoires.
column7: Sevada Hovsepyan(Idiap Research Institute); Imen Ben Mahmoud(Idiap Research Institute); Vanessa Rüegg(University of Zurich); Marta Manser(University of Zurich); Mathew Magimai.-Doss(Idiap Research Institute)

column4: Continual Generalized Category Discovery for Acoustic Signals via Instance-Adaptive Regularization and Dynamic Teacher Guidance
column6: Acoustic perception systems must continually adapt to emerging sound categories, yet real-world annotation is often unavailable or costly. Continual Generalized Category Discovery (C-GCD) addresses this challenge by retaining previously learned classes while discovering novel categories from unlabeled streaming data. However, directly transferring vision-based C-GCD methods to audio leads to marked performance degradation because acoustic signals exhibit complex spectrotemporal structures, strong class overlap, and severe base-class bias. We therefore propose an audio-oriented C-GCD framework with instance-adaptive regularization to balance consolidation and exploration, GMM-based adaptive thresholding, and an EMA-updated dynamic teacher for stable pseudo-label generation. Experiments on LibriSpeech and ShipsEar show consistent gains in novel-class discovery and old-class retention. On ShipsEar, our method achieves 74.14% cumulative average accuracy, surpassing Happy by 4.84 percentage points.
column7: Qisheng Xu(National University of Defense Technology; National Key Laboratory of Parallel and Distributed Computing); Shanhao Han(National University of Defense Technology; National Key Laboratory of Parallel and Distributed Computing); Hui Geng(National University of Defense Technology; National Key Laboratory of Parallel and Distributed Computing); Yulu Fang(National University of Defense Technology; National Key Laboratory of Parallel and Distributed Computing); Yunsheng Xiong(National University of Defense Technology; National Key Laboratory of Parallel and Distributed Computing); Yutao Dou(Hunan University); Kele Xu(National University of Defense Technology; National Key Laboratory of Parallel and Distributed Computing)

column4: I'll Keep an Ear Out: Teaching AudioLLMs Proactive Audio Assistance
column6: Audio large language models (AudioLLMs) operate reactively, responding only when queried. We introduce proactive audio assistance, where an AudioLLM monitors an audio stream and autonomously decides when to alert the user from a single natural-language intent, motivated by wearable applications for Deaf and Hard of Hearing users. We propose Interrupt and Silent Modeling (ISM), a model-agnostic paradigm that embeds proactive decisions into LLM decoding via two special tokens: and , capturing four states: onset detection, sustained-relevance triggering, irrelevance suppression, and de-duplication. Applied to Qwen2-Audio-7B, ISM achieves 99.6% interrupt F1 and perfect de-duplication recall on ESC-50. On noisy Epic-Sounds kitchen audio, ISM achieves the highest interrupt F1 without domain-specific training, the only method maintaining strong onset detection without over-triggering or over-suppression. Streaming evaluation confirms real-time viability with 3.5-second average latency.

column4: STSR: High-Fidelity Speech Super-Resolution via Spectral-Transient Context Modeling
column6: Speech super-resolution (SR) requires a delicate balance between preserving global harmonic coherence and sharp local transients. While diffusion-based models achieve impressive fidelity, their computational demands limit practical use; conversely, efficient time-domain architectures often struggle to capture the long-range spectral dependencies essential for precise harmonic alignment. We introduce STSR, an end-to-end MDCT-domain framework designed to bridge this gap. STSR leverages a Spectral-Contextual Attention mechanism with hierarchical windowing to aggregate non-local context, ensuring consistent harmonic restoration up to 48 kHz. To prevent the loss of transient clarity in compressed spectral representations, we incorporate a sparse-aware regularization strategy. Experimental results demonstrate that STSR surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in both perceptual quality and zero-shot generalization, establishing a robust, real-time paradigm for high-fidelity speech restoration. Samples can be found online.
column7: Jiajun Yuan(Wuhan University); Xiaochen Wang(Wuhan University); Yulin Wu(Jianghan University); Chenhao Hu(Xiaomi Corporation); Xueyang Lv(Xiaomi Corporation)

column4: A Novel Transfer Learning Approach for Room Impulse Response Estimation and Speech Dereverberation Across Geometrically Diverse and Data-Scarce Environments
column6: Accurate Room Impulse Response estimation is critical for audio reproduction, echo cancellation, and speech dereverberation. Traditional methods are computationally expensive and generalize poorly across room shapes and materials. We propose a novel transfer learning framework that adapts models trained on data-rich rectangular rooms to L-shaped and irregular geometries with limited measurements. Our geometry-aware encoder extracts shape-invariant features, while a physics-informed decoder enforces echo sparsity and energy decay. Uniquely, we freeze the encoder during fine-tuning, updating only the decoder-achieving 56% lower MSE and 37% lower LSD on unseen target geometries with merely 10 training rooms. Downstream speech dereverberation validates practical utility with PESQ of 3.24 vs. 2.78 and STOI of 0.89 vs. 0.79 compared to Generative Adversarial Networks baselines.
column7: Shahab Pasha(Shahab Pasha, University of Western Australia); Jiahong Zhao(Jiahong Zhao, Institute of Sound and Vibration Research, University of Southampton); Hualin Ren(Hualin Ren, University of Wollongong); Christian Ritz(Christian Ritz, University of Wollongong)

column4: HWB-plus: A Lightweight Speech Bandwidth Extension Method with Separate Modeling for Consonants and Vowels
column6: Speech Bandwidth Extension (BWE) aims to reconstruct the missing high-frequency components of narrowband signals for enhanced perceptual quality. However, existing methods often face a trade-off between performance and resource efficiency--a critical constraint for edge device deployment. This paper proposes an improved lightweight BWE approach based on HWB-Net, which achieves performance improvement with almost no change in model parameters and computational load. The key innovations are: (1) Dual-WGMM, grounded in STRAIGHT's periodic/aperiodic decomposition, including ConsWGMM (for high-frequency consonants) and VowelWGMM (for mid-to-low frequency vowels); (2) mel-scale initialization for VowelWGMM. Evaluated on the VCTK dataset, the proposed method outperforms SOTA lightweight models (HWB-Net, BAE-Lite) by significant margins across DNSMOS P.808, PESQ, and NISQA. This work provides a practical BWE solution for real-time communication on edge devices.
column7: Xin Liu(Inner Mongolia University); Xueliang Zhang(Inner Mongolia University)

column4: USDnet++: Distilling Signal Processing Based Dereverberation for Unsupervised Neural Speech Dereverberation
column6: Given a set of unlabeled reverberant speech signals, the recent USDnet model can learn to effectively perform unsupervised single-speaker speech dereverberation. This paper proposes USDnet++, which extends USDnet by leveraging signal processing based dereverberation results to improve the training of USDnet. The rationale is that the dereverberation result produced by signal processing algorithms typically has a higher signal-to-noise (SNR) of the target speech and hence could be leveraged as a weak supervision to improve the training of USDnet. In this paper, we employ weighted prediction error (WPE) and convolutional beamforming (WPD) to derive the signal processing based dereverberation result for improving USDnet. Evaluation results on the WSJ0CAM-DEREVERB dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of USDnet++.
column7: Ruizhe Pang(Southern University of Science and Technology); Shulin He(Southern University of Science and Technology); Jingqi Sun(Southern University of Science and Technology); Zhong-Qiu Wang(Southern University of Science and Technology)

column4: EffVOC: Low-Delay Efficient Speech Waveform Reconstruction from Spectral Representations Without Phase
column6: The Griffin-Lim algorithm has been a seminal contribution for phase reconstruction from amplitude spectrograms, however, requiring (infinitely) high algorithmic delay. Its low-delay variant suffers in speech quality. Recent (generative) neural network methods improve on speech quality still at medium to high algorithmic delay, but often they are complex and optimized only for one specific input representation. We build upon an efficient low-delay speech vocoder and propose EffVOC, which supports synthesis of wideband (WB) or fullband (FB) speech from either amplitude spectrum or Mel coefficient inputs. We evaluate both input representations across multiple model sizes in a unified framework and compare against state of the art. Results show that our proposed low-delay (20 ms vs. 32 ms or more) efficient approach marks a new SOTA by achieving top-ranked subjective MOS scores (WB: 4.17/4.15, FB: 4.14/4.11) for amplitude spectrum/Mel representations, very close to ground truth.
column7: Renzheng Shi(TU Braunschweig); Simon Welker(Universität Hamburg); Timo Gerkmann(Universität Hamburg); Tim Fingscheidt(TU Braunschweig)

column4: Your U-Net Dereverberation Model is Secretly an RIR Encoder
column6: In this work, we analyze the ability of NCSN++ U-Net based audio dereverberation models to capture global room characteristics in their intermediate representations. Through an empirical study of both a state-of-the-art diffusion-based model and a discriminative counterpart, we show that deeper layers encode structured room impulse response (RIR)-dependent embeddings. Moreover, the discriminative ability of this implicit room representation correlates with dereverberation performance across objective metrics. Motivated by this observation, we propose a training strategy that explicitly conditions the network on pre-trained RIR embeddings, obtained via self-supervised contrastive learning. Incorporating RIR conditioning improves representation quality, accelerates convergence, and enhances dereverberation performance, while significantly reducing the number of reverse diffusion steps required by the diffusion-based model during inference.
column7: Sina Khanagha(University of Hamburg); Timo Gerkmann(University of Hamburg)

column4: FastWave: Optimized Diffusion Model for Audio Super-Resolution
column6: Audio Super-Resolution is a set of techniques aimed at high-quality estimation of the given signal as if it would be sampled with higher sample rate. Among suggested methods there are diffusion and flow models (which are considered slower), generative adversarial networks (which are considered faster), however both approaches are currently presented by high-parametric networks, requiring high computational costs both for training and inference. We propose a solution to both these problems by re-considering the recent advances in the training of diffusion models and applying them to super-resolution from any to 48 kHz sample rate. Our model called FastWave has around 50 GFLOPs of computational complexity and 1.3 M parameters and can be trained with less resources and significantly faster than the majority of recently proposed diffusion- and flow-based solutions. FastWave also has comparable performance to state-of-the-art models. We provide our implementation on GitHub.
column7: Nikita Kuznetsov(HSE University; VK LLC); Maksim Kaledin(HSE University)

column4: LavaSR: Fast and Flexible Audio Bandwidth Extension via Vocos
column6: We propose a Vocos-based bandwidth extension model that enhances audio at 8–48 kHz by generating missing high-frequency content. Inputs are resampled to 48 kHz and processed by a neural vocoder backbone, enabling a single network to support arbitrary upsampling ratios. A lightweight Linkwitz-Riley-inspired refiner merges the original low band with the generated high frequencies via a smooth crossover. On validation, the model achieves competitive log-spectral distance while running at a real-time factor of 0.0001 on an NVIDIA A100 GPU and 0.0053 on an 8-core CPU, demonstrating practical, high-quality BWE at extreme throughput.
column7: Yatharth Sharma(New York)

column4: Adaptive Oscillatory Inductive Bias for Modeling Sharp Prosodic Dynamics in Diffusion-Based TTS
column6: Diffusion-based text-to-speech (TTS) models have achieved significant improvements in speech quality. However, modeling sharp prosodic transitions and rapid pitch variations in expressive speech remains challenging. Existing diffusion-based TTS decoders commonly utilize periodic nonlinearities such as Snake activation function to capture harmonic structures, but this activation funcation provides limited adaptability when modeling abrupt amplitude and frequency variations. In this paper, we investigate the role of oscillatory inductive bias in diffusion-based TTS decoders and introduce an adaptive oscillatory nonlinearity that enables controllable periodic modulation while maintaining signal stability through a linear bypass component. We refer the resulting TTS system as OscillaTTS. Experiments on the LJSpeech and Emotional Speech Dataset show consistent improvements across objective and subjective evaluations, indicating improved modeling of expressive prosodic dynamics.
column7: Sandipan Dhar(Sony Research India); Nirmesh J. Shah(Sony Research India); Ashishkumar P. Gudmalwar(Sony Research India); Pankaj Wasnik(Sony Research India)

column4: Word-level Emotional Intensity Control in TTS via Emotion Residual Vectors
column6: Modern emotional text-to-speech (TTS) models typically rely on utterance-level conditioning. However, natural emotional speech requires fine-grained variations across words to achieve nuanced, human-like expressiveness. To address this, we introduce emotion residual vectors (ERVs), which capture neutral-to-emotional deviations in word-aligned self-supervised speech embeddings as an annotation-free cue for local prosody. To stabilize intensity control, we compress ERVs into a low-dimensional bottleneck space and train a RoBERTa-based predictor to infer the projected vectors from text and emotion. During inference, the predicted vectors are converted into additive hidden-state offsets and injected into a neutral-conditioned TTS model, enabling continuous word-level intensity control. Experimental results show that our method improves local emotional controllability while preserving naturalness compared to controllable emotional TTS baselines.
column7: Ji-Hyun Park(Hanyang University); Nam-Seok Song(Hanyang University); Joon-Hyuk Chang(Hanyang University)

column4: Continuous Time-Varying Emotion Control Zero-Shot Text-To-Speech With Emotion Orthogonal LoRA
column6: High-quality emotional text-to-speech (TTS) often depends on large scale corpora and coarse discrete emotion labels, which limits fine-grained and time-varying control in practice. We address this by integrating continuous Valence, Arousal, and Dominance (VAD) control into a pretrained model via low-rank updates inserted into the backbone transformations. Our Emotion Orthogonal LoRA (EO-LoRA) uses three separate low-rank branches aligned to valence, arousal, and dominance, and an orthogonality regularizer encourages the branches to capture distinct effects. We further introduce Flow-DGPO, a reinforcement learning alignment stage for flow matching TTS that improves emotion controllability while preserving intelligibility and speaker similarity. Experiments show that our method improves continuous and time-varying emotion control while maintaining synthesis quality with limited training data.
column7: Chenchen Wan(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Minchuan Chen(Ping An Technology); Yan Shi(Ping An Technology); Peng Qi(Shanghai Jiao Tong University Chongqing Artificial Intelligence Research Institute); Shaojun Wang(Ping An Technology); Jing Xiao(Ping An Technology)

column4: ETC-TTS: Emotion Trajectory Learning for Controllable Emotional Text-to-Speech
column6: Emotional text-to-speech (TTS) systems have achieved high speech quality, yet controllable emotion intensity modeling remains challenging. Existing approaches control emotion embeddings via scaling or interpolation at inference time, so intermediate emotional states are not explicitly learned. To address this limitation, we propose Emotion Trajectory learning for Controllable emotional TTS (ETC-TTS), a framework that models emotion intensity as continuous trajectories in latent style space. A residual vector quantization (RVQ)-based style extractor provides emotion-aware representations, and a flow-matching objective learns trajectories between neutral and target emotions. Unlike prior methods, ETC-TTS learns emotion transitions during training, enabling stable intensity control. Experiments on Korean and English datasets show improved controllability while preserving speech quality. Subjective and objective evaluations confirm more stable emotional expressions than baseline methods.
column7: Gaeun Kim(Hanyang University); Jaeuk Lee(Hanyang University); Joon-Hyuk Chang(Hanyang University)

column4: Beyond One-Size-Fits-All: Personalized and Culturally Adaptive Emotional TTS via Interactive Optimization of Individual Emotion Perception Spaces
column6: The rise of conversational AI has increased interest in emotional Text-to-Speech (TTS). Most systems rely on discrete emotion labels, which fail to capture the nuanced nature of human affect. Recent models employ dimensional representations such as Russell's arousal-valence (A-V) model, offering finer control. However, emotional perception varies across individuals and cultures, which may cause mismatches between modeled and perceived emotions. We propose a personalized and culturally adaptive emotional TTS framework that performs interactive optimization of individualized A-V perception spaces using an Interactive Genetic Algorithm. By adapting emotion representations to each listener, the system produces speech with more perceptually aligned emotional expression than models using averaged A-V values. Evaluations with Japanese, Chinese, and Indonesian participants highlight the importance of personalization and cultural adaptation for moving beyond one-size-fits-all emotional TTS.
column7: Wangzixi Zhou(Nara Institute of Science and Technology); Bagus Tris Atmaja(Nara Institute of Science and Technology); Sakriani Sakti(Nara Institute of Science and Technology)

column4: Cross-modal Consistency Guidance for Robust Emotion Control in Auto-Regressive TTS Models
column6: While Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems enable emotional control via natural-language instructions, expressiveness, naturalness, and speech quality degrade when the target emotion conflicts with the textual semantics. We propose a Cross-modal Consistency Guided Classifier-Free Guidance (CCG-CFG) method with dynamic scales based on the degree of inconsistency between the text emotion and the explicit speech emotion, replacing the dropout condition with the text emotion. We also distill the CCG-CFG guidance signal using a hard-sample mining strategy, improving the TTS model's emotional alignment capability. Evaluations on five emotional corpora and two TTS benchmarks show that our approaches applied to CosyVoice2 achieve up to a 12% absolute improvement in emotion-recognition accuracy and a 10% relative improvement in subjective scores, outperforming baselines including HierSpeech++, Qwen3-TTS, and the original CosyVoice2, while preserving intelligibility, naturalness, and high speech quality.
column7: Yizhou Peng(Nanyang Technological University); Yukun Ma(Alibaba); Chong Zhang(Alibaba); Yi-Wen Chao(Nanyang Technological University); Chongjia Ni(Alibaba); Bin Ma(Alibaba); Eng Siong Chng(Nanyang Technological University)

column4: A Large-Scale Dataset of Listener Impressions of Emotional TTS
column6: We present the first large-scale dataset for speech quality assessment of emotional synthesized speech. The dataset consists of 18,208 speech samples in five emotional styles from 13 state-of-the-art synthesis systems and natural emotional speech, along with ratings from 262 listeners for quality and several aspects of emotional content, including perceived emotional categories, how well the speech matches the target emotion, valence, arousal, and dominance. Analyses of the ratings show the relationships between the different types of ratings, and experiments using pretrained emotion recognizers, speech quality predictors, and LLM-as-judge prediction approaches reveal reasonable correlations with human ratings in some cases, with room for improvement and varying results observed depending on the emotion category. This dataset will be made public to the research community as a resource for the developing automatic speech quality assessment models for emotional synthesized speech.
column7: Erica Cooper(National Institute of Information and Communications Technology); Xiaoxue Gao(A*STAR); Takuma Okamoto(National Institute of Information and Communications Technology); Tomoki Toda(Nagoya University; National Institute of Information and Communications Technology); Nancy Chen(A*STAR); Hisashi Kawai(National Institute of Information and Communications Technology)

column4: DECRA: Dynamic Emotion Control for Real-time Speech Anonymization
column6: Real-time speaker anonymization requires neutralizing or controlling emotional states with causal, low-latency synthesis to prevent leakage of sensitive paralinguistic information. However, most expressive VC systems operate offline and rely on global style conditioning, which limits real-time use and dynamic emotion control. In addition, speaker representations commonly used for VC entangle speaker identity with emotional attributes, making emotion control weaker and less reliable. We propose DECRA1, a real-time streaming VC system that performs closed-loop, time-varying prosody control. It conditions synthesis on continuous valence–arousal (VA) trajectories predicted online by a causal speech emotion recognition (SER) model, while disentangling speaker identity from emotion. The resulting system is streamable end-to-end, with <80 ms GPU latency. Experiments show improved VA-space emotion steering over SOTA baselines and demonstrate dynamic, time-varying emotion control.
column7: Ghady Nasrallah(Texas A&M University); Waris Quamer(Texas A&M University); Mu-Ruei Tseng(Texas A&M University); Ricardo Gutierrez-Osuna(Texas A&M University)

column4: Emo-BPO: Emotion Bidirectional Preference Optimization for Diffusion-based Emotional TTS
column6: Diffusion-based TTS has demonstrated strong capability in emotional speech generation. However, existing emotion alignment methods primarily reinforce target emotional expressions while overlooking modeling of competing emotional modes, limiting fine-grained controllability. This issue becomes more pronounced under classifier-free guidance (CFG), which relies on contrasting conditional trajectories to shape generation. We propose Emotion Bidirectional Preference Optimization (Emo-BPO), a simple effective framework that jointly learns emotion-aligned and emotion-contrastive score functions from reordered same-text emotional pairs. Our method requires neither auxiliary reward models nor additional annotations, and can be seamlessly integrated into existing diffusion-based TTS systems to improve emotional controllability and expressiveness.
column7: Jiacheng Shi(William & Mary); Hongfei Du(William & Mary); Xinyuan Song(Emory University); Y. Alicia Hong(George Mason University); Yanfu Zhang(William & Mary); Ye Gao(William & Mary)

column4: DeSRPA: Decoupled Speech Role-Playing Agent via Inference-Time Intervention
column6: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized text-based role-playing, creating immersive Speech Role-Playing Agents (SRPAs) requires a seamless bridge between cognitive reasoning and paralinguistic nuances. Current SRPAs primarily rely on End-to-End (E2E) fine-tuning. However, this paradigm suffers from poor generalization to unseen characters due to its reliance on role-specific data, while imposing a “modality alignment tax” that degrades intrinsic LLM reasoning capabilities. We propose DeSRPA, an agentic framework for character role play via inference-time intervention on frozen backbones. It employs a dual-level Control Vector (CV) mechanism Internal Cognitive Steering and External Expressive Rendering to synchronize “mind” and “voice”. Experiments on SpeechRole and OmniCharacter benchmarks demonstrate that DeSRPA significantly outperforms E2E baselines in personality and emotional consistency. It achieves high speech naturalness, narrowing the gap with proprietary models like GPT-4o Audio, while remaining a scalable and training-free paradigm.
column7: Wenqiu Tang(Nagoya University); Zhen Wan(National Institute of Informatics); Takahiro Komamizu(Nagoya University); Ichiro Ide(Nagoya University)

column4: EmoInstruct-TTS: Dual-Path Instruction-Guided Emotional Speech Synthesis
column6: Instruction-based controllable speech synthesis enables users to specify emotions through natural language. However, existing approaches often rely on coarse emotion labels and lack explicit modeling of fine-grained intensity. We propose EmoInstruct-TTS, a dual-path instruction-guided framework for emotional speech synthesis. We introduce Emotion2embed, a supervised semantic-acoustic emotion embedding covering 48 emotional states, including fine-grained categories and intensity levels. To infer embeddings from free-form instructions, we design an Instruction-Conditioned Emotion Flow Model (ICE-Flow) that generates acoustically grounded emotion representations. The inferred embeddings are integrated into an LLM-based synthesis pipeline to provide explicit emotional control while preserving semantic planning. Experiments show improved emotional controllability and speech naturalness over strong baselines.
column7: Minghui Wu(University of Science and Technology of China; iFLYTEK Research); Ganjun Liu(University of Science and Technology of China; iFLYTEK Research); Zikun Fang(University of Science and Technology of China); Ting Meng(iFLYTEK Research); Hongchuan Wu(iFLYTEK Research); Bingao Xu(iFLYTEK Research); Yonglong Cai(iFLYTEK Research); Jiasheng Chen(Huawei); Jun Du(University of Science and Technology of China)
