column4: ZeroSyl: Simple Zero-Resource Syllable Tokenization for Spoken Language Modeling
column6: Pure speech language models aim to learn language directly from raw audio without textual resources. A key challenge is that discrete tokens from self-supervised speech encoders result in excessively long sequences, motivating recent work on syllable-like units. However, methods like Sylber and SyllableLM rely on intricate multi-stage training pipelines. We propose ZeroSyl, a simple training-free method to extract syllable boundaries and embeddings directly from a frozen WavLM model. Using L2 norms of features in WavLM's intermediate layers, ZeroSyl achieves competitive syllable segmentation performance. The resulting segments are mean-pooled, discretized using K-means, and used to train a language model. ZeroSyl outperforms prior syllabic tokenizers across lexical, syntactic, and narrative benchmarks. Scaling experiments show that while finer-grained units are beneficial for lexical tasks, our discovered syllabic units exhibit better scaling behavior for syntactic modeling.
column7: Nicol Visser(Stellenbosch University); Simon Malan(Stellenbosch University); Danel Slabbert(Stellenbosch University); Herman Kamper(Stellenbosch University)

column4: Towards Data-free and Training-free Compression for Speech Foundation Models Using Parameter Clustering
column6: This paper presents a novel data-free and training-free compression approach for speech foundation models using channel-wise clustering via k-means. More fine-grained, mixed sparsity pruning by layer-level varying number of parameter clusters is also explored. Experiments conducted on the LibriSpeech dataset suggest that when operating with pruning sparsity of 50% on HuBERT-large, consistent WER reductions of 27.73%/18.61% absolute (34.37%/21.91% relative) over the magnitude-based pruning were obtained on the test-clean and test-other subsets before fine-tuning and 0.19%/0.79% absolute (3.36%/4.62% relative) after fine-tuning with only 3 epochs. Similar WER reductions of 2.86%/5.02% absolute (59.21%/55.29% relative) were observed against magnitude-based pruning on Whisper-large-v3 at 10% sparsity, all with no significant WER increase relative to the uncompressed baseline.
column7: Haoning Xu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Zhaoqing Li(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Huimeng Wang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Youjun Chen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Chengxi Deng(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Mengzhe Geng(National Research Council Canada); Xunying Liu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)

column4: OnDA: On-device Channel Pruning for Efficient Personalized Keyword Spotting
column6: Always-on keyword spotting (KWS) demands on-device adaptation to cope with user- and environment-specific distribution shifts under tight latency and energy budgets. This paper proposes, for the first time, coupling weight adaptation (i.e., on-device training) with architectural adaptation, in the form of online structured channel pruning, for personalized on-device KWS. Starting from a state-of-the-art self-learning personalized KWS pipeline, we compare data-agnostic and data-aware pruning criteria applied on in-field pseudo-labelled user data. On the HeySnips and HeySnapdragon datasets, we achieve up to 9.63× model-size compression with respect to unpruned baselines at iso-task performance, measured as the accuracy at 0.5 false alarms per hour. When deploying our adaptation pipeline on a Jetson Orin Nano embedded GPU, we achieve up to 1.52×/1.57× and 1.64×/1.77× latency and energy-consumption improvements during online training/inference compared to weights-only adaptation.
column7: Matteo Risso(Politecnico di Torino); Alessio Burello(Politecnico di Torino); Daniele Jahier Pagliari(Politecnico di Torino)

column4: Sub-Model Short-Term Memory Convolutions for Keyword Spotting Systems on Device
column6: Keyword Spotting (KWS) is becoming increasingly important as voice-controlled devices grow more widespread. While voice interaction with smartphones and smart TVs is already common, deploying KWS on heavily resource-constrained edge devices such as wearables remains challenging. These systems must meet high accuracy requirements while operating under strict constraints on computational power, memory footprint, and real-time latency. In this work, we present an application of the STMC (Short-Term Memory Convolutions) framework to adapt a modular CNN model for online, LSTM-like inference. Our approach reduces power consumption and redundant computations while maintaining the stability and simplicity of training CNNs. We achieve up to 82% and 46% MCPS reduction compared to equivalently frequent standard CNN execution and vanilla STMC, respectively. The best configuration achieves 93.8% accuracy on the 11-class Google Speech Commands task and 97.1% on the same task with zero-padded data.
column7: Paweł Warlewski(Samsung R&D Institute Poland); Artur Czeczko(Samsung R&D Institute Poland); Artur Szumaczuk(Samsung R&D Institute Poland); Grzegorz Stefański(Samsung AI Center Warsaw); Szymon Klimaszewski(Samsung R&D Institute Poland)

column4: An Efficient vLLM-Based Inference Pipeline for Unified Audio Understanding and Generation
column6: While Large Multimodal Models excel in comprehension, high-throughput inference engines lack native support for multimodal generation. This is severe in Speech Language Models, where generating multi-layered audio tokens via decoupled AR+NAR or synchronous Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) with delay-pattern interleaving conflicts with standard single-stream loops. We present a vLLM-based inference pipeline for unified speech understanding and generation. We extend autoregressive decoding to natively execute delay-pattern de-interleaving and coordinated multi-stream sampling, integrating an on-GPU acoustic decoder for end-to-end waveform synthesis. Crucially, we overcome the shared intuition that Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) halves throughput. By co-scheduling paired conditional and unconditional requests within a continuous batch, our CFG implementation sustains 80% of non-CFG throughput, absorbing dual-request and logit merging overheads. We open-source our framework1.
column7: Haoran Wang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Carnegie Mellon University); Jinchuan Tian(Carnegie Mellon University); Siddhant Arora(Carnegie Mellon University); Shinji Watanabe(Carnegie Mellon University)

column4: Audio-NSP: Data-Centric Semi-Autoregressive Generation for Large Audio-Language Models
column6: Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) suffer from high latency due to the autoregressive decoding of long audio sequences. We propose Audio-NSP (Next Sequence Prediction), a framework that activates semi-autoregressive parallel generation in pre-trained LALMs solely through data-centric Supervised Fine-Tuning. By restructuring training sequences with blockwise attention, Audio-NSP enables simultaneous multi-token prediction without architectural modifications. Crucially, applying this to audio reveals a decoding dilemma caused by the entropy gap between deterministic text and highly variable audio tokens. To resolve this, we introduce a modality-aware dynamic truncation strategy. It applies strict thresholds for text and lenient thresholds for audio, preventing degeneration into single-step decoding while preserving fidelity. Experiments show Audio-NSP achieves speedups of up to 3.42x while significantly outperforming Multi-Token Prediction baselines in quality preservation.
column7: Liang Cao(Tsinghua University); Xize Cheng(Zhejiang University); Dongjie Fu(Zhejiang University); Weihao Wu(Tsinghua University); Fuming You(Tencent); Zhiyong Wu(Tsinghua University); Haifeng Hu(Tencent)

column4: Improving streaming ASR with foundation models using emission policies
column6: Speech Foundation Models (SFMs) have achieved state-of-the-art results in offline ASR, yet their application in streaming environments remains limited due to the performance degradation caused by restricted context. In this work, we propose a model-agnostic, training-free streaming pipeline designed to wrap around ASR models in a "black box" manner. Our approach integrates three key components: a sliding window audio buffer for incremental data ingestion, token-level timestamp management to eliminate redundant output, and text-only emission policies to govern output timing. We systematically evaluate several emission policies, assessing their impact on the latency-accuracy trade-off across three English datasets. Results show that our pipeline enables timestamp-producing SFMs like Parakeet and Canary to achieve near-offline transcription quality in real-time environments without requiring access to internal model tensors.
column7: Gerard Mas Mollà(Universitat Politècnica de València); Albert Sanchis(Universitat Politècnica de València); Alfons Juan(Universitat Politècnica de València)

column4: AdaTS: Adaptive Token Sampling for Efficient Speech Language Models
column6: Speech Language Models (SLMs) have demonstrated strong speech understanding capabilities by incorporating speech tokens into large LMs (LLMs). However, most designs are i) token-intensive, as a large part of the LLM context is allotted to speech tokens, and ii) inefficient, as speech tokens are often temporally redundant, hindering SLMs’ capabilities to handle long-form tasks. To address both issues, we propose AdaTS, a dynamic sampling method that adaptively merges tokens where the speech signal is less informative. Our approach reduces the length of the speech signal seen by the LLM by 2× or more, with performance often better than standard downsampling across automatic speech recognition (ASR), speech question-answering (SQA), and speech translation (ST). Through an extensive empirical analysis, we show how SLMs using AdaTS retain strong speech understanding capabilities, while substantially reducing token redundancy and inference cost by 40%.
column7: Sonal Sannigrahi(Universidade de Lisboa; Instituto de Telecomunicações); Giuseppe Attanasio(Instituto de Telecomunicações); André F. T. Martins(Universidade de Lisboa; TransPerfect)

column4: Merging the Knowledge of LLMs for Automatic Speech Recognition
column6: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems, trained on paired speech-text data, have been improved by leveraging language models (LMs) trained on text-only data. LM fusion methods such as shallow fusion and density ratio are well-established methods that incorporate external LMs during ASR decoding. However, they incur additional computational costs due to LM inference, which is particularly problematic for recent larger LMs. In this study, we propose incorporating external LMs via model merging. This method integrates the LMs directly into the parameters of an LLM-based ASR model, requiring no additional computational cost at inference. We formulate domain extension and transfer via arithmetic operations on LoRA parameters. Experimental evaluations were conducted for the domain adaptation of LLM-based ASR trained on CSJ and LibriSpeech. We show that our LM merging consistently improved the ASR performance in the target domains, without degrading inference speed or memory footprint.
column7: Hayato Futami(Kyoto University); Tatsuya Kawahara(Kyoto University)

column4: Scaling few-shot spoken word classification with generative meta-continual learning
column6: Few-shot spoken word classification has largely been developed for applications where a small number of classes is considered, and so the potential of larger-scale few-shot spoken word classification remains untapped. This paper investigates the potential of a spoken word classifier to sequentially learn to distinguish between 1 000 classes when it is given only five shots per class. We demonstrate that this scaling capability exists by training a model using the Generative Meta-Continual Learning (GeMCL) algorithm and comparing it to repeatedly trained or finetuned baselines. We find that GeMCL produces exceptionally stable performance, and although it does not always outperform a repeatedly fully-finetuned HuBERT model nor a frozen HuBERT model with a repeatedly trained classifier head, it produces comparable performance to the latter while adapting 2 000 times faster, having been trained on less than half of the data for two orders of magnitude less time.
column7: Louise Beyers(Bytefuse); Batsirayi Mupamhi Ziki(Bytefuse); Ruan van der Merwe(Bytefuse)

column1: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Area 12 - Poster 2 - Audio Language Models: Reasoning, Reliability, and Multimodal Understanding

column4: Hearing the Order: Investigating Position Bias in Large Audio-Language Models
column6: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are often used in tasks that involve reasoning over ordered options. An open question is whether their predictions are influenced by the order of answer choices, which would indicate a form of position bias and undermine their reliability. In this paper, we identify and analyze this problem in LALMs. We demonstrate that no model is immune to this bias through extensive experiments on six LALMs across three widely used benchmarks and their spoken counterparts. Shuffling the order of answer options can cause performance fluctuations of up to 24% and even change model rankings, raising concerns about the reliability of current evaluation practices. We also study permutation-based strategies and show that they can mitigate bias in most cases. Our work represents the first systematic investigation of this issue in LALMs, and we hope it raises awareness and motivates further research in this direction.
column7: Yu-Xiang Lin(National Taiwan University); Chen-An Li(National Taiwan University); Sheng-Lun Wei(National Taiwan University); Po-Chun Chen(National Taiwan University); Hsin-Hsi Chen(National Taiwan University; NTU AI Research Center (AINTU)); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University; NTU Artificial Intelligence Center of Research Excellence (NTU AI-CoRE))

column4: Nudging Hidden States: Training-Free Model Steering for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Audio-Language Models
column6: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting has been extended to large audio-language models (LALMs) to elicit reasoning, yet enhancing its effectiveness without training remains challenging. We study inference-time model steering as a training-free approach to improve LALM reasoning. We introduce three strategies using diverse information sources and evaluate them across four LALMs and four benchmarks. Results show general accuracy gains up to 4.4% over CoT prompting. Notably, we identify a cross-modal transfer where steering vectors derived from few text samples effectively guide speech-based reasoning, demonstrating high data efficiency. We also examine hyperparameter sensitivity to understand the robustness of these approaches. Our findings position model steering as a practical direction for strengthening LALM reasoning.
column7: Lok-Lam Ieong(National Taiwan University); Chia-Chien Chen(National Taiwan University); Chih-Kai Yang(National Taiwan University); Yu-Han Huang(National Taiwan University); An-Yu Cheng(National Taiwan University); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University)

column4: MUGEN: Evaluating and Improving Multi-audio Understanding of Large Audio-Language Models
column6: While multi-audio understanding is critical for large audio-language models (LALMs), it remains underexplored. We introduce MUGEN, a comprehensive benchmark evaluating this capability across speech, general audio, and music. Our experiments reveal consistent weaknesses in multi-audio settings, and performance degrades sharply as the number of concurrent audio inputs increases, identifying input scaling as a fundamental bottleneck. We further investigate training-free strategies and observe that Audio-Permutational Self-Consistency, which diversifies the order of audio candidates, helps models form more robust aggregated predictions, yielding up to 6.28% accuracy gains. Combining this permutation strategy with Chain-of-Thought further improves performance to 6.74%. These results expose blind spots in current LALMs and provide a foundation for evaluating complex auditory comprehension.
column7: Chih-Kai Yang(National Taiwan University); Yun-Shao Tsai(National Taiwan University); Yu-Kai Guo(National Taiwan University); Ping-Le Tsai(National Taiwan University); Yen-Ting Piao(National Taiwan University); Hung-Wei Chen(National Taiwan University); Ting-Lin Hsiao(National Taiwan University); Yun-Man Hsu(National Taiwan University); Ke-Han Lu(National Taiwan University); Hung-yi Lee(NTU AI-CoRE)

column4: From Noisy Speech to Accurate APIs: LLM-driven Embedding Steering for Resilient Tool Retrieval
column6: Embedding-based tool retrieval is challenging and often fails in real deployments because API descriptors are inconsistent to what the embedding models are originally trained with and often require fine-tuning or retraining from scratch. The challenge is further amplified in speech driven queries, where background noise can degrade automatic speech recognition (ASR) outputs. We present a training free offline method that leverages an LLM to generate diverse, user-style synthetic queries, tasks, and scenarios for each tool, and then average (or steer) the embeddings to form a semantically enriched tool representation. To evaluate the robustness, we simulate realistic speech conditions-including reverberation and additive noise prior to ASR- and present experiments using multiple embedding models and tool datasets. Our results show that the proposed method provides a simple yet effective way to enhance tool retrieval reliability without requiring any model retraining.
column7: Catalin Zorilă(Toshiba Europe Ltd); Qingxiuxiong Dong(Toshiba Corporation); Rama Doddipatla(Toshiba Europe Ltd)

column4: A Reranker for Orchestrating Heterogeneous Speech and Text Retrievers
column6: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems have attracted significant interest for their ability to mitigate hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs). Although knowledge databases for RAG are increasingly diversifying to include various modalities such as speech and text, research on handling such multi-modal database scenarios remains limited. In this paper, we propose STEREO (Speech and Text Reranking Orchestrator), a reranker based on speech and text retrievers that aggregates disparate modality databases. To address the lack of specialized training data, we first curate a dataset comprising queries, mixed-modality evidence, and their corresponding relevance ranks. We then train the reranker and evaluate its effectiveness in both single-modality and mixed-modality scenarios. Our results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm excels at selecting the most relevant evidence, thereby significantly improving downstream question-answering performance.
column7: Inho Kim(Korea Institute of Energy Technology); Sumyeong Ahn(Korea Institute of Energy Technology)

column4: Do What I Say: A Spoken Prompt Dataset for Instruction-Following
column6: Speech Large Language Models (SLLMs) have rapidly expanded, supporting a wide range of tasks. These models are typically evaluated using text prompts, which may not reflect real-world scenarios where users interact with speech. To address this gap, we introduce DoWhatISay (DOWIS), a multilingual dataset of human-recorded spoken and written prompts designed to pair with any existing benchmark for realistic evaluation of SLLMs under spoken instruction conditions. Spanning 9 tasks and 11 languages, it provides 10 prompt variants per task-language pair, across five styles. Using DOWIS, we benchmark state-of-the-art SLLMs, analyzing the interplay between prompt modality, style, language, and task type. Results show that text prompts consistently outperform spoken prompts, particularly for low-resource and cross-lingual settings. Only for tasks with speech output, spoken prompts do close the gap, highlighting the need for speech-based prompting in SLLM evaluation.
column7: Maike Züfle(Karlsruhe Institute of Technology); Sara Papi(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Fabian Retkowski(Karlsruhe Institute of Technology); Szymon Mazurek(ACC Cyfronet AGH, AGH University of Krakow); Marek Kasztelnik(ACC Cyfronet AGH); Alexander Waibel(Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Carnegie Mellon University); Luisa Bentivogli(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Jan Niehues(Karlsruhe Institute of Technology)

column4: All That Glitters Is Not Audio: Rethinking Text Priors and Audio Reliance in Audio-Language Evaluation
column6: Large Audio-Language Models show consistent performance gains across speech and audio benchmarks, yet high scores may not reflect true auditory perception. If a model can answer questions without processing the acoustic signal, the benchmark fails as a measure of auditory understanding. We present a diagnostic framework using two axes: text prior, which measures answerability from text and general knowledge alone, and audio reliance, which assesses actual dependency on the acoustic signal. Evaluating eight LALMs across three benchmarks, we find that models retain 60-72% of their full-audio scores even without any audio input. Moreover, among items that require audio, only 3.0-4.2% need the complete audio clip; the majority can be resolved using localized fragments. These findings challenge the assumption that benchmark performance equals robust audio understanding, and we conclude with practical guidelines for improving evaluation reliability and benchmark design.
column7: Leonardo Haw-Yang Foo(National Taiwan University); Chih-Kai Yang(National Taiwan University); Chen-An Li(National Taiwan University); Ke-Han Lu(National Taiwan University); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University)

column4: ADALA: A Wake-up Word Detection Framework Based on Adaptive Semi-supervised learning and Large Language Model
column6: The efficacy of Wake-up Word (WUW) detection is often constrained by poor generalization to unseen negative samples, exacerbating the trade-off between wake-up rate and false activation rate. To address this limitation, we introduce ADALA, a novel WUW detection framework that integrates ADAptive semi-supervised learning with a LArge language model. Specifically, a Large Language Model (LLM) is fine-tuned via Reinforcement Learning (RL) to dynamically generate new and effective hard-negative samples. These synthetically generated negatives are subsequently combined with real-world data within a semi-supervised learning scheme to continuously enhance the WUW model. Experimental results validate our approach, demonstrating that ADALA achieves a superior performance equilibrium, significantly reducing the false activation rate (3.19%) on datasets of phonetically similar words while preserving a high wake-up rate (90.43%).
column7: Nianhang Tang(HUST; National Engineering Research Center of Digital Home Networking); Chaoyi Sun(HUST); Chao Cai(HUST)

column4: Said Aloud, Read Different: Cross-Modal Instability in Multimodal Models
column6: Multimodal foundation models are increasingly used in speech-first assistants that must interpret spoken queries and produce visually grounded decisions. Yet it remains unclear whether semantically equivalent queries yield consistent judgments across modality (text vs. speech) and language (English vs. Arabic). We introduce a speech-augmented visually grounded contrastive triplet benchmark spanning 10,150 culturally grounded images from 18 MENA countries, where each image is paired with one supported statement and two plausible but unsupported alternatives. We define contrastive instability as the conditional rate at which a model fails to resolve all statements within a triplet, isolating fragmented reasoning from complete failure. Evaluating recent multimodal models under text and speech in English and Arabic, we find that modality and language shifts introduce substantial triplet-level inconsistencies that are not fully captured by aggregate accuracy, with speech amplifying partial failures. We make the benchmark publicly available to the community.
column7: Basel Mousi(HBKU); Fahim Dalvi(HBKU); Shammur Absar Chowdhury(HBKU); Firoj Alam(HBKU); Nadir Durrani(HBKU)

column4: When Does Quality-Aware Multimodal Fusion Matter? A Leakage-Safe Diagnostic for Decision-Level Dependence
column6: Many multimodal systems estimate the reliability of each modality and weight their contributions to the final prediction. However, it remains unclear whether these scores influence model decisions or merely correlate with performance. We propose a simple diagnostic to test whether reliability information is used during inference. After training, the model and inputs are fixed while reliability scores are permuted across test examples. If predictions depend on these scores, performance should degrade. Experiments on StressID for stress recognition and CMU-MOSEI for sentiment analysis show that permuting reliability scores leaves performance unchanged despite substantial potential gains from selecting the best modality per example. In positive controls where reliability signals identify the correct modality, the same frozen fusion rules yield significant improvements, indicating that reliability signals influence fused decisions only when they reliably predict unimodal correctness.
column7: Jaden Moon(Dartmouth College); Arvind Pillai(Dartmouth College); Andrew Campbell(Dartmouth College)

column4: Generating Synthetic Doctor-Patient Conversations for Long-form Audio Summarization
column6: Long-context audio reasoning is underserved in both training data and evaluation. Existing benchmarks target short-context tasks, and the open-ended generation tasks most relevant to long-context reasoning pose well-known challenges for automatic evaluation. We propose a synthetic data generation pipeline designed to serve both as a training resource and as a controlled evaluation environment, and instantiate it for first-visit doctor-patient conversations with SOAP note generation as the task. The pipeline has three stages—persona-driven dialogue generation, multi-speaker audio synthesis with overlap/pause modeling, room acoustics, and sound events, and LLM-based reference SOAP note production—built entirely on open-weight models. We release 8,800 synthetic conversations with 1.3k hours of corresponding audio and reference notes. Evaluating current open-weight systems, we find that cascaded approaches still substantially outperform end-to-end models.
column7: Yanis Labrak(Idiap Research Institute); David Grünert(University of Zurich); Severin Baroudi(Idiap Research Institute; Université de Toulon, Aix Marseille Univ); Jiyun Chun(The Ohio State University); Pawel Cyrta(Stenograf); Sergio Burdisso(Idiap Research Institute); Ahmed Hassoon(Johns Hopkins University); David Liu(Colorado School of Mines); Adam Rothschild(Allegheny Health Network); Reed Van Deusen(University of Pittsburgh Medical Center); Petr Motlicek(Idiap Research Institute); Andrew Perrault(The Ohio State University); Ricard Marxer(Université de Toulon, Aix Marseille Univ; ILLS, CNRS); Thomas Schaaf(Solventum; Carnegie Mellon University)

column4: Voice of India: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Real-World Speech Recognition in India
column6: Existing Indic ASR benchmarks often use scripted, clean speech and leaderboard driven evaluation that encourages dataset specific overfitting. In addition, strict single reference WER penalizes natural spelling variation in Indian languages, including non standardized spellings of code-mixed English origin words. To address these limitations, we introduce Voice of India, a closed source benchmark built from unscripted telephonic conversations covering 15 major Indian languages across 139 regional clusters. The dataset contains 306230 utterances, totaling 536 hours of speech from 36691 speakers with transcripts accounting for spelling variations. We also analyze performance geographically at the district level, revealing disparities. Finally, we provide detailed analysis across factors such as audio quality, speaking rate, gender, and device type, highlighting where current ASR systems struggle and offering insights for improving real world Indic ASR systems.
column7: Kaushal Bhogale(IIT Madras); Manas Dhir(Josh Talks); Amritansh Walecha(Josh Talks); Manmeet Kaur(Josh Talks); Vanshika Chhabra(Josh Talks); Aaditya Pareek(Josh Talks); Hanuman Sidh(Josh Talks); Sagar Jain(Josh Talks); Bhaskar Singh(Josh Talks); Utkarsh Singh(Josh Talks); Tahir Javed(IIT Madras); Shobhit Banga(Josh Talks); Mitesh M. Khapra(IIT Madras)

column4: CalliOpeNLP: A Standalone Digital Health Voice Data Collection Research Tool
column6: Obstacles reported in manual health voice data collections include addressing compliance, annotation standards (e.g., labels, segmentation, transcription), security, interoperability (i.e., streamlined transfer), and in-person interaction bias. Automation is a logistical solution to mitigate these manual voice collection challenges. This paper introduces CalliOpeNLP, a new python-based open-source automated tool designed to support researchers working on clinical voice health data biobanks. While private commercial fee-based automated voice data collection software exist, CalliOpeNLP offers a free, standalone automated option which avoids unsecure data transfer. CalliOpeNLP includes computer-generated spoken- text instructions for 18 clinically validated voice tasks. CalliOpeNLP records, labels, and tracks patients' compliance using low latency voice-to-text transcript analytics. This tool provides a new practical application enhancing automated voice data collection capabilities.
column7: Brian Stasak(The University of Sydney); Rebecca Li(The University of Sydney); Antonia Chacon(The University of Sydney); Rebecca Black(The University of Sydney); Cate Madill(The University of Sydney)

column4: Pronunciation and Intonation Structured Markup (PRISM): A Dataset for Australian English Pronunciation Feedback
column6: While automated speech technologies for pronunciation learning are increasingly used, most tools offer limited feedback and lack scientific grounding. Phonetic variability in ESL speech and world Englishes is often ignored. We developed a curated dataset to support personalised feedback for Australian English pronunciation. Word-level forced alignment and manual annotation were applied to a demographically stratified subset of the CommonVoice corpus. Linguistically informed coding classes, such as vowels and tune types, were used to label “errors” (pronunciation differences from AusEng). This paper outlines the scientifically grounded annotation framework, presenting preliminary findings on error patterns across three accent groups: Hong Kong, South Asia, Indonesia. We also address challenges in using open data, including demographic imbalance. This work highlights collaboration between phonetics and computer science and provides an open-access dataset with a transparent framework.
column7: Olga Maxwell(University of Melbourne); Uy Thinh Quang(University of Melbourne); Debbie Loakes(University of Melbourne); Adele Gregory(University of Melbourne); Robert Turnbull(University of Melbourne)

column4: Collection and Curation of a Spontaneous Multilingual Speech Corpus for Low-Resource Himalayan Languages
column6: Advancing speech technology for underrepresented languages requires carefully collected and well-documented data resources. In this work, we introduce a spontaneous multilingual speech corpus consisting of 320 native speakers of Bodo, Dzongkha, Gorkhali (Nepali), and Sherpa. These languages span the Tibeto-Burman and Indo-Aryan families and include both tonal and non-tonal systems. The corpus contains spontaneous speech recorded under consistent recording and curation protocols. We describe the participant selection process, recording design, and metadata organization used to maintain consistency across languages. Acoustic analysis highlights systematic differences in pitch, energy, and temporal dynamics among the languages. In addition, language identification experiments show that these distinctions remain learnable, achieving up to 92.95% accuracy and demonstrating the usefulness of the corpus for computational documentation and modeling of linguistically diverse speech communities.
column7: Abhijit Sinha(National Institute of Technology); Subham Kutum(National Institute of Technology); Udara Laxman Kumar(National Institute of Technology); Paban Sapkota(National Institute of Technology); Hemant Kumar Kathania(National Institute of Technology)

column4: Spontaneous Dialect-Aware Speech Corpus for Low-Resource Dakhini, A Southern Indo-Aryan Language: Methods, Challenges, and Insights
column6: Dakhini, a contact variety spoken in the Deccan region of India, remains severely underrepresented in curated speech resources despite widespread conversational use. This work presents a data-centric study aimed at informing systematic Dakhini speech corpus development. Using telephonic conversational recordings, we examine factors relevant to corpus development, including context-driven code-switching and speaker variation across gender and educational backgrounds. Phonological reductions, auxiliary omission, and participial variation are observed in spontaneous speech, while formal contexts trigger shifts toward standardized Hindi/Urdu forms. These patterns highlight the importance of speaker stratification and dialect-aware annotation when curating low-resource conversational datasets. Our findings provide guidelines for developing Dakhini speech corpora and lay groundwork for dialect-sensitive ASR and conversational modeling in under documented language varieties.
column7: Anindita Mondal(IIIT Hyderabad); Priyanka Kommagouni(Independent Researcher)

column4: Toward Multimodal Industrial Fault Analysis: A Single-Speed Chain Conveyor Dataset with Audio and Vibration Signals
column6: We introduce a multimodal industrial fault analysis dataset collected from a single-speed chain conveyor (SSCC) system, targeting system-level fault detection in production lines. The dataset consists of multimodal signals, including three audio and four vibration channels. It covers normal operation and four representative fault types under multiple speeds, loads, and both clean and realistic factory-noise conditions reproduced on-site. It is explicitly designed to support channel-wise analysis and multimodal fusion research. We establish standardized evaluation protocols for unsupervised fault detection with normal-only training and supervised fault classification with balanced dataset splits across different operating conditions and fault types. A unified channel-wise kNN baseline is provided to enable fair comparison of representation quality without task-specific training. The dataset offers a practical and extensible benchmark for robust multimodal industrial fault analysis.
column7: Zhang Chen(Duke Kunshan University); Yucong Zhang(Wuhan University; The Chinese University of Hong Kong (Shenzhen)); Xiaoxiao Miao(Duke Kunshan University); Ming Li(The Chinese University of Hong Kong (Shenzhen); Wuhan University)

column4: Improving multichannel speech enhancement through accurate room-acoustic simulations
column6: Room-acoustic simulations are widely used to augment training data for deep-learning-based speech enhancement. While most pipelines rely on simplified geometrical acoustics, wave-based approaches offer greater physical accuracy. In this work, we examine how simulation fidelity affects multichannel speech enhancement performance. To this end, we train SpatialNet on datasets augmented with different room-acoustic simulation methods and evaluate the resulting models on measured data. We compare lower-fidelity datasets based on geometrical acoustics with a high-fidelity dataset using advanced acoustic modelling and a hybrid combination of wave-based and geometrical acoustics simulations. Training on the high-fidelity dataset results in an up to 38% relative reduction in median word error rate compared to the lower-fidelity alternatives. These results show that augmentation with high-fidelity room-acoustic simulations directly translates into improved multichannel speech enhancement performance.
column7: Georg Götz(Treble Technologies); Alessia Milo(Treble Technologies); Steinar Guðjónsson(Treble Technologies); Daniel Gert Nielsen(Treble Technologies); Jesper Pedersen(Treble Technologies); Finnur Pind(Treble Technologies)

column4: Data Filtering Trade-offs in Self-Supervised Speech Representation Learning: A Study on Unconstrained Broadcast Audio
column6: When processing raw broadcast audio for self-supervised learning (SSL) pretraining, initial filtering decisions include whether to retain only speech and restrict to the target language. While common in prior work, these choices rely on heuristics without systematic evaluation. We present a controlled comparison of 4 filtering strategies of increasing selectivity on Finnish broadcast data: no filtering, energy-based voice activity detection (VAD), neural VAD, and neural VAD with language identification (LID). Energy-based VAD consistently degrades representation quality compared to no filtering. Neural VAD substantially improves ASR, especially when combined with LID (up to 12.7% absolute WER reduction using 42% of the data), but increasingly selective filtering degrades general audio understanding by up to 9 percentage points. We show that no single strategy is universally optimal and quantify trade-offs between preprocessing cost, downstream accuracy, and generalizability.
column7: Yaroslav Getman(Aalto University); Tamás Grósz(Walton Institute); Tommi Lehtonen(Finnish Arts and Culture Agency); Mikko Kurimo(Aalto University)

column4: Collecting Prosody in the Wild: A Content-Controlled, Privacy-First Smartphone Protocol and Empirical Evaluation
column6: Collecting everyday speech data for prosodic analysis is challenging due to the confounding of prosody and semantics, privacy constraints, and participant compliance. We introduce and empirically evaluate a content-controlled, privacy-first smartphone protocol that uses scripted read-aloud sentences to standardize lexical content (including prompt valence) while capturing naturalistic variation in prosodic delivery. The protocol performs on-device prosodic feature extraction, deletes raw audio immediately, and transmits only derived features for analysis. We deployed the protocol in a large study (N = 560; 9,877 recordings), evaluated compliance and data quality, and conducted diagnostic prediction tasks on the extracted features, predicting self-reported speaker sex and momentary affective states (valence, arousal). We discuss implications and directions for advancing and deploying the protocol.
column7: Timo K. Koch(University of St. Gallen; LMU Munich); Florian Bemmann(LMU Munich; University of Mannheim); Ramona Schoedel(LMU Munich; University of Psychology); Markus Buehner(LMU Munich); Clemens Stachl(University of St. Gallen)

column4: From Game-Based Annotation to Representation Probing: Cross-Validated Prosodic Speech and Privacy Implications
column6: Building upon a prosodic speech corpus collected through a web-based interactive game, this paper examines its value for analyzing biometric speaker attributes, such as gender and age, and for LLM-level representation analysis. The corpus was designed so that players serve as both performers and annotators, creating a self-validating mechanism in which each utterance is evaluated through independent human judgments. This design enables systematic assessment of annotation consistency and label robustness. We evaluate the corpus through emotion recognition and probing of LLM-aligned speech representations. Results show that prosodic embeddings encode stable affective patterns while emotional attributes remain identifiable in intermediate representations, raising privacy considerations.
column7: Sia Vosh Sepanta(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Roberto Zamparelli(Cimec University of Trento); Alessio Brutti(Fondazione Bruno Kessler)

column4: Automatic Curation of Large-Scale, High-Quality, Multi-Category Music Source Separation Dataset
column6: The scale, audio quality, and granularity of instrument categories in datasets are critical factors limiting the performance of music source separation. Web crawling provides large-scale data but often introduces label noise and mismatches. We propose an automated method for constructing large-scale, high-quality, multi-category music source separation datasets. The approach comprises 4 steps: (1) designing a fine-grained 7-category musical instrument taxonomy; (2) training instrument-specific single-source detectors to identify segments containing only the target instrument; (3) retrieving plenty of raw audio data from public platforms using multilingual keywords; and (4) automatically cleaning the raw data with the detectors to produce a high-quality dataset. Our detector achieves 97.14% average accuracy across seven categories. Training SOTA models with the cleaned data yields an average SDR improvement of 1.16,dB on standard benchmarks, confirming the dataset's effectiveness.
column7: Yu Ji(Xiaomi Inc.); Shuo Yang(Xiaomi Inc.); Yuetonghui Xu(Central Conservatory of Music); Mengmei Liu(Xiaomi Inc.); Qiang Ji(Xiaomi Inc.); zerui Han(Xiaomi Inc.)

column4: Leveraging Discriminative Capabilities of Self-Supervised Neural Audio Fingerprinting for Efficient Speech Data Annotation
column6: Self-supervised neural audio fingerprinting methods have achieved great results in music retrieval systems. We show how such methods can be applied to efficiently organize speech data annotation tasks. First, they can be used to remove duplicates, which we successfully apply to industry-specific data, resulting in halving the number of data samples that need to be annotated. Second, we show that despite being trained only on music, the embeddings produced by neural fingerprinting methods are better at capturing acoustical properties of speech than speech-specific models, such as WavLM. We leverage this property of the embeddings and show how to subsample large datasets while preserving dataset diversity and avoiding biases towards overrepresented data points, using a technique known as farthest point sampling. This allows annotators to focus their already limited and valuable time on diverse data samples while avoiding duplicate and similar samples.
column7: Kemal Altwlkany(Infobip; University of Sarajevo); Elmedin Selmanovic(University of Sarajevo)

column4: Cognitive-Heuristic Guided Multimodal Data Augmentation for Alzheimer’s Disease Detection Using LLM and TTS
column6: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, and early detection is critical for intervention. Speech offers a non-invasive, accessible biomarker for AD detection, but suffers from severe data scarcity. Existing augmentation methods in text or speech enrich training data but often neglect cognitively relevant patterns. We propose a cognitive-heuristic guided multimodal generative augmentation frame work that explicitly incorporates AD-related cognitive declines. Our method integrates retrieval-augmented generation with large language models for cognitively informed text generation, and an attribute-guided text-to-speech system to reproduce AD-related acoustic features. This design captures both linguistic and acoustic alterations associated with cognitive decline. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that our augmented data consistently enhances performance, highlighting the efficacy of cognition-driven multimodal synthesis for speech-based AD detection.
column7: Yu Jiang(Tianjin University); Cheng Gong(TeleAI); Bin Wen(Tianjin University); Ruihao Jing(TeleAI); Tianrui Wang(Tianjin University); Shansong Liu(TeleAI); Boyu Zhu(TeleAI); Yuheng Lu(Tianjin University); Xuanchen Li(Tianjin University); Xiao Wei(Tianjin University); Chunyu Qiang(Tianjin University); Xiao-Lei Zhang(TeleAI); Longbiao Wang(Tianjin University); Jianwu Dang(Tianjin University)

column1: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 09:00-11:00 - Show And Tell 3 - Speech and Language Processing for Health and Accessibility

column4: Sound Reactor Mission: Gamified Misophonia Assessment to Bridge the Gap in Audiology and Hearing Care
column6: Misophonia causes strong emotional and physiological reactions to specific everyday sounds, yet audiology lacks a standardised, scalable assessment pathway. Sound Reactor Mission (SRM) is a browser-based, gamified speech-in-noise assessment requiring only headphones. In a six-minute space mission, participants complete adaptive Speech Reception Threshold estimation, select a personally annoying masker, compare speech intelligibility across three masker conditions, and complete an Acceptable Noise Level measure. Pilot data (N = 14; 100% completion; mean time = 6.5 min) showed lower intelligibility for the selected annoying sound (59.2%) than for synthetic (71.7%) and standard masking noise (86.3%). The live Interspeech demonstration lets attendees complete the mission and compare their results with other delegates.
column7: Jorge Mejia(National Acoustic Laboratories); Jan-Willem Wasmann(Radboud University Medical Center); Jane Gregory(University of Oxford)

column4: An Immersive VR System for Experiencing Spatial Speech-in-Noise Challenges in Clinical Audiology
column6: Clinical hearing test results can be difficult for patients and families to connect with real-world listening difficulties, making it harder to explain why everyday communication is challenging and how hearing devices and strategies can help. This paper presents a VR-based immersive listening demonstration system on Apple Vision Pro that allows patients to experience common listening challenges directly. The system places users in one of three 3D environments (café, train station, and living room) with a target speaker, competing talkers, and spatially rendered environmental noise. Users listen to short dialogues and answer comprehension questions, while clinicians configure difficulty through presets that vary signal-to-noise ratio, source count, and spatial separation. The system is designed as a portable clinical demonstration tool, not a diagnostic assessment.
column7: Nicky Chong-White(National Acoustic Laboratories); Thomas Ho(National Acoustic Laboratories)

column4: ELSI: An Interface for Standardizing Child-Centered Datasets, Applying Machine Learning Models, and Extracting Metrics
column6: The ExELang Legacy Support Interface (ELSI) is an open-source interface designed to support researchers studying language acquisition in diverse communities around the world. ELSI enables users, regardless of technical expertise, to standardize child-centered datasets, apply machine learning models trained on child-centered audio (e.g., speaker diarization, phoneme counts), and extract key metrics such as child vocalization count, adult vocalization count, and conversational turns. During the Show and Tell, we will demonstrate how to use the interface by walking through dataset standardization, model execution, and metric extraction. We expect ELSI to be particularly valuable for researchers who maintain large child-centered audio datasets and wish to leverage open-source machine learning tools without requiring advanced programming skills.
column7: Kaveri K. Sheth(Ecole Normale Supérieure); Loann Peurey(Ecole Normale Supérieure); Sho Tsuji(Ecole Normale Supérieure); Alejandrina Cristia(Ecole Normale Supérieure)

column4: Demonstration of Embedded Systems for Clinical Speech Analysis
column6: Interest in applying computational speech analysis tools for clinical purposes has grown alongside improvements in software. However, many existing tools rely on specialized hardware uncommon in routine clinical settings, separating data collection, analysis, and reporting in both time and space. Embedded systems can integrate sensors, graphics processing units, and displays into a single bedside platform, enabling speech analysis at the point of care. This approach could provide timely results that can be incorporated into urgent clinical decision-making. Here, we demonstrate the novel use of an embedded system to execute the core components of a computational speech analysis pipeline currently used to evaluate patients with psychiatric disorders, enabling end-to-end processing directly at the bed-side.
column7: Jeremiah B Joyce(Mayo Clinic); Erik Clemens(Mayo Clinic); Sanjeev Mishra(Mayo Clinic); Josh Boesche(Mayo Clinic); David Johnson(Mayo Clinic); Marie Reyes(Mayo Clinic)

column4: The TinyExplorer Ecosystem: Open tools for studying infants’ auditory and visual experiences
column6: Studying young children’s everyday learning environments remains difficult because existing methods often fail to capture the dynamic, multimodal, and socially embedded nature of children’s experiences in naturalistic settings. Recent advances in technology, including more user-friendly hardware and AI-powered software, are creating new opportunities to study young children’s everyday auditory and visual experiences in rich and scalable ways by utilising head-mounted cameras (headcams). However, the widespread use of headcams in research is still limited by two major barriers: (a) developing safe, lightweight, child-friendly recording systems, and (b) the time-intensive process of manual audio and video annotation. The TinyExplorer Ecosystem is an open-source platform designed to address these challenges by combining wearable egocentric recording hardware (TinyExplorer Gear) with locally run AI-powered annotation tools (TinyExplorer Detection App). The TinyExplorer Detection App currently integrates automated face detection and is being expanded to include hand detection, hand-object interaction annotation, and audio processing. Together, these tools support scalable, reproducible research on children’s real-world learning environments.
column7: Cátia M Oliveira(Cardiff University); Teodor Y. Nikolov(Cardiff University); Tamas Foldes(University of Surrey); Charlotte Bocchetta(Cardiff University); Hana D'Souza(Cardiff University)

column4: Head-Worn Dipole Microphone Array-based Speech Enhancement System for Single-Sided Deafness
column6: People with single-sided deafness (SSD) struggle to hear on their deaf side. However, conventional hearing aids typically have forward directionality to enhance speech from the front of the listener, making them poorly suited to SSD users, who need improved intelligibility of lateral speech. This gap motivates dedicated hardware and signal processing for hearing aids targeting the lateral direction. In this work, we construct a MEMS dipole microphone array with a side-directed beam to enhance sounds arriving laterally. We measured the array's transfer functions on a dummy head and simulated a noisy scenario. Beamforming with an array of two dipole and one omnidirectional microphones improved SDR by 0.78 dB and ESTOI by 0.04 for lateral speech, compared to a 3-channel omnidirectional array colocated. Our show-and-tell features audio demos and live real-time beamforming to show the potential of dipole microphones for this application and raise awareness of SSD in the community.
column7: Ken Takaki(The University of Tokyo); Kouei Yamaoka(The University of Tokyo); Yoshihiro Kawahara(The University of Tokyo)

column4: BetterSpeak: An Atypical Speech to Typical Speech Platform for Dysarthric Speakers
column6: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems offer immense potential for individuals with dysarthria, yet traditional models fail severely due to high inter- and intra-speaker variability and data scarcity. To address this, we present BetterSpeak, a mobile ASR platform powered by our novel Two-Phase Personalized Conformer Adaptation Pipeline. The pipeline employs a resource-efficient transfer learning strategy, first adapting a robust Conformer model to the general dysarthric vocabulary, and then rapidly personalizing its acoustic encoder using limited, publicly available dysarthric speech samples. We detail the platform's functionalities and demonstrate how this personalized, data-efficient approach is crucial for providing children with an accessible, high-accuracy medium for communication, thereby fostering a better social and digital life.
column7: Seyed Reza Shahamiri(University of Auckland); Zihan Zhong(University of Auckland); Qianli Wang(University of Auckland); Satwinder Singh(University of Auckland)

column4: ClinAware: Speech Enhancement Needs Clinical Awareness
column6: Speech enhancement is widely used to improve speech intelligibility in noisy conditions, while speech is increasingly investigated as a non-invasive modality for neurological applications. In telehealth and home-based assessments, speech enhancement is used as a preprocessing step. Its effects on clinically relevant speech biomarkers remain poorly understood. This demonstration presents an interactive system that allows users to explore the effect of speech enhancement methods on neurological voice biomarkers and a downstream risk indicator. Simulating a noisy environment or using noisy speech input, multiple enhancement methods are compared through spectrogram visualizations, quantitative biomarker changes, and corresponding shifts in a lightweight, interpretable risk score. The demo highlights that speech intelligibility improvement does not necessarily imply biomarker preservation, and it motivates a clinically informed design for future enhancements.
column7: Pramod H. Kachare(Infosys Limited); Chetana Amancharla(Infosys Limited)

AI in Communication Sciences: Necessity, Opportunity or Threat?
column5: John H. L. Hansen, Emma Power, Visar Berisha, Karen Hirschausen, Brendan Lonergan, Nicky Chong-White (Facilitator)
column6: Bringing together experts from research and clinical practice, this session will put the opportunities, risks and realities of AI in speech pathology and audiology up for debate. From its potential to improve care and accessibility to the ethical, professional and implementation challenges it presents, expect differing perspectives, challenging questions and a lively debate on what AI should, and should not, mean for the future of the field.
column8:

With more than 975 scientific publications and 14 textbooks, Professor Hansen has made significant contributions to speech technology, machine learning and human communication. Berisha’s work has been featured by The New York Times, ESPN, NPR, The Wall Street Journal, and international media. He was the 2023-2024 ISCA Distinguished Lecturer.

She has a strong interest in clinical excellence, professional development and translating evidence-based practice into meaningful, client-centred care.


Brendan Lonergan is the President of Hearing Matters Australia Inc., He has been wearing hearing aids since 2009 and has been totally deaf in his right ear since 2010 he also has moderate to moderately severe hearing loss in his Left ear and currently uses a Resound Vivia 9 Bi Cros hearing aid system and remote mic technology. column4: Relating the Neural Representations of Vocalized, Mimed, and Imagined Speech
column6: We investigated the relationship among neural representations of vocalized, mimed, and imagined speech recorded using publicly available stereotactic EEG recordings. Most prior studies have focused on decoding speech responses within each condition separately. Here, instead, we explore how responses across conditions relate by training linear spectrogram reconstruction models for each condition and evaluate their generalization across conditions. We demonstrate that linear decoders trained on one condition generally transfer successfully to others, implying shared speech representations. This commonality was assessed with stimulus-level discriminability by performing a rank-based analysis demonstrating preservation of stimulus-specific structure in both within- and across-conditions. Finally, we compared linear reconstructions to those from a nonlinear neural network. While both exhibited cross-condition transfer, linear models achieve superior stimulus-level discriminability.
column7: Maryam Maghsoudi(University of Maryland); Rupesh Chillale(University of Maryland); Shihab A Shamma(University of Maryland)

column4: Subject-Invariant Dynamic Graph Modeling for Cross-Subject EEG Imagined Speech Decoding
column6: Decoding imagined speech using EEG-based Brain-Computer Interfaces suffers from substantial performance degradation when applied to unseen subjects due to strong inter-subject variability. We propose a subject-invariant dynamic graph modeling framework for cross-subject EEG-based imagined speech decoding. The method integrates multi-view dynamic connectivity priors with channel-wise graph attention and incorporates adversarial subject disentanglement using a gradient reversal layer to suppress subject-specific information. Evaluation under a strict leave-one-subject-out protocol across 15 subjects achieves average classification accuracies of 31.20% ± 3.12% and 30.36% ± 4.05% on two independent datasets. The results demonstrate consistent cross-subject generalization and highlight the importance of structured connectivity modeling and subject-invariant training for robust EEG-based speech decoding.
column7: Saravanakumar Duraisamy(University of Luxembourg); Luis A. Leiva(University of Luxembourg)

column4: Exploiting EEG-based Gamma-Band Time Frequency Feature in WaveNet Decoder Framework for High-Fidelity Speech Reconstruction
column6: This paper presents a novel speech synthesis framework that reconstructs audible speech directly from invasive electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings, enabling a communication option for individuals with severe speech difficulties. The framework exploits time-frequency features extracted from the high-gamma band (70-170 Hz), strongly linked to speech production and perception, and maps them to speech representations using a WaveNet-based decoder. This framework comprises stacked causal dilated convolutional residual blocks with gated activations to capture both short-term articulatory patterns and long-range temporal relationships while maintaining causality. Residual and skip connections enhance feature propagation and stabilize training. Experimental results demonstrate strong correlations between predicted and actual spectrograms, highlighting both robustness and inter-subject variability, thereby advancing state-of-the-art neural speech decoding for brain-computer interfaces (BCIs).
column7: Rantu Buragohain(Indian Institute of Technology Jammu); Saket Maheshwari(GLA University); Karan Nathwani(Indian Institute of Technology Jammu)

column4: More than a feeling: Expressive style influences cortical speech tracking in subjective cognitive decline
column6: Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) doubles dementia risk. This study investigates how self-perceived cognitive worsening shapes neural dynamics during naturalistic speech perception. EEG was collected from 60 cognitively normal older adults as they listened to speech varied in prosodic contexts, categorized by expressive style (scrambled, descriptive, dialogue, exciting). Encoding models mapping three speech representations—acoustic, subsyllabic segmentation and phonotactic features—to ongoing EEG signals were built. Cortical tracking strength (CTS) showed that models fitted with subsyllabic linguistic features outperformed acoustic ones. Crucially, greater SCD severity was associated with weaker CTS of (1) subsyllabic linguistic but not acoustic features, and (2) prosodically flat speech (scrambled and descriptive). Thus, the CTS of higher-level linguistic features while listening to prosodically flat speech may serve as a potential neural marker for early-stage cognitive decline.
column7: Matthew King-Hang Ma(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Yun Feng(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Cloris Pui-Hang Li(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Manson Cheuk-Man Fong(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University)

column4: Bayesian Generalized Additive Multilevel Models for Accurate ERP Latency Estimation under Moderate Downsampling
column6: Estimating when event-related potential (ERP) effects begin and end helps characterize the timing of neural processing, but fitting single-trial Bayesian Generalized Additive Multilevel Models (GAMMs) at high sampling rates is computationally demanding. Downsampling can reduce this burden, but balancing accurate latency estimation with manageable computational cost is a key challenge. This study compared ERP latency estimates derived from Bayesian GAMMs across sampling rates, from full resolution down to an extreme downsampled rate, in a passive oddball paradigm. The mismatch negativity latency remained stable from full to moderate resolutions, with little shift in onset. In contrast, the late discriminative negativity showed a later onset and shorter duration as the sampling rate decreased. At the extreme resolution, both components remained detectable, but with reduced temporal precision. Overall, downsampling can reduce computational cost, but extreme downsampling should be avoided.
column7: Zixia Fan(Macquarie University); Ronny Kurniawan Ibrahim(Macquarie University); Joshua Penney(Macquarie University); Felicity Cox(Macquarie University)

column4: DisenEEG-Net: Disentangling EEG features via sufficient information bottleneck and adversarial learning for cross-subject auditory attention detection
column6: Cross-subject generalization remains a major challenge in EEG-based Auditory Attention Decoding (AAD), limiting the development of neuro-steered hearing devices. This challenge arises from large inter-subject variability in EEG signals and the difficulty of learning discriminative, subject-invariant representations. We propose DisenEEG-Net, an end-to-end feature disentanglement framework based on information theory and adversarial learning. It employs a parallel Transformer encoder to extract latent EEG representations, which are then decomposed into orthogonal task- and subject-specific subspaces. A sufficient information bottleneck retains essential subject information while suppressing task leakage, and adversarial training enforces subject invariance in task features. A decoder preserves feature fidelity during disentanglement. Results show that our proposed DisenEEG-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance under cross-subject settings on the KUL, DTU, and AVED datasets.
column7: Tasleem Kausar(CUHK-Shenzhen); Yuan Liao(CUHK-Shenzhen); Haoqi Hu(CUHK-Shenzhen); Siqi Cai(HIT Shenzhen); Haizhou Li(CUHK-Shenzhen)

column1: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 4 - Oral 5 - Speaker Diarization 2

column4: ASR-Synchronized Speaker-Role Diarization
column6: Speaker-role diarization (RD), e.g., doctor vs. patient, is often more practically useful than conventional speaker diarization (SD), which assigns generic labels, e.g., speaker-1, speaker-2. For joint ASR+RD, the current best model uses a single transducer to serially predict words and roles (at speaker turns), but at the cost of degraded ASR performance. To address this, we adapt a recent dual-transducer ASR+SD model for ASR+RD. We first show that SD and RD are fundamentally different tasks, exhibiting different dependencies on acoustic and linguistic cues. We then propose (1) task-specific predictors, (2) use of higher-layer ASR encoder features as input to the RD encoder, and (3) cross-entropy loss along the 1-best ASR path instead of the full RNNT loss. Experiments on a public and a private dataset of doctor-patient conversations show that our method outperforms the best baseline by relative 6.2% and 4.5%, respectively, in role-based word diarization error rate (R-WDER).
column7: Arindam Ghosh(Solventum Health Information Systems); Mark Fuhs(Solventum Health Information Systems); Bongjun Kim(Solventum Health Information Systems); Anurag Chowdhury(Solventum Health Information Systems); Monika Woszczyna(Solventum Health Information Systems, USA)

column4: Delayed-Commitment Online Speaker Tracking for Robust Many-Speaker Diarization
column6: Online speaker diarization--determining "who spoke when" in real time--is critical for meeting transcription, yet scaling to many speakers remains challenging. Within the clustering paradigm, we propose an online diarization system with no explicit speaker-count cap. Its core module, Delayed-Commitment Online Speaker Tracking (DC-OST), labels each embedding immediately but defers new-speaker registration until sufficient evidence accumulates. DC-OST also incorporates an adaptive distance threshold to suppress spurious registrations. Under system voice activity detection, the proposed system achieves 9.53% and 9.12% DER at 0.5 s latency on VoxConverse and VoxSRC-23--up to 21 and 28 speakers, respectively--outperforming both DIART and Sortformer. Moreover, a per-speaker-count analysis shows that our system maintains consistent accuracy as the number of speakers grows, unlike baseline systems whose performance degrades.
column7: Youngki Kwon(NAVER Cloud Corporation); Hee-Soo Heo(NAVER Cloud Corporation); Minjae Lee(NAVER Cloud Corporation); Han-Gyu Kim(NAVER Cloud Corporation); Bong-Jin Lee(NAVER Cloud Corporation)

column4: Multi-Speaker Embeddings With Weakly Supervised Speaker Activity Detection For Granular Speaker Diarization
column6: In this paper, we present a novel weakly supervised multi-speaker embedding model for extracting embeddings and corresponding frame-level voice and speaker activity from multi-speaker utterances. The proposed model has two major advantages compared to traditional cascaded and hybrid end-to-end diarization approaches. First, it removes the dependency and computational overhead of external VAD and speaker segmentation models in the diarization pipeline. Second, instead of relying on coarse speaker boundaries derived from overlapping window embeddings, our approach provides frame-level speaker boundaries for multiple speakers within each window, without relying on labeled frame-level training data. Our proposed system achieves an average relative improvement of 13.7% in confusion error rate over our previous speaker diarization system across the AMI, VoxConverse and DIHARD III benchmarks.
column7: Jenthe Thienpondt(Ghent University); Kris Demuynck(Ghent University)

column4: Neural Multichannel Distant Speaker Diarization and Source Separation with Beta Speaker Activity Prior
column6: Distant speaker diarization remains challenging due to adverse acoustic conditions, varying numbers of speakers and overlapping speech. While data-driven approaches have shown strong performance, model-driven methods offer a compelling alternative by leveraging spatial information from multichannel recordings. This paper is motivated to propose a Bayesian diarization model for a model-driven method called neural FCASA to enhance its robustness. Specifically, we propose a beta prior over speaker activity and hence a variational lower bound objective that can be seen as a regularized continuous speaker activity score in place of the original cross-entropy loss to train the diarization model. Our experiments show significant improvements in terms of Diarization Error Rate by at least 3% (16% relatively) and Jaccard Error Rate by at least 4% (20% relatively) on the AMI dataset compared to the baseline.
column7: Sicheng Mao(Telecom Paris); Mathieu Fontaine(Telecom Paris); Anthony Larcher(Universite du Mans); Roland Badeau(Telecom Paris)

column4: Two-Level Uncertainty Suppression for Robust Meeting Diarization
column6: Real-meeting diarization is challenged by uncertainty propagation, where boundary ambiguity from rapid speaker turns and overlap destabilizes downstream speaker assignment. We propose a two-level uncertainty suppression framework. For segmentation, linguistically contextualized representations from an OWSM-Encoder are integrated into WavLM via Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) reducing boundary ambiguity in high-activity regions. For clustering, Known-Seed Guided Clustering (KSGC) leverages known-speaker embeddings to stabilize global assignment under mixed known/unknown-speaker conditions. On AMI, AliMeeting, and AISHELL-4, FiLM reduces DER by up to 1.8 points over WavLM-large, with largest gains in boundary-ambiguous scenarios. KSGC further improves DER by up to 2.62 points under mixed conditions, especially in meetings with frequent speaker turns. These results suggest that addressing uncertainty-related errors at complementary levels improves robustness in meeting diarization.
column7: Shuhei Asaka(Institute of Science Tokyo); Muhammad Shakeel(Honda Research Institute Japan); Chikara Maeda(Honda Research Institute Japan); Benjamin Yen(Institute of Science Tokyo); Takeshi Ashizawa(Institute of Science Tokyo); Naoaki Sumida(Honda Research Institute Japan); Kazuhiro Nakadai(Institute of Science Tokyo)

column4: Hierarchical Permutation Consistency Learning for Self-Conditioned End-to-End Speaker Diarization
column6: Self-conditioned (SC) end-to-end neural diarization (EEND) iteratively refines speaker predictions across layers. However, conventional layer-wise permutation invariant training (PIT) independently determines the optimal speaker permutation at each layer. This layer-specific permutation selection causes hierarchical permutation inconsistency (HPI), propagating permutation noise into the SC path and disrupting training stability. To resolve this, we propose two frameworks: Group-Wise PIT (GW-PIT) and Continuous Influence PIT (CI-PIT). While GW-PIT enforces a global permutation constraint, CI-PIT applies soft regularization by aggregating layer-wise cost matrices using Gaussian weighting. This promotes permutation consistency across the hierarchy while preserving local representation flexibility. Experimental results on CALLHOME demonstrate that the proposed CI-PIT suppresses permutation noise, stabilizes training dynamics, and achieves DER improvements for 2- and 3-speaker scenarios.
column7: Bongsu Jung(Incheon National University); Wooil Kim(Incheon National University)

column1: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 5 - Oral 5 - Audio Foundation Models and Generation

column4: SAM: A Mamba-2 State-Space Audio-Language Model
column6: We present SAM, a State-space Audio-language Model that integrates an audio encoder with a Mamba-2 backbone. SAM-2.7B achieves 21.1 mAP on AudioSet and 17.6 SPICE on AudioCaps, matching or surpassing larger 7B transformer-based models with fewer parameters. We further provide the first systematic, representation-level analysis of how SSMs interact with audio encoder outputs: (1) joint audio encoder finetuning is essential, supported by accuracy gains and observed adaptation of token representation rank and similarity across different SSM sizes; (2) despite linear scaling, SSMs benefit more from compact, information-rich audio token representations than from excessively long token sequences; and (3) incorporating instruction-following supervision substantially improves reasoning ability, boosting MMAU-Sound accuracy from 22.8 to 56.8. Through comprehensive experiments and analysis, we establish practical design principles for SSMs as strong, scalable backbones for audio-language models.
column7: Taehan Lee(Sogang University); Jaehan Jung(Sogang University); Hyukjun Lee(Sogang University)

column4: Samsone: A Family of Open Small Audio Language Models for On-Device Inference
column6: The success of Large Audio Language Models has driven the development of massive multimodal networks exceeding billions of parameters. However, the demand for privacy-preserving, low-latency processing has shifted focus toward Small Audio Language Models (SALMs) capable of on-device execution. In this paper, we introduce Samsone, a family of SALMs designed for edge computing. Our core model, Samsone-134M, establishes a new state-of-the-art for its size class across multiple benchmarks. We further explore the scaling laws of SALMs by introducing Samsone-99M and Samsone-356M. Despite their compact footprint, the Samsone family delivers performance competitive with models orders of magnitude larger. To foster open research and reproducibility, we train Samsone on publicly available data. We release the training code, model weights, mobile-optimized checkpoints and provide an open-source Android application to demonstrate real-time on-device inference of Samsone.
column7: Piotr Masztalski(Samsung R&D Institute Poland; AGH University of Kraków); Michal K. Grzeszczyk(Samsung R&D Institute Poland); Olaf Sikorski(Samsung R&D Institute Poland)

column4: FreeSonic: Training-Free Temporal-Aware Decoupled Attention for Precise Audio Editing
column6: Text-to-audio (TTA) generation has made significant strides, yet achieving precise and consistent audio editing remains a major challenge. However, existing methods struggle to balance temporal consistency with background preservation. In this paper, we propose FreeSonic, a training-free framework leveraging the state-of-the-art Rectified Flow-based TangoFlux model. FreeSonic utilizes an optimized inversion-reverse process and joint text-audio attention maps for precise target segment extraction. For content editing, a novel scheduled attention decoupling confines modifications to target regions while preserving original acoustic context. Furthermore, task-oriented noise injection enhances versatility for tasks such as audio removal and non-rigid replacement. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that FreeSonic achieves a superior balance by providing a high-fidelity and efficient solution for precise and consistent audio editing. Project and demos: https://free-sonic.github.io/.
column7: Yuxuan Jiang(Tsinghua University); Mingyang Han(Alibaba Group); Yusheng Dai(Monash University); Andong Wang(Renmin University of China); Tianhong Zhou(Tsinghua University); Jiaxin Ye(Fudan University); Dongxiao Wang(Alibaba Group); Haoxiang Shi(Alibaba Group); Boyu Li(Alibaba Group); Jun Song(Alibaba Group); Cheng Yu(Alibaba Group); Bo Zheng(Alibaba Group); Weibei Dou(Tsinghua University); Zehua Chen(Tsinghua University); Jun Zhu(Tsinghua University)

column4: Resonate: Reinforcing Text-to-Audio Generation via Online Feedback from Large Audio Language Models
column6: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become an effective paradigm for enhancing Large Language Models (LLMs) and visual generative models. However, its application in text-to-audio (TTA) generation remains largely under-explored. Prior work typically employs offline methods like Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and leverages Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP) models as reward functions. In this study, we investigate the integration of online Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) into TTA generation. We adapt the algorithm for Flow Matching-based audio models and demonstrate that online RL significantly outperforms its offline counterparts. Furthermore, we incorporate rewards derived from Large Audio Language Models (LALMs), which can provide fine-grained scoring signals that are better aligned with human perception. With only 470M parameters, our final model, Resonate, establishes a new SOTA on TTA-Bench in terms of both audio quality and semantic alignment.
column7: Xiquan Li(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Junxi Liu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Wenxi Chen(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute); Haina Zhu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute); Ziyang Ma(X-LANCE Lab, Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute); Xie Chen(X-LANCE Lab, Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute)

column4: GACA-DiT: Diffusion-based Dance-to-Music Generation with Genre-Adaptive Rhythm and Context-Aware Alignment
column6: Dance-to-music (D2M) generation aims to compose music that is rhythmically and temporally aligned with dance. Prior methods rely on coarse rhythm embeddings (e.g., global motion features or binarized joint rhythms), which discard fine-grained motion cues and weaken alignment. In addition, temporal mismatches introduced by feature downsampling further impair synchronization. We propose GACA-DiT, a diffusion transformer-based framework for rhythm-consistent and temporally aligned music generation. It contains two key modules: (1) a Genre-Adaptive rhythm extraction module that integrates multi-scale temporal–spatial analysis with adaptive joint weighting to capture fine-grained, genre-aware rhythm patterns; and (2) a Context-Aware temporal alignment module that leverages learnable queries to align music latents with relevant dance rhythms. Experiments on AIST++ and TikTok demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both objective metrics and human evaluation.
column7: Jinting Wang(The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)); Yan Rong(The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)); Chenxing Li(Tencent AI Lab); Li Liu(The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou))

column4: Rethinking Speech Foundation Model Fine-tuning: Better SFT or Better Match?
column6: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is widely used to adapt self-supervised speech representations to downstream classification tasks. Small gains observed under a single pretrained checkpoint are often interpreted as method-level improvements, i.e., a higher attainable performance ceiling. We show that such conclusions are not always reliable because SFT outcomes depend strongly on the specific pretrained instance. We conduct a systematic study on three SUPERB classification tasks, evaluating eight SFT variants across nine pretrained checkpoints from wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, and WavLM, with multi-seed repetitions on representative base-scale models. We find that the identity of the statistically indistinguishable top-group SFT recipe is often checkpoint-dependent, with limited transferability across pretrained instances. These findings suggest that many reported downstream gains reflect instance and seed dependent elicitation match, rather than universally improving the attainable performance ceiling.
column7: Wangjin Zhou(Kyoto University); Yizhou Zhang(Kyoto University); Yichi Wang(Kyoto University); Tatsuya Kawahara(Kyoto University)
