column4: FlowEdit: Associative Memory for Lifelong Pronunciation Adaptation in Flow-Matching TTS
column6: Flow-matching text-to-speech systems achieve remarkable zero-shot quality but remain static after deployment: pronunciation errors on out-of-vocabulary proper nouns persist unless the model is retrained. We introduce FlowEdit, a lifelong adaptation framework for frozen flow-matching TTS that learns pronunciation corrections as latent conditioning edits rather than weight updates. When corrective feedback is provided, FlowEdit optimizes a token-level perturbation in the text embedding space, then stores the correction in a Modern Hopfield Network serving as content-addressable episodic memory. At inference, corrections are retrieved via soft attention with a similarity gate, enabling fuzzy morphological matching. On our curated benchmark of 312 multilingual proper nouns across 18 language families, FlowEdit reduces target-word Phoneme Error Rate by 92.7% relative to the zero-shot baseline while maintaining identical general-speech quality. Corrections complete in approximately 15 seconds on a single GPU.
column7: Harshit Singh(University Of Maryland); Ayush Pratap Singh(TU Darmstadt); Nityanand Mathur(Smallest AI)

column4: Privacy and quality trade-off in real-time speaker anonymization via editing of age and sex attributes
column6: Speaker anonymization aims to alter attributes in the speech signal to hide the identity of the speaker. While such attribute modifications can effectively hide speaker identity, they often degrade the quality of the synthesized speech. In this work, we present a systematic analysis of the privacy-quality trade-off by isolating two key attributes (age and sex) in a streaming speech synthesis system. We use objective metrics (speaker cosine similarity as a proxy of identity and DNS-MOS for speech quality) and perform linear regression to quantify how attribute shifts impact privacy and quality, and validate these trends with perceptual listening tests. Our results reveal that privacy degrades faster than quality as modifications increase, giving rise to an optimal anonymization region where moderate attribute changes achieve effective identity suppression with minimal naturalness loss. These findings provide actionable guidance for tuning any attribute-based anonymization system.
column7: Waris Quamer(Texas A&M University); Ricardo Gutierrez-Osuna(Texas A&M University)

column4: RIVET: Robust Idempotent Voice Attribute Editing
column6: Voice attribute editing models modify characteristics such as age and gender while preserving speaker identity. In large-scale speech datasets, however, attribute annotations are often noisy or inconsistent, which can cause conditional generative models to produce unstable edits. In this work, we show that idempotency provides an effective mechanism for improving robustness to noisy labels. An idempotent operator is one for which repeated application does not change the result, i.e., f(f(x)) = f(x). Enforcing this property acts as an implicit regularizer that reduces sensitivity to mislabeled examples. We introduce RIVET, a training framework that incorporates an idempotency objective to improve robustness to label noise. We evaluate RIVET under controlled label noise and on the GLOBE dataset with naturally noisy annotations. RIVET im-proves editing success and better preserves speaker identity than standard training, showing that idempotency improves robustness in voice editing models. Code is available online.
column7: Dareen Alharthi(Carnegie Mellon University); Bhuvan Koduru(Carnegie Mellon University); Rita Singh(Carnegie Mellon University); Bhiksha Ramakrishnan(Carnegie Mellon University)

column4: FineCombo-TTS: Collaborative and Precise Controllable Speech Synthesis Using Text Descriptions and Reference Speech
column6: Controllable text-to-speech (TTS) has become a key research focus. However, methods based on either reference speech or text descriptions lack flexibility and precise control, and recent joint approaches remain loosely coupled, with speech modeling timbre and text controlling global style. We propose FineCombo-TTS, a unified framework for speech synthesis grounded in reference speech and guided by text descriptions, enabling flexible and precise control over acoustic attributes. Instead of explicit attribute disentanglement, we learn a unified acoustic representation and introduce a Conditional Flow Matching (CFM)-based Speech Variance Predictor to model fine-grained reference-to-target transformations guided by text descriptions. To support relative attribute control, we construct FineEdit, a structured paired dataset that explicitly encodes source-to-target attribute variations. Experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves flexible, precise, and expressive controllable TTS.
column7: Shuoyi Zhou(Tsinghua University); Yixuan Zhou(Tsinghua University); Peiji Yang(Tencent); Yifan Hu(Inner Mongolia University); Yicheng Zhong(Tencent); Zhisheng Wang(Tencent); Zhiyong Wu(Tsinghua University)

column4: Edit Content, Preserve Acoustics: Imperceptible Text-Based Speech Editing via Self-Consistency Rewards
column6: Imperceptible text-based speech editing modifies spoken content through transcript manipulation while preserving acoustic continuity. Prior acoustic-space approaches suffer from content–style entanglement, causing unstable generation and boundary artifacts. We introduce a framework guided by the principle 'Edit Content, Preserve Acoustics'. Editing is conducted in a stable semantic space, while acoustic realization is handled by a Flow Matching decoder. To ensure perceptual consistency, we propose Self-Consistency Rewards Group Relative Policy Optimization, which leverages a pre-trained Text-to-Speech model as an implicit critic, together with intelligibility and duration constraints. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art autoregressive and non-autoregressive baselines in intelligibility, robustness, and perceptual quality.
column7: Yong Ren(Chinese Academy of Sciences; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences); Jiangyan Yi(Tsinghua University); Jianhua Tao(Tsinghua University); Tao Wang(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Le Xu(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Zhengqi Wen(Tsinghua University)

column4: Bagpiper-Edit: Zero-Shot Open-Ended Audio Editing via Rich-Caption
column6: Current text-guided audio editing methods rely on paired training data, predefined operation templates, and separate processing pipelines across speech, music, and sound. We present Bagpiper-Edit to enable open-ended audio editing via free-form natural language instructions. We reformulate audio editing as a rich-caption rewriting task by treating a rich caption as the semantic representation of an audio clip. The user request is translated into an edited caption, which then guides Bagpiper-Edit to generate the target edited audio with the original audio as contextual acoustic anchor. This unlocks the potential of free-form editing, and circumvents the need for paired audio-editing training data, enabling powerful zero-shot editing capabilities. Evaluations across speech, audio, and free-form editing show Bagpiper-Edit maintains good consistency to the original audio and achieves similar performance to other expert models in most cases. Demo: https://bagpiper-edit.github.io
column7: Xun Gong(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Jinchuan Tian(Carnegie Mellon University); Haoran Wang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); William Chen(Carnegie Mellon University); Shinji Watanabe(Carnegie Mellon University); Yamin Qian(Shanghai Jiao Tong University)

column4: SEA-MDD: Self-adapting Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis Models via Test-Time Training
column6: Mispronunciation detection and diagnosis (MDD) assists second language (L2) learners in improving pronunciation. However, the substantial variability in learner proficiency and the diverse mispronunciation types hinder the development of reliable MDD systems. Large-scale annotation to cover all mispronunciations is prohibitively expensive. To address this data scarcity, we propose SEA-MDD, a SElf-Adapting MDD method that leverages Test-Time Training (TTT) to effectively adapt trained models to new speech samples. Specifically, we integrate multilayer perceptron (MLP)-based TTT modules into Transformer blocks of wav2vec 2.0. The parameters of TTT modules are updated during both training and test time via self-supervised learning. This design enables trained models to adjust dynamically to novel inputs, mitigating performance degradation commonly observed in prior MDD models when exposed to diverse speech distributions. Experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
column7: Minglin Wu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Helen Meng(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)

column4: Mixture-of-Accent-Adapters for Robust ASR: Injecting Accent Cues into Pretrained Whisper
column6: Accented speech remains a key challenge for inclusive ASR, yet adapting large pretrained models often relies on costly full fine-tuning. Moreover, previous methods lack integration of accent-specific adapters, controlled encoder-level accent-cue injection, and multitask supervision for specialization regulation and gender information leakage mitigation. We propose Mixture-of-Accent-Adapters (MoAA), a novel adaptation framework for Whisper that enables on-demand specialization while defaulting to the frozen backbone when unnecessary. A pooled-state control bottleneck estimates accentedness, guiding accent-cue injection via weighted retrieval from a learnable soft accent codebook and routing lightweight accent-specialist adapters, while calibrating a gated blend with the backbone. An adversarial gender head reduces leakage, and reference-free hallucination suppression mitigates rare decoding artifacts. On AESRC benchmark, MoAA achieves 7.49% WER and 3.81% CER.
column7: Mehedi Hasan Bijoy(Aalto University); Yaroslav Getman(Aalto University); Tamás Grósz(South East Technological University); Mikko Kurimo(Aalto University)

column4: Contrastive Regularization for Accent-Robust ASR
column6: ASR systems based on self-supervised acoustic pretraining and CTC fine-tuning achieve strong performance on native speech but remain sensitive to accent variability. We investigate supervised contrastive learning (SupCon) as a lightweight, accent-invariant auxiliary objective for CTC fine-tuning. An utterance-level contrastive loss regularizes encoder representations without architectural modification or explicit accent supervision. Experiments on the L2-ARCTIC benchmark show consistent WER reductions across multiple pretrained encoders, with up to 25—29% relative reduction under unseen-accent evaluation. Analysis using within-transcript cosine dispersion indicates that SupCon promotes more compact and stable representation geometry under accent variability. Overall, SupCon provides an effective and model-agnostic regularization strategy for improving accent robustness.
column7: Van-Phat Thai(Air Traffic Management Research Institute, Nanyang Technological University); Aradhya Dhruv(Air Traffic Management Research Institute, Nanyang Technological University); Duc-Thinh Pham(Air Traffic Management Research Institute, Nanyang Technological University; Center of AI Research, VinUniversity); Sameer Alam(Air Traffic Management Research Institute, Nanyang Technological University)

column4: Exploring the potential and limitations of Model Merging for Multi-Domain Adaptation in ASR
column6: Model merging is a scalable alternative to multi-task training that combines the capabilities of multiple specialised models into a single model. This is particularly attractive for large speech foundation models, which are typically adapted through domain-specific fine-tuning, resulting in multiple customised checkpoints, for which repeating full fine-tuning when new data becomes available is computationally prohibitive. In this work, we study model merging for multi-domain ASR and benchmark 11 merging algorithms for 10 European Portuguese domains, evaluating in-domain accuracy, robustness under distribution shift, as well as English and multilingual performance. We further propose BoostedTSV-M, a new merging algorithm based on TSV-M that mitigates rank collapse via singular-value boosting and improves numerical stability. Overall, our approach outperforms full fine-tuning on European Portuguese while preserving out-of-distribution generalisation in a single model.
column7: Carlos Carvalho(INESC-ID; Universidade de Lisboa); Francisco Teixeira(INESC-ID); Thomas Rolland(INESC-ID); Alberto Abad(INESC-ID; Universidade de Lisboa)

column4: Activation Steering for Accent Adaptation in Large Audio Language Models
column6: Accent variability remains a major source of errors in automatic speech recognition, yet most adaptation methods rely on parameter fine-tuning without understanding where accent information is encoded. We treat accent variation as an interpretable subspace in hidden representations and investigate whether it can be identified and controlled directly in activation space. We extract layer-wise encoder activations and estimate mean-shift directions capturing accent-induced representation shifts. By injecting these directions into individual layers and measuring how they align accented and standard embeddings, we derive a layer-wise accent sensitivity profile, revealing that accent information concentrates in a narrow band of middle encoder layers. Leveraging this structure, we further introduce parameter-free accent steering that modifies representations during inference without updating model weights. Experiments across eight accents show consistent word error rate reductions.
column7: Jinuo Sun(The University of Melbourne); Yang Xiao(The University of Melbourne); Sung Kyun Chung(The University of Melbourne); Qiuchi Hu(The University of Melbourne); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University); Eun-Jung Holden(The University of Melbourne); Ting Dang(The University of Melbourne)

column4: AccentDrift: Real-time Streaming Accent Conversion via Sparse Speech Tokenization
column6: Although recent speech AI advances have enabled real-time speech understanding and generation, real-time accent conversion (AC) for second-language (L2) speakers in real-world interactions remains underexplored. In this paper, we present AccentDrift, a real-time streaming AC system that preserves linguistic content and speaker identity while transforming speech into a target accent with low latency. From an information bottleneck perspective, we adopt sparse speech tokenization to extract linguistic information from continuous speech. An accent adapter injects accent style into sparse semantic tokens, followed by a timbre adapter that hierarchically generates speaker-specific acoustics. To support streaming, we adopt a cache-aware streaming architecture and parallel streams, achieving 520 ms latency. AccentDrift outperforms prior parallel AC models, and demonstrates the feasibility of generating native-like accents for L2 speakers. Audio samples are available at https://accentdrift.github.io/demo/.
column7: Sang-Hoon Lee(Ajou University); Heejin Choi(Samsung Research); Joun Yeop Lee(Samsung Research); Sangjun Park(Samsung Research)

column4: Mitigating Speaker Leakage in Cascaded Multi-talker ASR with Diarization-based Transcript Correction
column6: While cascaded multi-talker ASR (MT-ASR) leverages state-of-the-art foundation models, its performance is often capped by speaker leakage during separation. Prior correction strategies primarily focus on lexical re-labeling for speaker attribution. We propose a complementary pruning-based paradigm that robustly identifies and removes leakage artifacts. Our method utilizes a pre-trained speaker diarization model as a multimodal verifier to prune transcribed segments satisfying a tripartite consensus of temporal containment, lexical cross-validation, and temporal alignment. Results on LibriMix, LibriSpeechMix, and the AMI Meeting corpus show our algorithm consistently reduces cpWER across diverse overlap conditions. Specifically, on subsets with high speaker leakage, our method achieves relative cpWER reductions of up to 29%, highlighting its effectiveness in enhancing the reliability of cascaded MT-ASR transcripts in complex acoustic environments.
column7: Hermann Yepdjio Nkouanga(Portland State University); Minwei Luo(Portland State University); Maggie Wigness(US Army Research Laboratory); Suresh Singh(Portland State University)

column4: Beyond Mimicry: Constrained Exploration with GRPO for Joint Multi-Talker ASR and Diarization under Unknown Speaker Counts
column6: Joint multi-talker ASR with speaker attribution and timestamps is particularly challenging when the speaker count is unknown and the output must follow a strict structure. We observe that Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)-only alignment of Speech-LLMs is brittle under dense overlaps, often leading to burst hallucinations and malformed speaker/timestamp tags. We propose a unified two-stage generative framework: (i) CoT-augmented SFT that infers the global speaker count before transcription, and (ii) GRPO-based constrained exploration guided by a Multi-dimensional Constraint-Aware Reward (MCAR) that directly optimizes permutation-invariant accuracy while enforcing counting, temporal, and structural constraints. On Libri3Mix and a Dynamic-Mix (2+3) set (speaker count unknown at test time), our model achieves 14.52%/9.24% cpWER and 1.95%/1.12% WDER, respectively, with GRPO yielding a 35%/54% relative cpWER reduction over SFT+CoT.
column7: Yunrui Cai(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Dingdong Wang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Lingwei Meng(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Xixin Wu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Zhiyong Wu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Tsinghua University); Helen Meng(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)

column4: KFC-KWS: Keyframe Fusion with CTC for User-Defined Keyword Spotting
column6: User-defined keyword spotting (KWS) enables personalized voice interaction by detecting user-specified keywords. A key challenge in this task is distinguishing target keywords from phonetically confusable alternatives. To address this challenge, we propose KFC-KWS, a multimodal framework that leverages connectionist temporal classification (CTC)-guided keyframe selection. Specifically, we exploit the peaky posterior distributions of CTC to identify high-confidence phoneme frames, enabling precise alignment across audio, phoneme, and text modalities. These keyframes are then fused with full-utterance representations through cross-attention to capture both local discriminative cues and global contextual information. On LibriPhrase, KFC-KWS achieves the best-balanced performance (98.73% AUC) and substantially outperforms advanced baselines on the challenging hard subset (97.65% AUC and 7.75% EER), demonstrating its effectiveness in discriminating between highly confusable keywords.
column7: Jin Li(Hangzhou Dianzi University); Wenbin Jiang(Hangzhou Dianzi University); Ji Hu(Hangzhou Dianzi University)

column4: Avoiding Catastrophic Forgetting in Text-Only Adaptation of LLM-based ASR via Multi-View Text Denoising
column6: Adapting LLM-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems to new domains using text-only data is challenging. Naively fine-tuning the LLM on target text disrupts the speech-text alignment learned by the projector, causing catastrophic forgetting. We propose a lightweight text-only adaptation strategy that formulates adaptation as a denoising task and introduces a multi-view noise-driven batching scheme to preserve alignment. Each mini-batch mixes paired source audio-text examples, projector-induced noisy transcripts, synthetically corrupted source transcripts, and corrupted target transcripts. This mixing enables domain adaptation while maintaining speech-text alignment. Our method requires no architectural changes or additional parameters and achieves up to 25.4% relative WER improvement over the non-adapted base model, outperforming recent text-only adaptation methods.
column7: Sergio Burdisso(Idiap Research Institute); Esaú Villatoro-Tello(Idiap Research Institute); Thibault Bañeras-Roux(Idiap Research Institute); Shashi Kumar(Idiap Research Institute; EPFL); Srikanth Madikeri(University of Zurich); Pradeep Rangappa(Idiap Research Institute); Manjunath K E(Uniphore); Petr Motlicek(Idiap Research Institute; Brno University of Technology); Andreas Stolcke(Uniphore)

column4: AQA-TTRL: Self-Adaptation in Audio Question Answering with Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
column6: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) exhibit strong capabilities in general audio understanding but remain static after deployment, limiting their adaptability to real-world data. Since supervised fine-tuning is costly, we propose AQA-TTRL, a novel framework for audio understanding that enables on-the-fly evolution via test-time reinforcement learning using only unlabeled test data. It generates pseudo-labels via majority voting and optimizes the model through reinforcement learning. To address the noise in self-generated labels, we introduce confidence weighting to adjust training signals. Furthermore, multiple-attempt sampling mitigates advantage collapse and stabilizes training. Across MMAU, MMAR, and MMSU, AQA-TTRL achieves significant average improvements of 4.42% for Qwen2.5-Omni 7B and 11.04% for the 3B model. Notably, the adapted 3B model outperforms direct inference of the unadapted 7B model, highlighting the effectiveness of test-time adaptation in audio understanding.
column7: Haoyu Zhang(The University of Tokyo); Jiaxian Guo(The University of Tokyo); Dong Yang(The University of Tokyo); Yusuke Iwasawa(The University of Tokyo); Yutaka Matsuo(The University of Tokyo)

column4: AFG-Bias: Acoustic-Fusion-Gated Biasing for Plug-and-Play Hotword Customization in LLM-Based ASR
column6: LLM-based ASR achieves strong transcription but struggles with rare domain-specific entities. Prior biasing methods either require architecture-specific training or rely on prompt injection, which suffers from scale collapse and hallucination. We propose AFG-Bias, a plug-and-play framework grounding hotword biasing in acoustic evidence without modifying LLM parameters. Cross-Modal Acoustic Retrieval (CAR) selects relevant hotwords from a large candidate list via sliding-window alignment, and Acoustic-Fusion Gating injects verified bias into decoding while suppressing hallucinations. On three LLM-ASR backbones, AFG-Bias achieves up to 74.1% relative CER reduction in financial and medical domains, and improves AISHELL-1 hotword F1 by up to 5.4 absolute points.
column7: Long Wu(Qifu Technology); Lingchao Zhao(Qifu Technology); Yuanzhong Zheng(Qifu Technology); Haojun Fei(Qifu Technology); Qing Yang(Qifu Technology)

column4: Decoding the Trade-off: A Large-Scale Analysis of Latency and Stability in LLM-based Speech Translation Cascades
column6: Real-time subtitling must balance low latency with stable translations. In segment-level cloud cascades, aggressive endpointing increases request rate and can push utilization beyond service capacity, triggering a backlog avalanche in which queueing delay dominates and "fast" settings become slower in steady state. We present RST, a reproducible KO→EN subtitle pipeline that distinguishes time-to-first-text (latency_first) and time-to-stable-text (latency_stable). On the full FLEURS corpus, we show that aggressive endpointing drives cascades into a backlog regime (median RTF > 1), where latency_stable grows over time. Whisper prompt conditioning further degrades short-chunk streaming ASR by +14-17 pp CER and can leak instructions. Sweeps reveal a clear stability boundary. We define an operational threshold as the most aggressive setting with median RTF ≤1, showing that throughput stability is essential for low-latency LLM-based cascades.
column7: Shinyoung Sun(Sogang University); Taehoon Kim(Sogang University)

column4: Fed-SpeechLLM: Federated Learning Speech Language Models for Multilingual ASR
column6: SpeechLLMs show strong promise for multilingual ASR, yet centralized training conflicts with privacy constraints over distributed, linguistically diverse data. This paper presents Fed-SpeechLLM, a federated learning framework for multilingual SpeechLLM-based ASR evaluated on a bilingual English and Italian setting. We study federated optimization under compounded non-IID conditions from acoustic and cross-lingual heterogeneity. Standard FL methods degrade when clients hold language-skewed distributions. Moreover, we propose language-aware gradient aggregation and a sampling clustering-based method to mitigate multilingual imbalance, using selective aggregation of speech encoders and projection layers with a frozen LLM backbone. Results confirm competitive performance against centralized training.
column7: Mohamed Nabih Ali(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Daniele Falavigna(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Alessio Brutti(Fondazione Bruno Kessler)

column4: Multi-Channel Differential ASR for Robust Wearer Speech Recognition on Smart Glasses
column6: With the growing adoption of wearable devices such as smart glasses for AI assistants, wearer speech recognition (WSR) is becoming increasingly critical to next-generation human-computer interfaces. However, in real environments, interference from side-talk speech remains a significant challenge to WSR and may cause accumulated errors for downstream tasks such as natural language processing. In this work, we introduce a novel multi-channel differential automatic speech recognition (ASR) method for robust WSR on smart glasses. The proposed system takes differential inputs from different frontends that complement each other to improve the robustness of WSR, including a beamformer, microphone selection, and a lightweight side-talk detection model. Evaluations on both simulated and real datasets demonstrate that the proposed system outperforms the traditional approach, achieving up to an 18.0% relative reduction in word error rate.
column7: Yufeng Yang(The Ohio State University); Yiteng Huang(Meta); Yong Xu(Meta); Li Wan(Meta); Suwon Shon(Meta); Yang Liu(Meta); Yifeng Fan(Meta); Zhaojun Yang(Meta); Olivier Siohan(Meta); Yue Liu(Meta); Ming Sun(Meta); Florian Metze(Meta)

column4: ESPnet3: Infrastructure for Scalable Speech and Audio Research in the Foundation Model Era
column6: Recent speech research involves increasingly large datasets, complex models, and diverse experimental workflows. However, existing frameworks require substantial engineering effort to support such experiments. We present ESPnet3, a speech and audio research framework built on a modular system architecture with configuration-driven dataset composition and unified Python-based workflows. ESPnet3 introduces a DataOrganizer abstraction for flexible dataset integration and dataset sharding for memory-efficient large-scale training, while allowing recipe-specific logic through lightweight stage overrides. In OWSM pre-training experiments, ESPnet3 reduces per-epoch training time by 21.1 minutes compared to ESPnet2 and achieves >80% GPU utilization in multi-node training. Fine-tuning experiments show that new models and datasets can be integrated with around 46 lines of additional code. ESPnet3 will be publicly released with model checkpoints and training logs.

column4: SCRIBE: Diagnostic Evaluation and Rich Transcription Models for Indic ASR
column6: Automatic speech recognition replaces typing only when correction costs less than manual entry, a threshold determined by error types, not counts: fixing a misrecognized domain term costs far more than inserting a comma. Word error rate (WER) fails on two fronts: it collapses distinct error categories into a single scalar, and it structurally penalizes agglutinative languages where valid sandhi merges inflate scores. We introduce SCRIBE, a diagnostic framework that provides categorical error decomposition into lexical, punctuation, numeral, and domain-entity rates through sandhi-tolerant alignment with domain vocabulary injection. Human validation confirms SCRIBE aligns with expert judgment where WER does not. We release SCRIBE, an LLM curation pipeline, benchmarks, and open-weight rich transcription models for Hindi, Malayalam, and Kannada.
column7: Kavya Manohar(Adalat AI); Arghya Bhattacharya(Adalat AI); Kush Juvekar(Adalat AI); Kumarmanas Nethil(Adalat AI)

column4: Audio-KWS-Gated Error Memory Retrieval for Incremental ASR Post-Correction
column6: ASR has improved, yet rare and domain-specific terms remain challenging. LLMs enable second-pass post-correction without retraining an ASR model. In long-running use, correction logs can be reused to fix recurring errors, but full-history prompting is limited by the LLM context window, and text-only selection is brittle when trigger terms are misrecognized. We propose an incremental post-correction framework with Audio-KWS-gated retrieval, where Audio-KWS detects keywords from audio to select relevant correction records within the context window. We proceed in three steps: (i) LLM-based error analysis extracts correction pairs to update a keyword inventory, (ii) Audio-KWS runs on audio to detect Top-N keywords and retrieve correction records (using phonetic readings as keywords for Japanese), and (iii) the LLM applies record-guided edits. On Earnings-21 and CSJ, our method achieves about 70% prompt reduction (Top-20 English; Top-10 Japanese) while improving WER/CER and Bias-F1.
column7: Taira Ashikawa(Toshiba Corporation); Daichi Hayakawa(Toshiba Corporation); Takehiko Kagoshima(Toshiba Corporation); Tomoki Watanabe(Toshiba Corporation)

column4: Voice Onset Time Categorical Perception in Mandarin-Speaking People Who Stutter: A Zoom-In Nonword Study
column6: As speech production and perception share neural mechanisms, people who stutter (PWS) may also exhibit atypical speech perception. The present study used a nonword continuum and a zoom-in design concentrating stimuli around the category boundary to analyze categorical perception of voice onset time (VOT) in Mandarin-speaking PWS. In identification, PWS showed a trend-level rightward boundary shift, requiring longer VOTs to perceive aspirated consonants. Unlike fluent controls, who displayed typical response delays near the boundary, PWS showed a reduced asymmetry, indicating inefficient access to phonemic categories. In discrimination, accuracy and reaction times did not differ between groups; however, more severe PWS responded faster to within-category stimuli. As accuracy remained stable, this likely reflects right hemisphere compensatory processing. Thus, PWS do not show impaired categorical perception per se but exhibit atypicality in forming and accessing category mappings.
column7: Yusuke Kiyama(Peking University); Xiyu Wu(Peking University)

column4: Learning to Hear Hesitation: Continual Learning for Disfluency-Aware ASR
column6: Despite advances in large-scale Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), disfluent speech remains challenging, as state-of-the-art systems are often optimized to omit disfluencies, leading to information loss and hallucinations. Prior work has focused on verbatim transcription and the integration of disfluency markers, but adapting models on limited datasets can lead to catastrophic forgetting of general-domain knowledge. We address this gap by leveraging continual learning (CL) with explicit disfluency tokens. We first introduce these tokens into a pretrained ASR model to establish stable token mechanisms, and then continue training on additional datasets with varying disfluency distributions. Through a detailed analysis of model dynamics during training, we identify a trade-off between marker learning and ASR performance, and a consistent cross-attention head mechanism shared across CL methods.

column4: Measuring Vocal Efficiency in Daily Life in Patients with Voice Disorders Using Wireless Accelerometer and Microphone Sensors
column6: Voice disorders are linked to inefficient phonation, with vocal efficiency (VE) measured in clinic. We studied ecological vocal efficiency (EVE) by estimating daily-life VE as SPL/Ps (dB/dB) using a wireless dual-sensor voice monitor: subglottal pressure (Ps) predicted from a neck-surface accelerometer (ACC) and sound pressure level (SPL) from a microphone. 14 females participated (7 with vocal fold nodules; 7 matched controls). In lab, VE was computed via a /p/-vowel sequence (loud-to-soft; 3 pitch levels). Participants completed 3 days of ambulatory monitoring (12 h/day), and EVE was computed. Patients showed lower EVE and reduced variability than controls in daily life (4.1 vs 4.7, effect size r = 0.67; SD 0.4 vs 1.0, r = 0.91); variability metrics separated groups better in field than in lab. Patients spent significantly more time outside the EVE normative range than controls (92 vs 36%; p = 0.03; r = 0.81). Preliminary results support EVE as an ecological marker of vocal function.
column7: Ahmed Yousef(MGH; Harvard Medical School); Emma Willis(MGH); Vahni Tagirisa(MGH); Robert Hillman(MGH; Harvard Medical School); Daryush Mehta(MGH; Harvard Medical School)

column4: Mispronunciation Modeling via PPG-Based Phone Editing: A Data Augmentation Framework for Dysarthric Speech Recognition
column6: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems face significant challenges in recognizing dysarthric speech due to severe acoustic variability, frequent mispronunciations, and extreme data scarcity. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel speaker-dependent data augmentation framework utilizing phonetic posteriorgram (PPG)-based phone editing. By quantifying individual pronunciation variations, our method selectively edits the phonetic representations of typical speech to emulate the mispronunciation patterns of target dysarthric speakers. This technique is further integrated with speaking style conversion and phonetic-level speed perturbation to comprehensively capture both the articulatory and prosodic characteristics of dysarthria. We evaluated our approach on the UASpeech corpus by fine-tuning a HuBERT ASR model. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively enhances recognition robustness, achieving an overall word error rate of 19.53%.
column7: Tsai-Hsiu Ko(National Cheng Kung University); You-Cyuan Jhuo(National Cheng Kung University); Chung-Hsien Wu(National Cheng Kung University)

column4: Modeling Lombard Effects in Voice Disorders Using Daily-Life Monitoring of Ambient Noise and Voice Acoustics
column6: Real-world Lombard effects—vocal adjustments in noisy environments—are overlooked in patients with voice disorders. We analyzed ambulatory data from 24 patients with phonotraumatic and non-phonotraumatic vocal hyperfunction (PVH and NPVH) and 18 healthy controls (2–4 days; ≥ 10 h/day), synchronizing equivalent ambient noise levels (Leq) with voice measures: SPL (sound level), F0 (pitch), CPP (cepstral peak prominence), and H1H2 (first minus second harmonic magnitude). We fit models predicting each voice measure from ambient noise (Leq mean, SD). With higher Leq, SPL, F0, and CPP rose and H1H2 fell; CPP showed the strongest correlation (r = 0.36–0.53). Nonlinear models fit best (max test r² = 0.32 for CPP). PVH had steeper SPL slope (0.65 dB/dB Leq mean; 0.86 dB/dB Leq SD) and larger CPP slope (0.18 dB/dB Leq mean) than NPVH. Real-world Lombard effects in patients were subtype-specific, with CPP capturing voice-quality effects beyond SPL and F0.

Yousef(Massachusetts General Hospital; Harvard Medical School); Trishul Chowdhury(Massachusetts General Hospital; Northeastern University); Gregory Ciccarelli(MIT Lincoln Laboratory); Thomas F. column4: A Transcript-anchored Pipeline With Large Language Models For Detecting Inappropriate Pauses In Dysarthric Speech
column6: Dysarthria, a motor speech disorder common after stroke, reduces intelligibility and often involves prosodic abnormalities such as inappropriate pauses (IPs). These provide critical cues for clinical assessment and treatment; however, reliable automatic evaluation remains challenging because transcript-level information is essential. We present an automated framework for IP detection using large language models (LLMs). The framework integrates verbatim automatic speech recognition, the Montreal Forced Aligner with refined temporal boundaries, LLM-guided lexical adaptation, and LLM-based classification with rationale generation. This pipeline enables accurate identification of IPs and provides precise time alignment in dysarthric speech. Experimental results demonstrate strong performance against expert evaluation, highlighting the effectiveness of LLM-guided processing. Overall, our study introduces a scalable and explainable approach for clinical and research assessment.
column7: Minsu Han(LG Electronics); Insung Lee(Sogang University); Taeyoung Jeong(Sogang University); Myoung-Wan Koo(Sogang University)

column4: Synergizing Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Alzheimer Detection with Language-Invariant Multimodal Bi-Geometric Adversarial Learning
column6: In this work, we study zero-shot cross-lingual speech-based Alzheimer's disease detection (SADD). We hypothesize that learning language-invariant multimodal representations by fusing multilingual speech and text pretrained models is essential for reliable transfer to unseen languages, as the two modalities capture complementary acoustic and linguistic markers of cognitive impairment while adversarial learning suppresses language-specific confounds. Empirical results in zero-shot cross-lingual evaluation substantiate the hypothesis, showing that multimodal fusion consistently outperforms unimodal baselines. To this end, we propose ORBIT, a novel framework that combines cross-attentive fusion, multi-tap language adversaries, and complementary spherical-hyperbolic geometric learning with consensus clustering. Across settings, ORBIT achieves the strongest performance compared to unimodal models and simple concatenation-based fusion baselines.
column7: Girish (Ulster University); Mohd Mujtaba Akhtar(Ulster University); Farhan Sheth(Manipal University); Muskaan Singh(Ulster University); Juliana Gerard(Ulster University); Paula McClean(Ulster University); Kongfatt Wong-Lin(Ulster University)

column4: CoSTA: Cognitive-State-Conditioned TTS Data Augmentation Using ASR Transcripts for Alzheimer’s Disease Detection
column6: Speech-based Alzheimer's Disease (AD) detection is constrained by scarce pathological speech data. To address this, we propose CoSTA, a Text-to-Speech (TTS)-based data augmentation framework. Specifically, we first develop two Cognitive-State-Conditioned (CS-Cond) TTS models by adapting CosyVoice2 and F5-TTS to synthesize speech with distinct AD and Healthy Control characteristics. Furthermore, by constructing a transcript pool comprising Manual Transcripts (MT) and 36 Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) transcripts, we investigate the impact of text sources on TTS-based augmentation. We also perform augmentation-factor analysis and test-time augmentation. Experiments on the ADReSS dataset show that CS-Cond TTS significantly improves synthetic speech utility, and ASR-driven augmentation frequently outperforms MT-driven augmentation. Finally, CoSTA yields a 4.16% gain over the baseline, achieving an audio-only accuracy of 85.83% on the ADReSS test set and outperforming prior methods.
column7: Yin-Long Liu(University of Science and Technology of China); Yuanchao Li(University of Edinburgh); Yiming Wang(University of Science and Technology of China); Yue Li(University of Science and Technology of China); Rui Feng(University of Science and Technology of China); Jiaxin Chen(University of Science and Technology of China); Shaobo Liu(University of Science and Technology of China); Liu He(University of Science and Technology of China); Yuang Chen(University of Science and Technology of China); Jiahong Yuan(University of Science and Technology of China); Zhen-Hua Ling(University of Science and Technology of China)

column4: WSG: Clinically-Informed Weighted Speech Graphs for Dementia Detection
column6: Early detection of dementia is critical, yet clinical assessments are often time-consuming and costly. Speech graphs offer a scalable, automated approach by modelling utterances as graphs to capture structural patterns that indicate cognitive decline. While existing methods overlook crucial information such as word meaning and pronunciation, this work proposes Weighted Speech Graphs (WSGs), integrating clinically motivated attributes into speech graphs, and presents a novel graph-derived feature set for dementia detection. Remarkably, just one or two features can achieve performance comparable to a full baseline feature set, while providing interpretable insights aligned with clinical observations. Furthermore, an open-source Python framework for graph construction, feature extraction and visualisation is released, promoting reproducibility and extensibility. Together, these advances bridge practical application and clinical insights in speech graph-based dementia detection.
column7: Yao Xiao(University of Sheffield); Fritz Peters(University of Sheffield); Madhurananda Pahar(University of Sheffield); Dorota A Braun(University of Sheffield); Caitlin H Illingworth(University of Sheffield); Stefan Goetze(University of Sheffield); Daniel Blackburn(University of Sheffield); Heidi Christensen(University of Sheffield)

column4: Etiology-Aware Speech Language Models for Dysarthric Speech Recognition
column6: Standard ASR systems ignore clinical context about speakers' neurological conditions, limiting their effectiveness on dysarthric speech. We propose etiology-aware speech language models that incorporate clinical knowledge to improve recognition. We compare four strategies: standard fine-tuning, auxiliary etiology classification, providing the condition as input context (hinting), and predicting the condition before transcribing within the same autoregressive stream. We find that predicting the condition before transcribing is the most effective strategy, achieving 7.77% WER on the Speech Accessibility Project dataset, a 6.4% relative reduction over standard fine-tuning. This approach requires no clinical labels at inference. Auxiliary classification reaches higher etiology accuracy yet fails to reduce WER, showing that clinical reasoning must occur within the generation stream to benefit recognition. Cross-dataset evaluation on TORGO confirms consistent gains across conditions.
column7: Moreno La Quatra(Kore University of Enna); Alkis Koudounas(Sony Group Corporation); Valerio Mario Salerno(Kore University of Enna); Sabato Marco Siniscalchi(Università degli Studi di Palermo)

column4: Confidence Score Guided Incremental and Speaker Adaptive Pseudo-Labeling for Semi-Supervised Elderly Speech Recognition
column6: This paper proposes a novel confidence score guided incremental and speaker adaptive pseudo-labeling approach for semi-supervised elderly speech recognition. It facilitates higher-quality pseudo-label selection and progressive refinement, while also mitigating speaker heterogeneity. A confidence estimation module is designed to rank the reliability of untranscribed data, enabling a curriculum learning trajectory that progressively folds in unlabeled data subsets from high to low confidence. Speaker-specific characteristics are captured through speaker adaptive training with learnable prompts. Experiments on the English DementiaBank Pitt and Cantonese JCCOCC MoCA elderly speech datasets suggest that the proposed method outperforms the semi-supervised baseline using no confidence scores guided incremental or speaker adaptive pseudo-labeling by statistically significant word error rate (WER) or character error rate (CER) reductions of 1.45% and 2.27% absolute (6.21% and 6.98% relative).
column7: Chengxi Deng(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Xurong Xie(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Shujie Hu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Jiajun Deng(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Mengzhe Geng(National Research Council Canada); Youjun Chen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Huimeng Wang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Haoning Xu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Guinan Li(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Xunying Liu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)

column4: Label Correction Enhanced Dual-Stream Multiple Instance Learning for Weakly-Supervised Depression Detection in Speech
column6: Automatic Depression Detection (ADD) in speech aims to estimate speaker's depressive state through speech-based intelligent methods, yet existing speech-based ADD works fail to jointly address inaccurate and inexact labels for ADD in weakly-supervised cases. To this end, we propose an approach of Label Correction enhanced Dual-stream Multiple Instance Learning (LC-DMIL) for weakly-supervised speech-based ADD. The proposed LC-DMIL includes a label correction module focusing on correcting inaccurate labels through fused likelihood-ratio-based and prototype-based correction strategies, and a depression detection module employing a dual-stream multiple instance approach towards the inexact labels. Experiments on weakly-supervised speech-based depression detection data indicate that, the proposed approach performs effectively for the weakly-supervised speech-based ADD.

Posts & Telecommun.; Graz University of Technology); Jin Qi(Nanjing Univ. Posts & Telecommun.); Feiyi Xu(Nanjing Univ. Posts & Telecommun.); Zhao Ren(University of Bremen); Björn W. column4: QC-GAN: A Parameter-Efficient Quaternion Conformer GAN for High-Fidelity Speech Enhancement
column6: We propose a parameter-efficient speech enhancement framework, Quaternion Conformer GAN (QC-GAN), which combines a Quaternion Conformer generator with MetricGAN-based training. The Hamilton product encodes the magnitude and phase via structured weight sharing, reducing the number of layer parameters while preserving their interdependencies. A metric-learning discriminator was employed to maximize perceptual quality by optimizing the approximate perceptual evaluation scores. On the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset, QC-GAN achieved a Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) score of 3.48 with only 0.89M parameters, delivering a performance comparable to state-of-the-art models at less than half their size. A 35K-parameter variant achieved a PESQ score of 3.23, surpassing conventional methods with significantly fewer parameters. Evaluation on the DNS-Challenge 3 dataset further confirmed generalization to real-world conditions.
column7: Shogo Yamauchi(The Asahi Shimbun Company); Hideaki Tamori(The Asahi Shimbun Company); Makoto Sakai(The Asahi Shimbun Company); Yosuke Yamano(The Asahi Shimbun Company); Tohru Nitta(Tokyo Woman's Christian University)

column4: SEMamba++: A General Speech Restoration Framework Leveraging Global, Local, and Periodic Spectral Patterns
column6: General speech restoration demands techniques that can interpret complex speech structures under various distortions. While State-Space Models like SEMamba have advanced the state-of-the-art in speech denoising, they are not inherently optimized for critical speech characteristics, such as spectral periodicity or multi-resolution frequency analysis. In this work, we introduce an architecture tailored to incorporate speech-specific features as inductive biases. In particular, we propose the Global, Local, and Periodic (GLP) module, a frequency feature extraction block that effectively and efficiently leverages the properties of frequency bins. Then, we design a multi-resolution parallel time-frequency dual-processing block to capture diverse spectral patterns, and a learnable mapping to further enhance model performance. With all our ideas combined, the proposed SEMamba++ achieves the best performance among multiple baseline models while remaining computationally efficient.
column7: Yongjoon Lee(Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)); Jung-Woo Choi(Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST))

column4: ABSE-NET: A Lightweight Neural Model for Active Binaural Speech Enhancement in Open-Fit Hearing Aids
column6: Open-fit hearing aids have attracted growing attention due to their superior wearing comfort. However, the open-fit design inevitably causes acoustic leakage into the ear canal, degrading the performance of existing binaural speech enhancement (BSE). To this end, we propose ABSE-NET, an active BSE framework integrating active noise control (ANC) with BSE to jointly enhance target speech and suppress acoustic leakage. The ABSE-NET pipeline cascades a binaural MVDR (BMVDR) with a lightweight neural network (LNN). The former achieves a coarse BSE, whereas the latter simultaneously cancels acoustic leakage and compensates for BMVDR-induced distortion. The LNN uses an encoder-decoder with a feature fusion module, which includes frequency-time dependency learning and convolutional attention blocks. Unlike traditional BSE+ANC solutions via adaptive filtering, ABSE-NET needs no in-ear microphone in practical deployment. Experiments validate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods. Code repository: https://github.com/Bream101/ABSE-NET.
column7: De Hu(Inner Mongolia University); Xue Du(Inner Mongolia University); Qingyin Zhao(Inner Mongolia University); Qintuya Si(Inner Mongolia University)

column4: A Fast Solver for Interpolating Stochastic Differential Equation Diffusion Models for Speech Restoration
column6: Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DPMs) are a well-established class of diffusion models for unconditional image generation, while SGMSE+ is a well-established conditional diffusion model for speech enhancement. One of the downsides of diffusion models is that solving the reverse process requires many evaluations of a large Neural Network. Although advanced fast sampling solvers have been developed for DPMs, they are not directly applicable to models such as SGMSE+ due to differences in their diffusion processes. Specifically, DPMs transform between the data distribution and a standard Gaussian distribution, whereas SGMSE+ interpolates between the target distribution and a noisy observation. This work first develops a formalism of interpolating Stochastic Differential Equations (iSDEs) that includes SGMSE+, and second proposes a solver for iSDEs. The proposed solver enables fast sampling with as few as 10 Neural Network evaluations across multiple speech restoration tasks.
column7: Bunlong Lay(University of Hamburg; HITeC Hamburg); Timo Gerkmann(University of Hamburg)

column4: Explicit Context-Driven Neural Acoustic Modeling for High-Fidelity RIR Generation
column6: Realistic sound simulation plays a critical role in many applications. A key element in sound simulation is the room impulse response (RIR), which characterizes how sound propagates within a given space. Recent studies have applied neural implicit methods to learn RIR using context information collected from the environment, such as scene images. However, these approaches do not effectively leverage explicit geometric information from the environment. To further exploit neural implicit models with direct geometric features, we present MiNAF, which queries a rough room mesh at given locations and extracts distance distributions as an explicit representation of local context. Our approach demonstrates that incorporating explicit local geometric features can better guide the model in generating more accurate RIR predictions. Through comparisons with conventional and state-of-the-art methods, we show that MiNAF performs competitively across various evaluation metrics.
column7: Chen Si(University of California San Diego); Qianyi Wu(Monash University); Chaitanya Amballa(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Romit Roy Choudhury(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)

column4: SCNet: Enhancing GAN-based Speech Generation with Subband Condition Network and Magnitude-aware Phase Loss
column6: Recent speech generation has been predominantly driven by GAN-based networks aimed at high-quality waveform synthesis from mel-spectrograms. However, these methods often operate as black-box models, leading to the loss of inherent spectral information. In this work, we propose SCNet, a GAN-based vocoder augmented with a Subband Condition Network to address this issue. Specifically, SCNet leverages a subband signal predicted by a lightweight condition network as prior knowledge. This subband signal is then transformed via STFT to obtain Fourier coefficients, which are integrated into the backbone for the enhanced reconstruction. Additionally, to mitigate the phase wrapping, we introduce a magnitude-aware phase loss that computes instantaneous phase errors weighted by the corresponding magnitude, emphasizing regions with higher energy. Experimental results demonstrate that SCNet achieves superior performance in both objective and subjective evaluations for high-quality speech generation.
column7: Nan Xu(Tencent); Mingxue Yang(UESTC‌)

column4: The Role of Laryngeal Position in the Articulation of American English Velar Stop Consonants
column6: This study re-examines the articulation of voiceless /k/ and voiced /ɡ/ velar stop consonants in American English (AE) by modeling movements of the hyoid bone (HY) and the tongue dorsum (TD) as articulatory gestures using dynamic analysis of ultrasound tongue recordings and multivariate statistical inference methods. HY was found to raise and advance for /k/ and lower and retract for /ɡ/ when TD reaches its target, both of which correlate with the high f0 peak for /k/ and the low f0 peak for /ɡ/ during their following and preceding vowels. /ɡ/ was produced with longer, larger, and faster TD raising toward the velar surface, indicating that /ɡ/ is conditioned by the full spatiotemporal expansion of the tongue with the maximal linguovelar contact. This study suggests that varying degrees of expansion of the tongue, linguovelar contact, and laryngeal positioning simultaneously condition the articulation of AE velar stops, all of which relate to their acoustic correlates.
column7: Daejin Kim(University of New Mexico)

column4: Band-Limited Cepstral Analysis of Speaker Sensitivity in Forensic Voice Comparison
column6: This study investigates where speaker-sensitive frequency regions (sub-bands) are located and how much speaker-discriminative information each region encodes. Likelihood-ratio-based forensic voice comparison experiments were conducted using Band-Limited Cepstral Coefficient (BLCC) matrices derived from a systematic scan of the 0–8 kHz full-band range with 0.6 kHz and 1.2 kHz sub bands. Approximately 30 seconds of running speech from 162 native male Australian English speakers were analysed. The results show that although all sub-bands contain useful speaker-specific information, frequencies above approximately 7kHz are the least informative, while the 0–0.6 kHz and 4–6 kHz regions provide strong speaker discriminative cues. The findings also illustrate the effectiveness of the BLCC method in accessing and analysing any local spectral region of interest.
column7: Shunichi Ishihara(Australian National University); Satoru Tsuge(Daido University); Frantz Clermont(Australian National University)

column4: Speaker-Specific and Language-Dependent Temporal Organization in Bilingual Political Speech
column6: Speech rhythm helps structure persuasive speech, but most empirical work examines monolingual English. This study asks how politicians organize timing when speaking Luxembourgish and French. We analyze 400 sentences from ten politicians, annotated for segments and pauses. We compute rhythm metrics, including means, variability, and pairwise variability indices for consonants and vowels. We quantify speaker and language contributions and test within-speaker language effects with paired t-tests. Results show that consonant-based metrics retain speaker-specific signatures, whereas vowel-based metrics are largely driven by language choice. French tokens display longer and more variable vowels and vocalic intervals, while consonant timing differences are smaller. No robust language by gender interactions emerge. These findings show that language choice systematically reorganizes rhythmic timing in bilingual public speech.
column7: Nina Hosseini-Kivanani(University of Luxembourg; Radio Télévision Luxembourg); Nafiseh Taghva(Shiraz University); Peter Gilles(University of Luxembourg); Oliver Niebuhr(University of Southern Denmark)

column4: Revisiting the NZE front vowel shift: evidence from New Zealand's largest and most linguistically diverse city
column6: Auckland is New Zealand's largest and most demographically diverse city, yet it has been largely ignored in research on New Zealand English (NZE). Recent work on Modern NZE in Auckland and the rediscovery of key historical commentary suggests the city has played a role in leading sound changes that make NZE distinct. This data also raises questions about the trajectory of NZE's much-discussed Short Front Vowel Shift. This paper explores 100 years of sound change in Auckland through a preliminary acoustic and statistical analysis of NZE's iconic /e, æ, ɪ/ vowels. We compare contemporary Aucklanders' (n=67) speech across two age groups with that of historical Aucklanders (n=8), integrating real and apparent-time analyses. Results show a rise and subsequent fall of /e/ and /æ/ over time, and early centralisation of /ɪ/ among historical speakers, contrasting previous research. Further investigation suggests /ɪ/ centralisation was initially phonologically conditioned by adjacent laterals.
column7: Brooke Ross(University of Auckland); Catherine Watson(University of Auckland); Elaine Ballard(University of Auckland); Miriam Meyerhoff(University of Oxford)

column4: Effects of body position on vowel formants in New Zealand English
column6: Speech is produced in everyday contexts that involve different body positions, yet body position is rarely modelled in acoustic analyses. This study tests whether static body position (supine, sitting, standing) affects vowel formants F1 and F2 in New Zealand English using a within-speaker /hVd/ list (11 vowels) from 9 speakers. Linear mixed-effects models with vowel, age, and sex show small position-related differences, with the clearest contrasts involving supine relative to sitting and standing. Position effects vary by vowel, age, and sex. Vowel-specific contrasts are significant for a small subset of vowels, most clearly in high-front categories for F2. In this dataset, F1 position differences are clearer for female speakers, and F2 position differences are significant in the younger female condition. These findings suggest that body position should be documented when interpreting or combining vowel-formant measurements across recording configurations.
column7: Qing Guan(The University of Auckland); Catherine I. Watson(The University of Auckland); C. T. Justine Hui(The University of Auckland)

column4: From onset to coda: spectral variation in normative Polish /s/ produced by children
column6: Sibilant fricatives are shaped by multiple linguistic and developmental factors, yet word-position effects in perceptually normative Polish /s/ remain underdescribed. This pilot study examines whether word-initial, word-medial, and word-final positions are associated with acoustic differences in /s/ produced by Polish-speaking preschool children aged 5-8 years. The dataset comprised 816 /s/ tokens from 102 children. Acoustic measures included spectral centroid (CoG), skewness, kurtosis, and spectral flux. Word position significantly affected the spectral properties of /s/: the strongest pairwise differences was present within word-initial and word-medial tokens (CoG, spectral flux, kurtosis, skewness), whereas medial-final contrasts were generally smaller and often non-significant, except for skewness.
column7: Joanna Walczak(Silesian University of Technology); Oliwia Skórzewska(Silesian University of Technology); Zuzanna Miodońska(Silesian University of Technology)

column4: Multi-Level Privacy-Preserving Dementia Detection from Speech via Targeted Adversarial Obfuscation and Representation Learning
column6: Speech recordings used for dementia detection inherently expose speaker identity, raising critical privacy concerns. Existing methods typically address only singular threats and fail to resolve the privacy–utility trade-off. We propose a multi-level framework designed to neutralize two distinct eavesdropping vectors. At the signal level, a Cumulative Signal Attack (CSA) concentrates perturbations in keyword-aligned regions to maximize transcription error (Word Error Rate WER = 1.00) while preserving vital prosodic biomarkers. At the feature level, a Gradient Reversal Layer (GRL) with Mutual Information (MI)-guided noise injection suppresses speaker-discriminative dimensions while retaining dementia-relevant diagnostic structure. Evaluated on the DementiaBank Pitt Corpus, our framework achieves near-chance speaker identification (Equal Error Rate EER = 0.59, F1 = 0.003) while maintaining strong dementia classification performance (F1 = 0.78, AUC = 0.86).
column7: Henriette Flore Kenne(University of Massachusetts Lowell); Raphael Anaadumba(University of Massachusetts Lowell); Mohammad Arif Ul Alam(University of Massachusetts Lowell)

column4: An Acoustic Investigation of Mid Front Vowel Harmony in Assamese
column6: Previous descriptions of Assamese have reported a pattern of vowel harmony in which a mid vowel is raised when followed by a close vowel in the subsequent syllable. Articulatory studies based on a single dialect have offered mixed findings, and systematic acoustic studies remain limited. This study provides an acoustic analysis of /ɛ/-raising in harmonic contexts across the three major dialect regions of Assamese. The data were drawn from 18 adult speakers (3 male and 3 female speakers per region), including both wordlist and connected speech recordings. F1 and F2 measurements were analysed using linear mixed-effects models with harmonic context, vowel duration, dialect, speech style, and gender as predictors. The results show consistent /ɛ/-raising in harmonic contexts across dialects. Although the harmony effect was evident across all dialects and speech styles, its magnitude varied across dialect–style combinations, particularly in vowel height (F1).
column7: Saurabh Nath(The Australian National University); Rosey Billington(The Australian National University); Danielle Barth(The Australian National University)
