column4: Automatic Detection of Stress from Speech in the Trier Social Stress Test
column6: Automatically detecting stress in speech provides an unobtrusive way to gain insights relevant to behavioral research or clinical assessment. This study investigates the automatic differentiation between a stressful and non-stressful situation, and the prediction of physiological and affective stress responses. Speech data was collected from 50 participants who either completed the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) or a non-stressful control condition. With a processing pipeline that included speaker diarization and machine learning models, we achieved stress detection performance significantly above a mean baseline. Moreover, relevant physiological and affective stress responses were partially predictable from acoustic-prosodic features. Feature-importance analyses identified the most informative predictors contributing to model performance. The findings demonstrate that speech can serve as a meaningful and unobtrusive indicator of multiple dimensions of the human stress response.
column7: Hanna Drimalla(Bielefeld University); Wieland R. Cremer(Bielefeld University); Christine Kraus(Bielefeld University); Oliver T. Wolf(Ruhr University Bochum)

column4: Looking for Affect in Spontaneous Finnish Speech through Linguistic Interpretability
column6: Existing research on affect in speech has shown how acoustic surface characteristics and content-related linguistic aspects of speech both relate to perceived emotional arousal and valence. However, it is not clear what the relative contributions of these two factors are in the perceptual process. This is especially true for Finnish, for which most existing studies focus on either acoustic-phonetic or text analysis. This paper presents a study where we systematically explore the combinatory role of text- and audio-based features in modeling the human perception of valence and arousal using a newly released affective speech corpus for spontaneous Finnish. We show that the combination of text- and audio-based features improves valence regression results over the individual modalities, whereas for arousal regression the complementary effect is not substantial. The results support prior findings from other languages, providing new data and knowledge on spontaneous Finnish speech.
column7: Kalle Lahtinen(Tampere University); Liisa Mustanoja(Tampere University); Okko Räsänen(Tampere University)

column4: Umm... With Transformers? Insights from Filled Pause Use across Four Slavic Parliaments
column6: Filled pauses (FPs) are a universal feature of spontaneous speech, yet most studies rely on small, single-language corpora, limiting the generalisability of their findings. We analyse ~4,000 hours of parliamentary speech across four related Slavic languages (Croatian, Czech, Polish, Serbian). FP occurrence is obtained via transformer-based automatic detection, while FP rate is modelled using Generalised Estimating Equations (GEE) with Mundlak correction to distinguish within-from between-speaker effects. We replicate a negative association of age and speech rate with FP rate, but find that gender effects are language-specific and directionally opposite to most prior literature. Novel analyses of sentiment, political orientation, and power status reveal a consistent positive association between sentiment and FP rate, alongside parliament-specific modulation by orientation and power status, with opposition speakers tending toward lower FP rates than governing coalition speakers.
column7: Ivan Porupski(Jožef Stefan Institute); Branimir Dropuljić(TransUnion; University of Zagreb); Nikola Ljubešić(Jožef Stefan Institute; University of Ljubljana; Institute of Contemporary History)

column4: Eye and Mouth Cues in Audiovisual Perception of Mandarin Irony: Evidence from Eye-tracking and Facial Masking
column6: Irony is a form of nonliteral language whose comprehension involves integrating auditory and visual cues. Although prosodic cues have been widely studied across languages, the role of facial cues remains underexplored. This study investigated perceptual strategies for different facial regions in decoding Mandarin ironic speech. 44 native speakers completed a perception experiment including ironic blame and praise and their literal counterparts under Visual-only, Audiovisual (quiet), and Audiovisual (noise) conditions. Eye-tracking measured fixation duration and pupil dilation. Results showed distinct visual patterns: ironic blame elicited longer fixations on the eyes, with no pupil-size differences across regions, whereas ironic praise prompted greater attention to the mouth across modalities, with larger pupil size during eye fixations in the quiet audiovisual condition. These findings reveal asymmetric visual processing across irony types and inform multimodal intention recognition.
column7: Shifeng Xia(Nanjing University of Science and Technology); Shanpeng Li(Nanjing University of Science and Technology)

column4: Do Speech Emphasis Models Generalize across Languages and Emotions?
column6: Prosodic emphasis varies across languages, emotions, and speaking styles, yet existing emphasis detection models are largely trained and evaluated on monolingual neutral read speech. We introduce MMEE (Multilingual Multi-Emotion Emphasis), a corpus of 10,000 professionally recorded expressive utterances (14.13 hours) across 7 languages and 34 emotion/style categories, with three-level perceptual labels (10 annotations per sample). We benchmark two state-of-the-art architectures under monolingual, cross-lingual, multilingual, cross-emotion, cross-dataset, and data-scale settings. Monolingual models show limited zero-shot transfer, degrading across typologically distant languages, while multilingual training substantially improves robustness. Models transfer robustly between high- and low-arousal emotions; bidirectional transfer between synthetic and perceptual benchmarks suggests shared prosodic structure; and performance stays robust even at smaller training scales.
column7: Megan Wei(Adobe Research; Brown University); Deepali Aneja(Adobe Research); Jiaqi Su(Adobe Research); Yunyun Wang(Adobe Research); Haonan Chen(Adobe Research); Zeyu Jin(Adobe Research)

column4: KuralHub: Exposing Typological Capability Frontiers in Multilingual Speech Emotion Recognition
column6: Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) advancements are constrained by high-resource bias, limiting global access. To address this, we introduce KuralHub, an open-science initiative democratizing SER for under-resourced languages. We evaluate 11 self-supervised models (WavLM, HuBERT, Wav2vec 2.0, Whisper) across 33 datasets in 29 diverse languages. Beyond standard benchmarking, our study reveals a critical typological bias: cross-lingual transferability is dictated more by structural linguistic properties than pre-training data volume. While models easily adapt to Mandarin or Amharic, they systematically fail on the Dravidian family. Crucially, we demonstrate that simply scaling model parameters fails to resolve this bottleneck. By exposing these linguistic capability frontiers, KuralHub provides a vital roadmap for developing equitable, typologically-aware speech technologies for all speakers.
column7: Luxshan Thavarasa(University of Moratuwa); Jubeerathan Thevakumar(University of Moratuwa); Thanikan Sivatheepan(University of Moratuwa); Uthayasanker Thayasivam(University of Moratuwa)

column4: YUE-PUB-Speech: A Speech-based Pragmatic Understanding Benchmark for Cantonese
column6: Pragmatic understanding is essential for natural human communication, yet most existing studies focus on text-only settings. In this paper we introduce YUE-PUB-Speech, the first multimodal pragmatic dataset for Cantonese, a low-resource language, constructed by sampling pragmatically rich texts and recording corresponding speech by trained annotators. The corpus provides paired text-speech instances that capture pragmatic meaning in spoken language without requiring fine-grained phonological or word-level alignment. Baseline experiments show that incorporating speech signals improves pragmatic understanding compared to text-only models, highlighting the importance of multimodal resources for pragmatic research in speech and language processing.
column7: Yajie Wen(South China Normal University); Ziwei Gong(Columbia University); Chengyan Wu(South China Normal University; Sun Yat-sen University); Xiyun Gong(Guangzhou College of Commerce); Yun Xue(South China Normal University); Julia Hirschberg(Columbia University); Bolei Ma(LMU Munich & Munich Center for Machine Learning)

column4: TIMBRE: Layer-Wise Cross-Lingual Speech Emotion Recognition Across 49 Layers and 26 Corpora
column6: We present the first large-scale layer-wise cross-lingual speech emotion recognition analysis: 49 layers of wav2vec2-xls-r-1b across 26 corpora, 23 languages and 14 families, a 49×26×26 tensor of 31,850 experiments. Under linear probing of mean-pooled representations, cross-corpus transfer peaks at layer 15 (31% depth, F1=0.392), the CRIS layer, and collapses by 24.6% at layer 45. Typology is associated with the shape of the layer profile: Romance languages show a U-shaped relative advantage, and the tonal advantage grows with depth. On the same 26×26 matrix with identical classifiers, mean-pooled wav2vec2 outperforms 27-dim acoustic features by 41% (F1: 0.355 vs. 0.252); acoustic features retain 71% of this baseline at a 3.7×10^7-fold lower complexity and prevail on only 3 of 26 corpora. Per-corpus expressiveness and elicitation style, rather than group or family membership, drive overall transferability.
column7: Anatoly Marchenko(Independent Researcher)

column4: Hearing Smiles in the Crowd: How Babble Noise Shapes Smiled Speech Perception
column6: In everyday communication, the auditory perception of smiled speech can be hindered by noise. We examined how multi-talker babble noise affected human auditory perception of smile-like speech, consisting of affective amused and mechanical spread-lip speech. Listeners completed two categorization tasks: 1) smile-like detection (smile-like vs. neutral speech) and, within smile-like speech, 2) smile-type categorization (amused vs. spread-lip speech). Results showed that increasing noise reduced perceptual sensitivity in both tasks while systematically altering response bias. In Task 1, as noise increased, participants' accuracy not only decreased but they were also less inclined to report hearing a smile. Similarly, in Task 2, an initial bias toward "amused" responses in quiet reversed under strong noise. These findings demonstrate that smile perception in noise reflects not only degraded sensory evidence but also adaptive shifts in decision strategy under uncertainty.
column7: Rong Li(University of Twente); Esther Janse(Radboud University); Dirk Heylen(University of Twente); Khiet Truong(Radboud University; University of Twente)

column4: Stress Detection Across Daily Activities: A Context-Aware Multimodal Framework with Trajectory and Ambient Speech
column6: Stress detection is widely studied for mental health monitoring, with most approaches relying on physiological signals such as HRV. These methods require wearable devices, limiting scalability in practical deployment. Audio signals, particularly speech, provide a non-intrusive alternative, yet models relying solely on sound lack robustness across contexts. Stress perception is inherently context-dependent and influenced by spatial factors beyond speech alone, especially for hospital workers in high-pressure clinical environments. This study proposes a context-aware framework extracting distinct features from speech and mobility trajectories. By employing a late fusion mechanism to combine vocal and movement embeddings, the proposed approach improves robustness, outperforming unimodal audio baselines on a hospital worker dataset. Experimental results show the framework improves the F1 score by 9.32% and the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) by 0.038 over the audio-only baseline.
column7: Wei-Heng Huang(National Tsing Hua University); Woan-Shiuan Chien(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Chi-Chun Lee(National Tsing Hua University)

column4: T-ORR: Text-Anchored Orthogonal Residual Rectification for Robust Multimodal Sarcasm Detection
column6: Sarcasm relies on a covert contradiction between intended connotation and literal text. In Multimodal Sarcasm Detection (MSD), conventional fusion models often obscure sparse incongruity cues by entangling features within a joint space. We propose Text-Anchored Orthogonal Residual Rectification (T-ORR), reframing MSD as a signal separation problem. T-ORR utilizes Dynamic Locality-Constrained Alignment to adaptively focus non-verbal streams on the specific words they modify. A Structure-Preserving Geometric Decomposition then employs QR projection to disentangle these signals into semantic Resonance and modality-specific Dissonance. Rather than standard fusion, a Contrastive Incongruity Routing (CIR) mechanism models the semantic distance between literal and incongruous states. Evaluations on MUStARD and MUStARD++ yield state-of-the-art results, suggesting geometric decoupling effectively isolates multimodal incongruities.
column7: Qi Chen(Tianjin Foreign Studies University); Junyi Chen(Beijing Language and Culture University); Jiabin Han(Tianjin Foreign Studies University); Hongjiao Yang(Tianjin Foreign Studies University)

column1: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 4 - Poster 4 - Speaker Privacy Preservation and Anonymization

column4: VerAno: Speaker Anonymization via Self-Supervised Tokenization and Conditional Flow Matching
column6: Effective speaker anonymization faces a critical bottleneck: balancing robust privacy protection with the preservation of downstream utility. To resolve this trade-off, we introduce VerAno, a novel framework that leverages a Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) to tokenize Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) speech features. By strategically constraining codebook size, VerAno achieves the self-supervised disentanglement of speaker-specific features from speaker-independent features. These discrete tokens are fused with pretrained speaker embeddings and processed by a flow-matching transformer to synthesize high-fidelity acoustic representations. Experimental evaluations on the VoicePrivacy Challenge datasets demonstrate that VerAno substantially outperforms baseline models. Furthermore, the system generalizes favorably across languages, demonstrating promising cross-lingual capabilities when applied to unseen data.
column7: Ngoc Hung Le(Soongsil University); Thien-Phuc Doan(Soongsil University); Thien An Nguyen(Soongsil University); Kyujin Kim(Soongsil University); Souhwan Jung(Soongsil University)

column4: Controlled Generation of Synthetic Speaker Vectors for Voice Anonymization
column6: Voice anonymization benefits from transparent control over the pseudo-speaker's voice. Anonymization approaches based on resynthesis substitute the original speaker vector with a different, often artificial, vector, but this does not allow for controlling which original speaker attributes are preserved. To address this, we extend one existing WGAN-based artificial vector generation method with attribute-label conditioning. We also introduce diffusion models as a robust alternative for generating speaker vectors, utilizing classifier guidance for label-informed synthesis. Evaluated using the Voice Privacy Challenge 2024 suite, both approaches demonstrate strong attribute control while maintaining competitive privacy and utility. Furthermore, we propose measures for diversity, originality, and naturalness of synthesized embeddings. Combined with TTS performance on challenging speech, these measures enable the selection of optimal generator configurations for the anonymization pipeline.
column7: Ekaterina Kolos(University of Stuttgart); Sarina Meyer(Institute for Natural Language Processing, University of Stuttgart); Ngoc Thang Vu(Institute for Natural Language Processing, University of Stuttgart)

column4: Child-Centric Voice Anonymization in Single and Multi-Speaker Speech via Domain-Adapted SSL Models
column6: Voice anonymization aims to protect speaker identity while preserving linguistic content and speech usability. However, most anonymization systems are developed on adult speech, leading to degraded performance when applied to child speech. This paper investigates child-centric anonymization by adapting a self-supervised learning (SSL) based anonymization pipeline to the child speech domain. The system is adapted using child speech from the MyST corpus and evaluated under both single-speaker and two-speaker mixture conditions. Experimental results show that child-domain adaptation improves intelligibility and perceptual quality while maintaining strong privacy protection. Extending the approach to multi-speaker further demonstrates that combining target speaker extraction with child-adapted anonymization provides privacy protection while preserving conversational structure. These findings highlight the importance of child-specific adaptation for practical speech anonymization systems.
column7: Pranav Tushar(Singapore Institute of Technology); Xiao Xiao Miao(Duke Kunshan University); Rong Tong(Singapore Institute of Technology)

column4: Reducing Speaker Residual by Considering Pinhole Effect in Voice Anonymization
column6: Voice anonymization aims to protect privacy by suppressing speaker identity while preserving linguistic content and prosody. However, residual speaker attributes in non-identity representations may still increase linkability and weaken privacy protection. To this end, this paper proposes a fine-tuning strategy with a pinhole loss for well-trained voice anonymization frameworks to further reduce residual speaker attributes. Inspired by the pinhole effect, the pinhole loss measures the linkability of anonymized utterances from the same source speaker. By minimizing this loss, linkability is reduced, thereby improving privacy protection. Experiments on multiple anonymization frameworks, pseudo-speaker generation methods, and datasets show improved privacy protection while maintaining utility. Audio samples can be found in https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Pinhole-loss-fine-tunning-4628.
column7: Zeyan Liu(University of Science and Technology of China); Weili Jiang(Ministry of Public Security); Liping Chen(University of Science and Technology of China); Kong Aik Lee(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Boyu Zhao(Ministry of Public Security); Kai Gao(Ministry of Public Security); Zhenhua Ling(University of Science and Technology of China)

column4: StreamVoiceAnon+: Emotion-Preserving Streaming Speaker Anonymization via Frame-Level Acoustic Distillation
column6: We address the challenge of preserving emotional content in streaming speaker anonymization (SA). Neural audio codec language models trained for audio continuation tend to degrade source emotion: content tokens discard emotional information, and the model defaults to dominant acoustic patterns rather than preserving paralinguistic attributes. We propose supervised finetuning with neutral-emotion utterance pairs from the same speaker, combined with frame-level emotion distillation on acoustic token hidden states. All modifications are confined to finetuning, which takes less than 2 hours on 4 GPUs and adds zero inference latency overhead, while maintaining a competitive 180ms streaming latency. On the VoicePrivacy 2024 protocol, our approach achieves a 49.2% UAR (emotion preservation) with 5.77% WER (intelligibility), a +24% relative UAR improvement over the baseline (39.7%→49.2%) and +10% over the emotion-prompt variant (44.6% UAR), while maintaining strong privacy (EER 49.0%).1
column7: Nikita Kuzmin(Nanyang Technological University; A*STAR); Kong Aik Lee(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Eng Siong Chng(Nanyang Technological University)

column4: Personal Attribute Leakage in Federated Speech Models
column6: Federated learning is a method proposed for privacy-preserving training of machine learning models. In this paper, we analyze the vulnerability of ASR models to attribute inference attacks in the federated setting. We test a non-parametric white-box attack method under a passive threat model on three ASR models: Wav2Vec2, HuBERT, and Whisper. The attack operates solely on weight differentials without access to raw speech from target speakers. We demonstrate attack feasibility on sensitive demographic and clinical attributes: gender, age, accent, emotion, and impaired speech. Our findings indicate that attributes that are underrepresented or absent in the pre-training data are more vulnerable to such inference attacks. In particular, information about accents can be reliably inferred from all models. Our findings expose previously undocumented vulnerabilities in federated ASR models and offer insights towards improved security.
column7: Hamdan Al-Ali(MBZUAI); Ali Reza Ghavamipour(Maastricht University); Tommaso Caselli(University of Groningen); Fatih Turkmen(University of Groningen); Zeerak Talat(University of Edinburgh); Hanan Aldarmaki(MBZUAI)

column4: A Large-Scale Per-Speaker Analysis of Re-identification Risk in Speech Anonymization
column6: Speech anonymization is commonly evaluated using average-case metrics such as the equal error rate, which can hide large disparities in re-identification risks across individuals. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale per-speaker privacy analysis using a linkability-based metric under a worst-case scenario. Nearly 5,000 speakers are evaluated across multiple anonymization systems, attacker architectures, and conversation lengths. While linkability scores are highly polarized at the speaker level, the sets of easy to re-identify and hard to re-identify speakers vary substantially across configurations. We show that no single factor explains speaker vulnerability. Instead, the re-identification risk emerges from the interaction between the attacker, the anonymizer, and the amount of available speech. These results challenge the notion of intrinsic speaker-level privacy risks and emphasize the need for evaluation protocols that are explicitly conditioned on the attacker and anonymizer.
column7: Orane Dufour(Université de Lorraine); Paul Magron(Université de Lorraine); Mickael Rouvier(Avignon University); Emmanuel Vincent(Université de Lorraine)

column4: Privacy-Preserving Speaker Verification with Multi-Granularity Feature Obfuscation
column6: To counter eavesdropping threats from recent advances in speech technology, this paper proposes a privacy-preserving speaker verification (SV) framework that protects both linguistic content and biometric identity. We leverage FAcodec to explicitly remove content-bearing information and selectively apply multi-granularity feature obfuscation to the remaining noncontent representations, preserving speaker-discriminative cues while discouraging faithful waveform reconstruction. Our results further indicate that ASR-based metrics such as Word Error Rate (WER) alone may not fully reflect perceptual privacy: even without content tokens, reconstructed speech can remain partially intelligible to listeners despite high WER. By substantially reducing perceptual intelligibility, our approach achieves an EER of 2.35% on VoxCeleb1-O, a 54.7% relative improvement over prior state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating a favorable balance between biometric utility and linguistic privacy.
column7: Hanseul Kim(Chosun University); Nam In Park(National Forensic Service); Chanjun Chun(Chosun University; Glosori Inc.)

column4: Imperceptible Voiceprint Protection via Human-Machine Perception Discrepancy Feature Disentanglement
column6: The proliferation of zero-shot voice cloning models increases the risk of unauthorized speaker impersonation. Although adversarial perturbation provides an effective defense, existing methods face a fundamental trade-off: strong perturbations introduce audible artifacts, while imperceptible ones may lack robustness when transferred to unseen systems. We introduce a two-stage framework exploiting human-machine perception discrepancy. We first train a disentanglement network to separate content and speaker information, then inject perturbations into the speaker embedding space where machines are sensitive but humans are not. Experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves 87.2% defense success rate, surpassing state-of-the-art embedding-level defenses by 7%, while maintaining a high MOS of 4.18 and demonstrating strong transferability to black-box voice cloning systems.
column7: Chenlong Xue(Army Engineering University of PLA); Meng Sun(Army Engineering University of PLA); Qiang Zhang(Army Engineering University of PLA); Xiongwei Zhang(Army Engineering University of PLA); Kunyuan Li(Army Engineering University of PLA); Yuan Liao(Chinese University of Hong Kong); Xiaoyi Ge(Information Support Force Engineering University); Kui Yao(Army Engineering University of PLA)

column4: Towards Privacy-Preserving ASR: Speaker-Level Machine Unlearning
column6: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems are commonly designed to transcribe linguistic content independently of speaker identity. However, speaker-specific information can persist within the latent representations of ASR models, raising privacy concerns when training data includes sensitive individuals. While machine unlearning has been studied in several speech tasks, applying speaker unlearning to ASR remains challenging due to the strong entanglement of linguistic and speaker-related information in speech representations. In this work, we conduct a layer-wise analysis of Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) based ASR representations, revealing that speaker identity is primarily encoded in intermediate encoder layers. Based on this observation, we explore a feature-level unlearning strategy that targets these identity structures. Experiments on the VCTK corpus show that the proposed approach removes the influence of specific speakers while maintaining robust transcription performance.
column7: Seaone Ok(Seoul National University); Seungu Han(Seoul National University); Eungbeom Kim(Seoul National University); Kyogu Lee(Seoul National University)

column4: NaVo: Natural Voice Protection against Voice Cloning Attacks via Generative Universal Adversarial Audio
column6: Proactive defense against voice cloning disrupts synthesis by injecting adversarial perturbations. However, prior methods rely on iterative optimization, often causing perceptual distortion and high latency that limit real-time deployment. We propose NaVo, a generative framework that produces natural-sounding universal adversarial audio. NaVo guides a latent diffusion–based text-to-audio model with fine-tuned low-rank adaptation modules tailored to gender and acoustic categories such as rain, music, and babble, enabling high-fidelity, speaker-independent adversarial audio generation. Unlike optimization-based approaches, NaVo supports real-time protection through simple audio mixing without gradient-based inference. It achieves a 76% defense success rate against a widely used commercial voice cloning system in a black-box setting. By jointly addressing universality, audio quality, and computational efficiency, NaVo offers a practical solution for proactive voice protection.
column7: Seoyoung Park(Soongsil University); Seungmin Kim(Soongsil University); Sohee Park(Soongsil University); Dain Kim(Soongsil University); Thien An Nguyen(Soongsil University); Thien-Phuc Doan(Soongsil University); Souhwan Jung(Soongsil University); Daeseon Choi(Soongsil University)

column4: DAST: A Dual-Stream Voice Anonymization Attacker with Staged Training
column6: Voice anonymization masks vocal traits while preserving linguistic content, which may still leak speaker-specific patterns. To assess and strengthen privacy evaluation, we propose a dual-stream attacker that fuses spectral and self-supervised learning features via parallel encoders with a three-stage training strategy. Stage I establishes foundational speaker-discriminative representations. Stage II leverages the shared identity-transformation characteristics of voice conversion and anonymization, exposing the model to diverse converted speech to build cross-system robustness. Stage III provides lightweight adaptation to target anonymized data. Results on the VoicePrivacy Attacker Challenge (VPAC) dataset demonstrate that Stage II is the primary driver of generalization, enabling strong attacking performance on unseen anonymization datasets. With Stage III, fine-tuning on only 10% of the target anonymization dataset surpasses current state-of-the-art attackers in terms of EER.1 .
column7: Ridwan Arefeen(Singapore Institute of Technology); Xiaoxiao Miao(Duke Kunshan University); Rong Tong(Singapore Institute of Technology); Timothy Liu(NVIDIA AI Technology Centre); Aik Beng Ng(NVIDIA AI Technology Centre); Simon See(NVIDIA AI Technology Centre)

column4: Carrier-Aware Sound Zone Control for Parametric Array Loudspeakers
column6: Parametric array loudspeakers (PALs) exploit ultrasonic carrier and nonlinear self-demodulation to generate directional speech and audio sound, offering advantages for spatial audio reproduction. While recent work extends linear-acoustic sound zone control (SZC) to PAL arrays by optimizing sideband excitations and achieves high acoustic contrast (AC), the carrier--essential for demodulation--remains unexplored as a control variable. We propose a carrier-aware SZC framework for PALs, treating the carrier as a new control dimension, with an alternating optimization for sideband and carrier weights. Simulations and experiments show that our method outperforms sideband-only control, yielding higher AC and demodulation efficiency. In experiments, broadband gains of 11.2 dB in AC and 7.0 dB in target-zone SPL are achieved under identical power constraints. The results establish the carrier as a key control variable for more efficient, high-performance spatial audio and speech rendering with PALs.
column7: Mengtong Li(Nanjing University); Tao Zhuang(Nanjing University); Yu Sun(Samsung Electronics (China)); Shaozhe Li(Nanjing University); Xuxiang Wu(Nanjing University); Jia-Xin Zhong(Nanjing University); Jing Lu(Nanjing University; Horizon Robotics)

column4: A Sparsity-Aware Robust Nonlinear Active Noise Control for Impulsive Noise Environments
column6: Functional link network (FLN) based active noise control (ANC) alogorithms offer strong nonlinear modeling capabilities but inevitably introduce redundant basis functions during expansion, leading to inefficient adaptation and degraded steady-state performance. To improve the performance, we propose a sparsity-aware robust nonlinear ANC algorithm that incorporates a reweighted zero-attracting (RZA) regularization term into the minimum-output-variance constrained filtered-s least mean p-power (MOV-FsLMP) framework. This mechanism acts as an online feature selector, effectively suppressing redundant coefficients induced by FLN expansion while preserving the inherent robustness against impulsive disturbances. Extensive simulations under α-state impulsive noise conditions demonstrate that the proposed algorithm consistently outperforms the conventional MOV-FsLMP, achieving a 1-2 dB improvement in steady-state mean square error (MSE) and a higher active noise reduction (ANR) under identical configurations, validating its practical effectiveness for nonlinear ANC applications.
column7: Hengwei Xu(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Hongqing Liu(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Liming Shi(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Lu Gan(Brunel University)

column4: NCPSZ: A Nonlinear Control Network for Miniature Loudspeakers in Personal Sound Zone Applications
column6: In personal sound zone (PSZ) systems, linear control methods suffer from significant performance degradation on devices with miniature loudspeakers due to severe nonlinear distortion (NLD). To overcome this limitation, we propose a nonlinear control network for PSZ (NCPSZ), a data-driven framework tailored for sound leakage prevention. We introduce an asymmetric dual-network architecture: a high-fidelity modeling network (ModelNet) characterizes the loudspeaker's nonlinear behavior offline, which supervises a lightweight, causal control network (CtrlNet) for real-time operation. Crucially, we employ an "anchor speaker" strategy, where the primary earpiece speaker maintains the target sound pressure in the bright zone (BZ), while the CtrlNet optimizes assisting speakers to actively cancel nonlinear leakage in the dark zone (DZ). Validated in a realistic smartphone leakage-prevention task, NCPSZ achieves a consistent acoustic contrast (AC) improvement of 3.78 dB over the linear VAST baseline and 1.80 dB over a parameter-matched causal CNN, demonstrating effective privacy protection under nonlinear regimes.
column7: Chen Gong(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Lei Zhou(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Chen Huang(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Hongqing Liu(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Liming Shi(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Lu Gan(Brunel University)

column4: LMPAN: A Lightweight Multi-Path Alignment Network for Joint Full-Duplex Acoustic Echo Cancellation and Noise Suppression
column6: We propose a lightweight multi-path alignment network (LMPAN) for on-device joint acoustic echo cancellation (AEC) and noise suppression (NS) in full-duplex spoken dialogue systems. To address hardware-induced distortions and dynamic acoustic conditions, we introduce three core innovations: (1) a multi-path alignment stage correcting temporal and energy mismatches across reference, linear AEC (LAEC) output, and microphone signals; (2) an attention-based mechanism that dynamically integrates enhanced LAEC and microphone features under varying acoustic scenarios; (3) a post-filtering module with a dynamic target generation strategy for downstream tasks (ASR, VAD). Furthermore, we adopt a two-stage training framework leveraging self-supervised learning representations to enhance perceptual quality. Experiments show that LMPAN, with only 480K parameters and 126 MACs, achieves performance comparable to the state-of-the-art lightweight model DeepVQE-S, while ensuring real-time inference capability.
column7: Chengwei Liu(Alibaba); Shaofei Xue(Alibaba); Haoyin Yan(Alibaba); Xiaotao Liang(Alibaba); Zheng Xue(Qwen Business Unit of Alibaba)

column4: Active Constructive Interference for Speech
column6: We introduce a new paradigm for active sound modification: Active Speech Enhancement (ASE). While Active Noise Cancellation (ANC) algorithms focus on suppressing external interference and traditional speech enhancement passively reconstructs degraded speech signals, ASE goes further by actively shaping the speech signal, both attenuating distortions and amplifying speech-relevant frequencies to improve intelligibility and perceptual quality. To enable this, we propose a novel Transformer-Mamba-based architecture, along with a task-specific loss function that jointly optimizes interference suppression and signal enrichment in an acoustic environment. Our method outperforms existing baselines across multiple speech processing tasks, including denoising, dereverberation, and declipping, demonstrating the effectiveness of active, targeted modulation in challenging acoustic environments. A demo and code are publicly available at github.com/ofiryaish/ASE-TM.
column7: Ofir Yaish(Ben-Gurion University of the Negev); Yehuda Mishaly(Tel Aviv University); Eliya Nachmani(Ben-Gurion University of the Negev)

column4: Predictive Directional Selective Fixed-Filter Active Noise Control for Moving Sources via a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network
column6: Directional Selective Fixed-Filter Active Noise Control (D-SFANC) can effectively attenuate noise from different directions by selecting the suitable pre-trained control filter based on the Direction-of-Arrival (DoA) of the current noise. However, this method is weak at tracking the direction variations of non-stationary noise, such as that from a moving source. Therefore, this work proposes a Predictive Directional SFANC (PD-SFANC) method that uses a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN) to capture the hidden temporal dynamics of the moving noise and predict the control filter to cancel future noise. Accordingly, the proposed method can significantly improve its noise-tracking ability and dynamic noise-reduction performance. Furthermore, numerical simulations confirm the superiority of the proposed method for handling moving sources across various movement scenarios, compared to several representative ANC baselines.
column7: Boxiang Wang(Nanyang Technological University); Zhengding Luo(Nanyang Technological University); Dongyuan Shi(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Junwei Ji(Nanyang Technological University); Xiruo Su(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Woon-Seng Gan(Nanyang Technological University)

column4: DDSN: A Physics-Aware Decoupled Dual-Stream Network for Speech Packet Loss Concealment
column6: Packet loss concealment (PLC) restores high-fidelity speech from impaired signals in real-time communication. Existing frequency-domain methods typically process real and imaginary spectra jointly. This coupled modeling overlooks the distinct wrapped phase and magnitude characteristics, causing phase misalignment and structural artifacts. We propose a Wrapped-Phase-Aware Decoupled Dual-Stream Network (DDSN) that explicitly separates magnitude and phase modeling. Using independent streams, DDSN adapts to the specific characteristics of spectral energy and temporal alignment. To facilitate interaction, our Scaled Asymmetric Residual Guidance (SARG) mechanism uses magnitude priors to guide phase reconstruction. A manifold-constrained trigonometric representation maintains the topological consistency of the phase. Experimental results demonstrate DDSN performs favorably against established baselines, maintaining stable reconstruction during long burst losses.
column7: Hao Tian(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Yonghui Liu(Fanvil Link Technology Co., Ltd); Jianbing Liu(Fanvil Link Technology Co., Ltd); Kai Niu(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Zhiqiang He(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications)

column4: A Causal Reference-Enhanced Keep-Speech Active Noise Control Method
column6: This paper proposes a causal, low-latency reference-enhanced keep-speech active noise control (KSANC) method, in which a deep neural network is used to enhance the reference signal by suppressing speech components while retaining noise. As a result, speech components in the error signal can be effectively preserved after control. The proposed method is validated through experiments using measured headphone impulse responses. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach improves speech intelligibility and speech quality in noisy conversational scenarios for headphone applications, compared with all baselines. Moreover, the method exhibits robustness to different speech signals and directions, noise types and directions, as well as varying signal-to-noise ratios. Listening examples are available at https://github.com/RaoLi666/RSE_KSANC.git.
column7: Li Rao(Nanjing University); Xiaobin Rong(Nanjing University; Nanjing Institute of Advanced AI); Yu Sun(Samsung Electronics (China)); Yiming He(Nanjing University); Kai Chen(Nanjing University); Haishan Zou(Nanjing University); Jing Lu(Nanjing University; Nanjing Institute of Advanced AI)

column4: Active Noise Control With a Gain Constraint for Micro-Loudspeakers
column6: The fixed-filter methods are widely employed in active noise control (ANC) systems due to their computational efficiency. They are typically designed to minimize the mean squared sound pressure at the error microphone, thereby attenuating disturbance components across the entire frequency spectrum. Due to the limited low-frequency reproduction capability of micro loudspeakers, this approach is prone to causing mechanical over-excursion. One solution is to cascade a high-pass filter before or after the control filter to limit the power of the output signal. But the group delay introduced by this filter increases the electronic latency. This paper proposes an ANC method with frequency-response gain constraints, where gain constraints are imposed on both the low-frequency range and the target noise reduction (NR) frequency range of the control filter's frequency response. Simulation and experimental results confirm the effectiveness of our proposed method in terms of NR performance.
column7: Zhenhua Cheng(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Yi Zhou(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Yin Liu(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Yu Zhao(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Liming Shi(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications)

column4: DiffVQE: Hybrid Diffusion Voice Quality Enhancement Under Acoustic Echo and Noise
column6: Acoustic echo and background noise pose challenges on speech enhancement in hands-free systems and speakerphones. Discriminatively trained end-to-end methods represent a powerful solution for joint acoustic echo control (AEC) and denoising. However, with the advent of generative methods, diffusion-based approaches have seen remarkable performance in speech enhancement tasks. In this work, to the best of our knowledge, we provide the first (still non-causal) diffusion-based AEC model (DiffVQE) that is reproducible in terms of topology, training data, and training framework. So far, without employing diffusion, Microsoft's discriminative DeepVQE model has been shown to excel any of the ICASSP 2023 AEC Challenge entries achieving remarkable performance. Using data from the Interspeech 2025 URGENT Challenge for a diverse, high-quality training dataset, our DiffVQE excels DeepVQE both in echo and noise control performance, as well as in computational complexity and model size.
column7: Haljan Lugo(Technische Universität Braunschweig); Ernst Seidel(Technische Universität Braunschweig); Pejman Mowlaee(GN Advanced Science); Ziyue Zhao(GN Advanced Science); Tim Fingscheidt(Technische Universität Braunschweig)

column4: HybridCodec: Fast Dual-Stream, Semantically Enhanced Neural Audio Codec
column6: The popularity of neural audio codecs as speech tokenizers has surged with the advent of Multimodal Large Language Models. New codec architectures with semantic and acoustic disentanglement have emerged. There are two main approaches to introduce semantic information into codec models: one distills semantic information from SSL representations into the first RVQ layer, while the other maintains separate streams for semantic and acoustic features. We propose HybridCodec, a unified architecture that combines both paradigms. It employs separate semantic and acoustic branches while distilling SSL representations into the semantic stream. This design ensures strong disentanglement without requiring an SSL model during inference. HybridCodec shows superior semantic specialization (RVQ-1) on in-domain test set and competitive reconstruction (RVQ-all). We demonstrate its robustness in out-of-domain and zero-shot cross-lingual settings, achieving a 3x speedup over existing dual-stream models.
column7: Arjun Gangwar(Indian Institute of Technology); S Umesh(Indian Institute of Technology)

column4: WavSLM: Single-Stream Speech Language Modeling via WavLM Distillation
column6: Large language models show that simple autoregressive training can yield scalable and coherent generation, but extending this paradigm to speech remains challenging due to the entanglement of semantic and acoustic information. Most existing speech language models rely on text supervision, hierarchical token streams, or complex hybrid architectures, departing from the single-stream generative pretraining paradigm that has proven effective in text. In this work, we introduce WavSLM, a speech language model trained by quantizing and distilling self-supervised WavLM representations into a single codebook and optimizing an autoregressive next-chunk prediction objective. WavSLM jointly models semantic and acoustic information within a single token stream without text supervision or text pretraining. Despite its simplicity, it achieves competitive performance on consistency benchmarks and speech generation while using fewer parameters, less training data, and supporting streaming inference.
column7: Luca Della Libera(Concordia University; Mila-Quebec AI Institute); Cem Subakan(Universite Laval; Concordia University; Mila-Quebec AI Institute); Mirco Ravanelli(Concordia University; Mila-Quebec AI Institute)

column4: VOSSA: Voiceprint Optimization for Streaming Speech Architectures
column6: Real-time voice conversion (VC) systems commonly rely on pretrained speaker embeddings from automatic speaker verification (ASV) models. While effective for speaker discrimination, these embeddings are trained to remain stable across phonetic and prosodic variations within-speaker, which may conflict with frame-level acoustic generation in streaming constraints. To address this issue, we propose VOSSA (Voiceprint Optimization for Streaming Speech Architectures), a speaker representation framework that extracts speaker information from intermediate content encoder layers and aggregates using attentive statistics pooling. The embedding is trained jointly with VC objectives, removing the need for a separate speaker encoder. Across six datasets, VOSSA improves F0 dynamics and vowel-discriminative acoustic cues while maintaining comparable NISQA-MOS, WER, and speaker similarity. Perceptual tests further indicate improvements in naturalness, speaker similarity, intelligibility, and vibrancy.
column7: Mu-Ruei Tseng(Texas A&M University); Waris Quamer(Texas A&M University); Ghady Nasrallah(Texas A&M University); Ricardo Gutierrez-Osuna(Texas A&M University)

column4: MeanVC 2: Robust Low-Latency Streaming Zero-Shot Voice Conversion
column6: Streaming zero-shot voice conversion (VC) has become increasingly popular due to its potential for real-time applications. The recently proposed MeanVC achieves lightweight streaming zero-shot VC, but it has several limitations: its chunkwise autoregressive denoising doubles the effective training sequence length, conversion quality degrades under small-chunk settings, and its timbre encoder directly relies on reference melspectrograms, making it sensitive to reference audio quality. To address these limitations we propose MeanVC 2. We introduce future-receptive chunking (FRC), which explicitly schedules past and future receptive fields across diffusion transformer decoder layers and removes clean-chunk teacher forcing. By incorporating bounded future context, FRC enables stable conversion with a 40 ms chunk size. We further introduce a universal timbre token encoder, which constructs a timbre representation from a global speaker embedding and retrieves fine-grained timbre cues via cross-attention, improving robustness to low-quality references and enhancing zero-shot speaker similarity. Experimental results show that MeanVC 2 significantly outperforms MeanVC, while reducing latency from 211 ms to 110 ms. Audio samples are publicly available. The source code will be publicly released.
column7: Guobin Ma(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Yuxuan Xia(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Yuepeng Jiang(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Dake Guo(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Hanke Xie(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Jingbin Hu(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Yanbo Wang(The University of New South Wales); Lei Xie(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Pengcheng Zhu(WeNet Open Source Community)

column4: FlashTTS: Fast Streaming TTS with MTP Acceleration and X-pred Mean Flow Distillation
column6: Recent progress in speech dialogue systems requires text-to-Speech (TTS) models to be faster and more responsive. Modern speech dialogue systems impose two primary requirements on TTS models: low latency and support for streaming inputs and outputs. However, most existing single-codebook LLM-based TTS methods rely on multi-stage pipelines that lack native streaming capabilities. These systems typically suffer from high end-to-end latency due to slow autoregressive prediction and multi-step flow matching. To address these limitations, we propose FlashTTS, an open-source and low-latency streaming TTS framework. FlashTTS introduces a lagged multi-track architecture that natively processes streaming text and speech inputs, thereby eliminating the need for sentence-level buffering. To accelerate acoustic generation, we integrate parallel Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) with an X-pred mean flow matching decoder. This configuration achieves high-fidelity token-to-mel generation in exactly two function evaluations (2-NFE). By jointly optimizing input processing and decoding efficiency, FlashTTS offers a practical foundation for real-time speech dialogue systems. Experiments show that FlashTTS substantially reduces First-Packet Latency to 325ms compared to robust streaming baselines, all while preserving strong zero-shot voice cloning and cross-lingual intelligibility. Speech samples are available. The model code and checkpoints will be released as open source.

Univ.); Wenhao Li(Northwestern Polytech. Univ.); Jingbin Hu(Northwestern Polytech. Univ.); Guobin Ma(Northwestern Polytech. Univ.); Huakang Chen(Northwestern Polytech. column4: Prosodic Boundary-Aware Streaming Generation for LLM-Based TTS with Streaming Text Input
column6: Streaming TTS that receives streaming text is essential for interactive systems, yet this scheme faces two major challenges: unnatural prosody due to missing lookahead and long-form collapse due to unbounded context. We propose a prosodic-boundary-aware post-training strategy, adapting a pre-trained LLM-based TTS model using weakly time-aligned data. Specifically, the model is adapted to learn early stopping at specified content boundaries when provided with limited future text. During inference, a sliding-window prompt carries forward previous text and speech tokens, ensuring bounded context and seamless concatenation. Evaluations show our method outperforms CosyVoice-Style interleaved baseline in both short and long-form scenarios. In long-text synthesis, especially, it achieves a 66.2% absolute reduction in word error rate (from 71.0% to 4.8%) and increases speaker and emotion similarity by 16.1% and 1.5% relatively, offering a robust solution for streaming TTS with incremental text.
column7: Changsong Liu(Nanyang Technological University); Tianrui Wang(Nanyang Technological University; Tianjin University); Ye Ni(Nanyang Technological University; Southeast University); Yizhou Peng(Nanyang Technological University); Eng Siong Chng(Nanyang Technological University)

column4: CTC-TTS: LLM-Based Dual-Streaming Text-to-Speech with CTC Alignment
column6: Large-language-model (LLM)-based text-to-speech (TTS) systems can generate natural speech, but most are not designed for low-latency dual-streaming synthesis. High-quality dual-streaming TTS depends on accurate text-speech alignment and well-designed training sequences that balance synthesis quality and latency. Prior work often relies on GMM-HMM based forced-alignment toolkits (e.g., MFA), which are pipeline-heavy and less flexible than neural aligners; fixed-ratio interleaving of text and speech tokens struggles to capture text-speech alignment regularities. We propose CTC-TTS, which replaces MFA with a CTC based aligner and introduces a bi-word based interleaving strategy. Two variants are designed: CTC-TTS-L (token concatenation along the sequence length) for higher quality and CTC-TTS-F (feature-dimension embedding stacking) for lower latency. Experiments show that CTC-TTS outperforms fixed-ratio interleaving and MFA-based baselines on streaming synthesis and zero-shot tasks.
column7: Hanwen Liu(Xinjiang University); Saierdaer Yusuyin(Xinjiang University); Hao Huang(Xinjiang University); Zhijian Ou(Tsinghua University)

column4: PF-D2M: A Pose-free Diffusion Model for Universal Dance-to-Music Generation
column6: Dance-to-music generation aims to generate music that is aligned with dance movements. Existing approaches typically rely on body motion features extracted from a single human dancer and limited dance-to-music datasets, which restrict their performance and applicability to real-world scenarios involving multiple dancers and non-human dancers. In this paper, we propose PF-D2M, a universal diffusion-based dance-to-music generation model that incorporates visual features extracted from dance videos. PF-D2M is trained with a progressive training strategy that effectively addresses data scarcity and generalization challenges. Both objective and subjective evaluations show that PF-D2M achieves state-of-the-art performance in dance-music alignment and music quality. Samples of PF-D2M are available at https://jakeoneijk.github.io/pfd2m_project
column7: Jaekwon Im(KAIST); Natalia Polouliakh(Sony CSL Tokyo); Taketo Akama(Sony CSL Tokyo)

column4: Streaming T5-based Text-to-Speech Synthesis with Limited Lookahead
column6: Streaming text-to-speech synthesis in cascaded LLM-TTS systems still faces latency challenges as most TTS models require full context before initiating generation. We present S5-TTS, a Streaming variant of T5-TTS that enables low-latency, word-by-word incremental speech synthesis through encoder-decoder language modeling and monotonic alignment learning. S5-TTS begins generating speech immediately after receiving the first few words, substantially reducing end-to-end response latency. To maintain quality under limited lookahead, we introduce a lookahead-causal masking mechanism with Conv-based auxiliary attention that preserves intelligibility and speaker similarity, and employ interleaved multi-source distillation to further restore naturalness. Experiments show that S5-TTS achieves comparable quality to full-context T5-TTS, supports zero-shot synthesis with high speaker similarity, and significantly reduces end-to-end latency for practical conversational AI systems.
column7: Muyang Du(NVIDIA, China); Jason Roche(NVIDIA, USA); Junjie Lai(NVIDIA, China)

column4: Learning to Wait: Real Streaming Speech-to-Text Translation with an LLM
column6: A streaming speech-to-text translation system outputs tokens as the audio comes in. The state of the art for streaming speech translation with an LLM is Bestow. Bestow's wait policy is fixed: it outputs tokens at a fixed cadence irrespective of the contents of the audio. On a test set, it often seems to perform well, but not in the real world. If no speech is heard immediately after the microphone is opened, then the fixed policy will force tokens out and produce hallucinations; if the speaker speaks fast, the system will fall behind. This paper instead proposes a wait policy that learns when to wait for more audio and when to emit tokens. On a test set, the model that uses this policy achieve better quality and/or better latency. Moreover, it is not susceptible to hallucinations for real-world data.
column7: Shucong Zhang(Samsung, AI Center-Cambridge); Titouan Parcollet(Samsung, AI Center-Cambridge); Rogier van Dalen(Samsung, AI Center-Cambridge)

column4: Leveraging Audio-LLMs to Filter Speech-to-Speech Training Data
column6: Large-scale mined corpora provide abundant training data for end-to-end speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) but may contain noise, misalignment, and semantic errors. Filtering noisy data is crucial to maintain robust speech translation performance. We study how to train an audio-language model to make keep/drop decisions on paired speech directly from audio. To obtain reliable supervision without manual labels, we adopt a scalable two-stage Rank→Distill strategy. A lightweight ranker generates keep/drop pseudo-labels from noisy speech pairs, then trains an audio large language model to predict keep/drop directly from raw paired speech. The resulting model jointly captures acoustic fidelity and cross-lingual semantic consistency for the selection of speech-conditioned data. Experiments on CVSS-C and SpeechMatrix show consistent improvements over unfiltered training, yielding up to +1.4 ASR-BLEU for end-to-end S2ST.
column7: Qixu Chen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)

column4: POTSA: A Cross-Lingual Speech Alignment Framework for Speech-to-Text Translation
column6: Speech Large Language Models have achieved breakthroughs in multilingual speech-to-text translation. However, existing approaches often overlook semantic commonalities across source languages, leading to biased translation performance. In this work, we propose POTSA (Parallel Optimal Transport for Speech Alignment), a new framework based on cross-lingual parallel speech pairs and Optimal Transport, designed to bridge high- and low-resource translation gaps. First, we introduce a Bias Compensation module to coarsely align initial speech representations. Second, we impose token-level OT constraints on a Q-Former using parallel pairs to establish fine-grained representation consistency. Then, we apply a layer scheduling strategy to focus OT constraints on semantically beneficial layers. Experiments on FLEURS show our method achieves SOTA performance, with +1.29 BLEU over five common languages and +2.93 BLEU on zero-shot languages, using only 10 hours of parallel speech per language.
column7: Xuanchen Li(Tianjin University); Chenrui Cui(Tianjin University); Tianrui Wang(Tianjin University; NTU Singapore); Meng Ge(Tianjin University); Zikang Huang(Tianjin University); Yizhou Peng(NTU Singapore); Jin Li(Tianjin University); Yuheng Lu(Tianjin University); Yu Jiang(Tianjin University); Nyima Tashi(Tibet University); Longbiao Wang(Tianjin University; Huiyan Technology); Jianwu Dang(Chinese Academy of Sciences)

column4: Automated Gradient-Driven Parameter Sharing for Low-Resource Multilingual Speech-to-Text Translation
column6: Multilingual S2T models typically use uniform sharing due to insufficient training data, which can lead to representation conflicts in low-resource scenarios. We present a gradient-driven framework that automatically discovers optimal parameter sharing configurations by analyzing inter-language gradient behaviors. Our approach integrates clustering for grouping, similarity analysis for shared-private ratios, and joint SVD with regularized CCA for subspace calibration. On four low-resource language pairs using the SeamlessM4T-Medium model, our Gradient-Driven Parameter Sharing (GDPS) framework achieves consistent improvements.
column7: Ruiyan Sun(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Satoshi Nakamura(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)

column4: Multilingual Multi-Speaker Unit Vocoders: A Systematic Analysis of Discrete Speech Representations
column6: Discrete speech units obtained via k-means clustering of self supervised embeddings entangle phonetic, speaker, and language information, causing speaker mixing and cross-lingual interference in multilingual multi-speaker speech generation. Despite growing use in Audio LLMs and speech to speech systems, unit vocoders remain underexplored. We analyze a BigVGAN based unit vocoder, across four Indian languages. We study the interaction between cluster size and conditioning strategies using WER, speaker similarity, and unit level metrics. Results show that cluster size governs intelligibility by improving phonetic discriminability, while explicit speaker conditioning is indispensable for preventing identity collapse. Language supervision yields further gains mainly at lower cluster sizes where units remain ambiguous. Our analysis shows similar phonemes across languages collapse to the same cluster IDs at smaller inventories, with larger clusters progressively separating them.
column7: Naman Kothari(National Institute of Technology); Arjun Gangwar(Indian Institute of Technology); Adarsh Arigala(Indian Institute of Technology); S Umesh(Indian Institute of Technology)

column4: Evaluation of forced alignment of code-mixed speech: the case of Hindi-English
column6: Code-mixed speech poses unique challenges to forced alignment: expanded inventories, orthographic errors, and speaker variation. We evaluate forced alignment of Hindi-English code-mixed speech using the Montreal Forced Aligner. We address 2 problems: (1) free variation involving native vs non-native pairs and (2) phonemic boundary detection for mid-utterance English words. Bootstrapping strategies substantially outperform unmodified lexicons. Acoustic models trained on sentence-level code-mixed data achieve a mean error of 4.15ms, ie. ten times lower than monolingual Hindi (38.18ms) or isolated English (37.58ms) alternatives. Principled lexicon design and code-mixed training data are both essential for reliable alignment of bilingual speech.
column7: Ayushi Pandey(Karya); Pamir Gogoi(Karya); Kevin Tang(Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf; University of Florida )

column4: Does Translation-Enhanced Speech Encoder Pre-training Affect Speech LLMs?
column6: Connecting a pre-trained speech encoder to a Large Language Model (LLM) is the standard architecture for building Speech LLMs. However, a structural misalignment exists between phonetically anchored encoders and semantically organized LLMs. To bridge this divide, the encoder benefits from objectives that emphasize semantic understanding over surface-level sound recognition. We argue that speech translation provides a principled way to achieve this. Unlike transcription, translation requires capturing meaning beyond phonetic similarity, since the source speech and the target text do not systematically align at the phonetic level. We experimentally evaluate the impact of incorporating translation objectives into speech encoder pre-training. Our results demonstrate that translation-enhanced pre-training significantly improves cross-modal integration and leads to superior performance across downstream Speech LLM tasks.
column7: Tomoya Mizumoto(SB Intuitions); Yusuke Fujita(SB Intuitions)

column4: PiDA: Phonetically-Informed Data Augmentation for Robust Vietnamese Speech Translation
column6: Cascaded speech translation (ST) systems suffer from error propagation when Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) outputs incorrect transcripts. We present the first systematic categorization of ASR errors for Vietnamese ST, classifying substitution errors by phonetic cause and quantifying their impact on downstream Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance using Linear Mixed-Effects Modelling. We confirm that most ASR substitution errors arise from phonetic confusions rather than random noise, and that these phonetic errors significantly degrade ST quality. Motivated by this finding, we propose Phonetically-Informed Data Augmentation (PiDA), which generates ASR-like corruptions by substituting words with phonetically similar alternatives using phonetic word embeddings. Fine-tuning on a PiDA-augmented version of FLEURS Vietnamese-English improves translation of erroneous ASR outputs (up to +2.04 BLEU over standard fine-tuning) while also slightly improving clean-text performance.
column7: Giang Son Nguyen(VinUniversity); Tung X. Nguyen(VinUniversity); Hieu Minh Truong(VinUniversity); Nhu Vo(VinUniversity; University of Technology Sydney); Wray Buntine(VinUniversity; Monash University); Dung D. Le(VinUniversity)

column4: MoVE: Translating Laughter and Tears via Mixture of Vocalization Experts in Speech-to-Speech Translation
column6: Recent Speech-to-Speech Translation (S2ST) systems achieve strong semantic accuracy yet consistently strip away non-verbal vocalizations (NVs), such as laughter and crying that convey pragmatic intent, which severely limits real-world utility. We address this via three contributions. First, we propose a synthesis pipeline for building scalable expressive datasets to overcome the data scarcity limitation. Second, we propose MoVE, a Mixture-of-LoRA-Experts architecture with expressive-specialized adapters and a soft-weighting router that blends experts for capturing hybrid expressive states. Third, we show pretrained AudioLLMs enable striking data efficiency: 30 minutes of curated data is enough for strong performance. On English-Chinese S2ST, while comparing with strong baselines, MoVE reproduces target NVs in 76% of cases and achieves the highest human-rated naturalness and emotional fidelity among all compared systems, where existing S2ST systems preserve at most 14% of NVs.
column7: Szu-Chi Chen(National Taiwan University); I-Ning Tsai(National Taiwan University); Yi-Cheng Lin(National Taiwan University); Sung-Feng Huang(NVIDIA); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University; NTU AI-CoRE)

column4: Cross-Modal Robustness Transfer (CMRT): Training Robust Speech Translation Models Using Adversarial Text
column6: End-to-End Speech Translation (E2E-ST) has made significant progress but often relies on curated datasets, overlooking challenges like robustness to inflectional morphology variations common in non-native and dialectal speech. In this work, we adapt an adversarial attack targeting inflectional morphology from the text domain to speech and demonstrate that E2E-ST models are highly vulnerable. While adversarial fine-tuning improves robustness in text, generating adversarial speech data is computationally difficult. To address this, we propose Cross-Modal Robustness Transfer (CMRT), a method that transfers robustness from text to the speech modality without requiring adversarial speech data. Experiments across four language directions show that CMRT improves adversarial robustness by over 3 BLEU points on average while maintaining performance on clean data.
column7: Abderrahmane Issam(Maastricht University); Yusuf Can Semerci(Maastricht University); Jan Scholtes(Maastricht University); Gerasimos Spanakis(Maastricht University)

column4: YODAS v3: Over 1 Million Hours of High-Bandwidth, Stereophonic, Multilingual Speech
column6: We present YODAS v3, a weakly-labeled speech corpus containing over 1.1 million hours of 48kHz multi-channel audio in 147 languages, released under a CC BY 3.0 license. YODAS v3 is not only the largest open speech dataset to date, but also the first truly large-scale speech corpus with high-fidelity stereo audio. We first provide the collection methodology for the corpus, where we introduce new techniques for gathering language-balanced speech data. The effectiveness of our approach is shown by the language distribution of the crawled data: 22 languages in YODAS v3 have over 10K hours and 73 languages have over 5K hours of data. We then conduct extensive analyses on the composition of the data, such as the distribution of languages, audio quality, and transcription quality. Finally, we train baseline speech recognition and neural codec models to show the effectiveness of the dataset. Download at https://huggingface.co/datasets/espnet/yodas3.
column7: William Chen(Carnegie Mellon University); Shinnosuke Takamichi(Keio University); Sayaka Shiota(Tokyo Metropolitan University); Satoru Fukayama(National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technolog (AIST)); Samuele Cornell(Carnegie Mellon University); Shinji Watanabe(Carnegie Mellon University)

column4: Inverse Text Normalization in Romanian: A Comparative Study of Rule-Based, Neural, and Large Language Model Approaches
column6: Inverse Text Normalization (ITN) converts spoken-form automatic speech recognition transcripts into standardized written text and is a critical post-processing step in speech systems. We present a comparative study of ITN in Romanian, evaluating rule-based grammars, neural sequence-to-sequence models, fine-tuned multilingual transformers, and large language models under a unified evaluation framework that separates copy and normalization errors. Experiments on 24k manually annotated spoken-written pairs, including out-of-distribution evaluation, reveal distinct trade-offs. Deterministic grammars provide high precision and efficiency but limited coverage, while neural models benefit from pretraining yet exhibit numerical instability. Few-shot LLM prompting achieves near-human accuracy and stronger cross-domain generalization at higher computational cost. Our results clarify accuracy-efficiency trade-offs and provide practical guidance for deploying ITN in speech pipelines.
column7: Oana Sirbu(University of Bucharest); Alexandra Diaconu(University of Bucharest); Sergiu Nisioi(University of Bucharest); Bogdan Alexe(University of Bucharest; Gheorghe Mihoc-Caius Iacob Institute of Mathematical Statistics and Applied Mathematics of the Romanian Academy)

column4: Audiovisual CXMI: Scene-based Context Tagging for Spoken Language Translation Evaluation
column6: Existing metrics assess translation quality at the sentence level but cannot measure how well a machine translation model utilizes context. Conditional Cross-Mutual Information (CXMI) quantifies context usage, yet considers only text, missing audiovisual cues that human translators exploit. We propose Audiovisual CXMI (AV-CXMI), an extension of CXMI with scene-based audiovisual tags extracted from video. Our framework first segments video into scenes via visual boundary detection refined by speaker analysis. Next, we extract structured tags capturing six contextual categories from multimodal streams, and finally, evaluate translation quality conditioned on the extracted tags. Experiments on Korean-English film translation show that the proposed AV-CXMI achieves significantly higher correlation with human judgment (Pearson r=0.400, p
column7: Dayeon Ku(Dept. of EECS); Hwayoung Park(Dept. of AI Convergence, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology); Hong Kook Kim(Dept. of EECS; Dept. of AI Convergence, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology; AunionAI Co., Ltd.)
