column4: DEBATE: A Dataset for Disentangling Textual Ambiguity in Mandarin Through Speech
column6: Despite extensive research on textual and visual disambiguation, disambiguation through speech (DTS) remains underexplored. This is largely due to the lack of high-quality datasets that pair spoken sentences with richly ambiguous text. To address this gap, we present DEBATE, a unique public Chinese speech-text dataset designed to study how speech cues and patterns such as pronunciation, pauses, stress, and intonation can help resolve textual ambiguity and reveal a speaker's true intent. DEBATE contains 1,001 carefully selected ambiguous utterances, each recorded by 10 native speakers to capture diverse spoken disambiguations. We detail the rigorous data pipeline and benchmark threelarge speech language models, revealing a significant gap between machine and human intent understanding. DEBATE represents the first effort of its kind and offers a foundation for building similar DTS datasets across languages and cultures.
column7: Haotian Guo(Hunan University); Jing Han(Hunan University; Yuelushan Center for Industrial Innovation); Yongfeng Tu(Malanshan Audio & Video Laboratory); Shihao Gao(Hunan University); Weihao Gan(Malanshan Audio & Video Laboratory); Zixing Zhang(Hunan University)

column4: Distilling Structured Reasoning into SpeechLLMs for Spoken Language Understanding
column6: Recent Speech Large Language Models (SpeechLLMs) have emerged as a promising approach for end-to-end Spoken Language Understanding (SLU). While adapting SpeechLLMs to specific SLU tasks such as intent classification requires alignment with task-specific label schemas, conventional fine-tuning still struggles to separate semantically adjacent intent categories. To address this, we propose Reasoning-Guided Fine-Tuning (RG-FT), which distills structured reasoning trajectories generated by DeepSeek-R1, comprising candidate enumeration, rejection reasoning, and label prediction, into SpeechLLMs as a multitask objective. Explicitly verbalizing why incorrect candidates are rejected forces the model to capture fine-grained distinctions and sharpen inter-class decision boundaries. At inference, only direct label prediction is used, incurring zero additional computational cost. Experiments on multiple SLU benchmarks and six SpeechLLMs demonstrate that RG-FT consistently improves SLU performance.
column7: Toshihiro Tsukagoshi(Shizuoka University); Natsuo Yamashita(Hitachi, Ltd.); Kota Dohi(Hitachi, Ltd.); Hiroaki Kokubo(Hitachi, Ltd.); Masaaki Yamamoto(Hitachi, Ltd.)

column4: Enhancing Audio Reasoning via Semantic Summary Prediction
column6: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) perform well on complex question answering but often show a reasoning gap, where explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reduces accuracy compared to direct answers. We hypothesize that long reasoning sequences shift attention away from the audio input. To address this, we propose SPARE (Semantic Prediction for Audio REasoning), which introduces a register token aligned with the final conclusion using a cosine similarity loss with a Sentence-BERT embedding. This conditions the model's latent space with the target semantic goal before reasoning begins. Experiments on MMAU and MMAR with SALMONN show improved zero-shot reasoning and stronger early attention to audio without additional inference cost.
column7: Francesco Bonzi(Concordia University; Mila - Quebec AI Institute); Pooneh Mousavi(Concordia University; Mila - Quebec AI Institute); Cem Subakan(Université Laval; Mila - Quebec AI Institute); Mirco Ravanelli(Concordia University; Mila - Quebec AI Institute)

column4: Incremental End-to-End Spoken Dialogue State Tracking with a Multimodal LLM and Reinforcement Learning
column6: End-to-end spoken dialogue state tracking (DST) infers belief states directly from speech, avoiding cascading errors in ASR-DST pipelines. This paper proposes an incremental DST method using a multimodal large language model (Qwen2.5-Omni-7B) that generates transcripts and symbolic state updates from raw audio. Unlike conventional approaches that regenerate the full state each turn, our method predicts only symbolic edit operations relative to the previous state, reducing output length and the risk of corrupting unchanged slots. We apply a two-stage training recipe: supervised fine-tuning followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which directly optimizes generation-level rewards for transcript accuracy, DST correctness, and format validity. Experiments on SpokenWOZ demonstrate that incremental updates substantially outperform full-state prediction, and GRPO further improves accuracy, achieving the best reported results on this benchmark.
column7: Tomoya Higuchi(The University of Electro-Communications); Michimasa Inaba(The University of Electro-Communications)

column4: Joint Speech And Text Training For LLM-based End-To-End Spoken Dialogue State Tracking
column6: End-to-end spoken dialogue state tracking (DST) is made difficult by having to handle speech input with scarce training data. Combining speech foundation encoders and large language models has emerged as an approach to alleviate this difficulty. Although this approach results in strong spoken DST models, achieving state-of-the-art performance in realistic multi-turn DST, it struggles to generalize across domains and requires annotated spoken DST training data for each domain of interest. However, collecting such data for every target domain is both costly and difficult. Noting that textual DST data is more easily obtained for various domains, in this work, we propose jointly training on available spoken DST data and written textual data from other domains as a way to achieve cross-domain generalization. We conduct experiments which show the efficacy of our proposed method for getting good cross-domain DST performance without relying on spoken training data from the target domains.
column7: Katia Vendrame(Brno University of Technology); Bolaji Yusuf(Brno University of Technology); Santosh Kesiraju(Brno University of Technology); Šimon Sedláček(Brno University of Technology); Oldřich Plchot(Brno University of Technology); Honza Černocký(Brno University of Technology)

column4: MAC-SLU: Multi-Intent Automotive Cabin Spoken Language Understanding Benchmark
column6: Spoken Language Understanding (SLU), which aims to extract user semantics for downstream tasks, is vital to task-oriented dialog systems. Existing SLU datasets generally lack diversity and complexity, and a unified benchmark for the latest Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) remains absent. This work introduces MAC-SLU, a novel Multi-Intent Automotive Cabin Spoken Language Understanding Dataset, which increases task difficulty with authentic and complex multi-intent data. Based on MAC-SLU, we benchmarked leading LLMs and LALMs, covering methods like in-context learning (ICL), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), as well as end-to-end (E2E) and pipeline paradigms. Experiments show that while LLMs and LALMs have the potential to complete SLU tasks through ICL, their performance still lags significantly behind SFT. Meanwhile, E2E LALMs demonstrate performance comparable to pipeline approaches and effectively avoid error propagation from speech recognition.
column7: Yuezhang Peng(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Chonghao Cai(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Ziang Liu(Central South University); Shuai Fan(AISpeech Co., Ltd.); Sheng Jiang(AISpeech Co., Ltd.); Hua Xu(AISpeech Co., Ltd.); Yuxin Liu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Sheng Wang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Qiguang Chen(Harbin Institute of Technology); Yao Li(Shanghai Aviation Electric Co., Ltd.); Kele Xu(National University of Defense Technology); Kai Yu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; AISpeech Co., Ltd.); Libo Qin(Harbin Institute of Technology); Xie Chen(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute)

column4: MSU-Bench: Towards Understanding the Conversational Multi-Speaker Scenarios
column6: Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) is moving from task-specific pipelines toward large audio language models (LALMs) that generate natural-language responses. However, existing speech benchmarks mainly focus on single-speaker settings or isolated subtasks, leaving speaker-centric understanding in realistic multi-speaker conversations insufficiently evaluated. We introduce MSU-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark for multi-speaker conversational understanding, covering 16 speaker-centric tasks and 2,300 QA instances in a two-tier framework from speaker grounding to dialogue reasoning. We build a Gemini-assisted annotation and QA generation pipeline with human-in-the-loop verification, achieving high QA validity and strong agreement between human answers and verified labels. We further analyze speaker-referencing schemes and diagnostic error types to reveal bottlenecks in speaker grounding and reasoning. Experiments reveal clear gaps across model families, with closed-source systems leading overall but all models still facing challenges in complex speaker grounding and multi-speaker reasoning. The benchmark annotations, metadata, and evaluation scripts are available at the official GitHub repository: ASLP-lab/MSU-Bench.
column7: Zhaokai Sun(ASLP@NPU; SZ Loop Area Inst.; Li Auto); Shuai Wang(Nanjing Univ.; SZ Loop Area Inst.); Zhennan Lin(ASLP@NPU); Chengyou Wang(ASLP@NPU); Dehui Gao(ASLP@NPU); Yuang Cao(ASLP@NPU); Chunjiang He(ASLP@NPU); Pan Zhou(Li Auto); Lei Xie(ASLP@NPU)

column4: MVCL-DAF++: Enhancing Multimodal Intent Recognition via Prototype-Aware Contrastive Alignment and Coarse-to-Fine Dynamic Attention Fusion
column6: Multimodal intent recognition (MMIR) suffers from weak semantic grounding and poor robustness under noisy or rare-class conditions. We propose MVCL-DAF++, which extends MVCL-DAF with two key modules: (1) Prototype-aware contrastive alignment, aligning instances to class-level prototypes to enhance semantic consistency; and (2) Coarse-to-fine attention fusion, integrating global modality summaries with token-level features for hierarchical cross-modal interaction. On MIntRec and MIntRec2.0, MVCL-DAF++ achieves new state-of-the-art results, improving rare-class recognition by +1.05% and +4.18% WF1, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of prototype-guided learning and coarse-to-fine fusion for robust multimodal understanding.
column7: Haofeng Huang(University of Shanghai for Science and Technology); Bin Li(CAS); Yifei Han(CAS); Long Zhang(CAS); Yangfan He(University of Minnesota-Twin Cities); Yaxin Xue(University of Leeds)

column4: PROGRESS: Coverage-guided RL to Train Search-augmented LLM Agent
column6: Existing search-augmented LLM agents are trained using Reinforcement Learning to boost its reasoning capabilities. However, these approaches primarily rely on outcome-level rewards which provide little supervision over search behavior and overlook agent's ability to decompose complex queries properly. To mitigate this issue, we propose PROGRESS which utilizes teacher-guided coverage reward to explicitly shape decomposed query generation of the policy model. During training, frozen teacher models are used to decompose complex queries into essential search queries. These essential search queries are utilized to guide the search behavior of the policy model. Integrated into an R1-style training framework, our approach provides lightweight guidance over query decomposition decisions without dense process-level supervision. Experiments show that coverage-guided RL improves overall task performance, highlighting the importance of explicitly supervising search strategies in agentic LLMs.
column7: Sudipta Paul(Samsung Electronics); Vijay Srinivasan(Samsung Electronics); Vivek Kulkarni(Samsung Electronics); Aounon Kumar(Samsung Electronics); Yashas Malur Saidutta(Samsung Electronics); Wenbo Li(Samsung Electronics); Srinivas Chappidi(Samsung Electronics)

column4: SFL-MTSC: Leveraging Semantic Frame-Level Multi-Task Self-Consistency for Robust Multi-Intent Spoken Language Understanding
column6: Prompt-based spoken language understanding (SLU) with large language models (LLMs) often suffers from inconsistent intent-slot structures due to decoding stochasticity, particularly in multi-intent scenarios. In view of this, we propose Semantic Frame-Level Multi-Task Self-Consistency (SFL-MTSC), a novel structured aggregation framework operating at the semantic frame level. Instead of output-level majority voting, SFL-MTSC decomposes predictions into intent-specific frames, applies domain-intent grouping and slot-level clustering, and evaluates cluster reliability using path support scoring. Reliable frames are retained and re-integrated to form the final prediction. Zero-shot experiments on the MAC-SLU benchmark dataset show improved slot F1 and overall accuracy over single-path inference, while intent accuracy remains largely stable across most settings.
column7: Po-Yen Chen(National Taiwan Normal University); Berlin Chen(National Taiwan Normal University)

column4: Selective Capability Unlearning in End-to-End Spoken Language Understanding
column6: Modern spoken language understanding (SLU) systems are increasingly deployed in real-world settings, where specific functionalities may need to be removed due to policy or safety constraints. In SLU, a functionality corresponds to an intent and its associated slot-generation behavior. However, in autoregressive models, suppressing a target intent does not eliminate the conditional mapping that generates slots conditioned on that intent. When the intent prefix is externally supplied, the model can reconstruct the original intent-slot structure. We identify this structural failure as capability persistence. We propose Binding Subspace (BSU), a representation-level framework that isolates and attenuates intent-conditioned directions underlying this mapping. Across SLU benchmarks, BSU substantially reduces forced-prefix recoverability while preserving retained performance.
column7: Akanksha Singh(IISER Bhopal); Vinod Kumar Kurmi(IISER Bhopal)

column4: GigaChat Audio: Time-aware Large Audio Language Model
column6: Temporal grounding in long recordings remains challenging for audio-conditioned LLMs. We present a time-aware audio LLM that answers questions with explicit timestamps over up to 120 minutes of input. Our approach interleaves periodic time markers with continuous audio tokens using large-scale synthetic supervision from a cascaded pipeline. Our model achieves strong temporal-grounding accuracy on short and long benchmarks and supports time-anchored fragment descriptions and summaries. Extensive ablations examine how time representation, marker frequency, tokenization, and duration-mixture design affect accuracy and computational cost. We release model weights and datasets to support further research on time-aware audio understanding, available at https://huggingface.co/ai-sage/GigaChat3.1-Audio-10B-A1.8B.
column7: Aleksandr Kutsakov(SaluteDevices); Mariia Sadovina(SaluteDevices); Georgii Gospodinov(SaluteDevices); Alexandr Maximenko(SaluteDevices); Oleg Kutuzov(SaluteDevices); Pavel Bogomolov(SaluteDevices); Fyodor Minkin(SaluteDevices)

column4: Multi-Phonation Graph Learning with Self-Supervised Speech Embeddings for ALS Detection and Progression Prediction
column6: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) progressively impairs speech motor control, making acoustic analysis a promising biomarker for severity and progression estimation. We propose a subject-level graph framework that aggregates multiple phonation recordings into a unique k-nearest-neighbor graph built from pretrained SSL embeddings of 2s segments. We compare four SSL front-ends (wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, data2vec-audio, and UniSpeech-SAT) and five graph neural networks (GCN, residual GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE, and GIN) on the SAND dataset tasks (339 participants: 205 ALS, 134 control): 5-class dysarthria severity and 4-class ALSFRS-R progression prediction. On the official validation set, the best configuration (HuBERT+GIN) achieves macro-F1 of 0.73 for Task 1 and 0.69 for Task 2, outperforming SAND validation baselines (0.61 and 0.58). These results highlight the potential of combining GNNs with pretrained cross-lingual speech representations for low-resource ALS detection and progression monitoring.
column7: Behrad TaghiBeyglou(Huawei Canada; University of Toronto); Fatemeh Bagheri(University of Toronto; North York General Hospital); Ervin Sejdic(University of Toronto; North York General Hospital)

column4: Synthetic Pathological Speech at Scale: A Flow Matching Approach for Clinical Data Augmentation
column6: Deep learning for pathological voice detection suffers from severe data scarcity. Traditional augmentation often fails to capture the non-linear glottal instabilities of voice disorders. We propose a flow-based generative framework to synthesize pathological and healthy vowel phonations using clinical status token conditioning. We investigate scaling laws by training supervised classifiers on synthetic datasets ranging from 100 to 100,000 samples. Experiments across four languages show that classifiers trained solely on 100k synthetic samples surpass real-only baselines by +3.9% accuracy and +13.3% sensitivity on held-out real data. Synthetic augmentation further improves zero-shot transfer across multiple datasets on multi-class pathology classification (+7.4%/+10.0% F1) and Parkinson's detection from vowels (+6.8% accuracy). Our findings demonstrate that flow-based generative scaling effectively addresses data scarcity while improving cross-domain robustness.
column7: Alkis Koudounas(Sony Group Corporation); Moreno La Quatra(Kore University of Enna); Quentin Jodelet(Sony Group Corporation); Hayato Futami(Sony Group Corporation); Valerio Mario Salerno(Kore University of Enna); Sabato Marco Siniscalchi(Università degli Studi di Palermo); Emiru Tsunoo(Sony Group Corporation)

column4: Learning to Attend to Depression-Related Patterns: An Adaptive Cross-Modal Gating Network for Depression Detection
column6: Automatic depression detection using speech signals with acoustic and textual modalities is a promising approach for early diagnosis. Depression-related patterns exhibit sparsity in speech: diagnostically relevant features occur in specific segments rather than being uniformly distributed. However, most existing methods treat all frames equally, assuming depression-related information is uniformly distributed and thus overlooking this sparsity. To address this issue, we propose a depression detection network based on Adaptive Cross-Modal Gating (ACMG) that adaptively reassigns frame-level weights across both modalities, enabling selective attention to depression-related segments. Experimental results show that the depression detection system with ACMG outperforms baselines without it. Visualization analyses further confirm that ACMG automatically attends to clinically meaningful patterns, including low-energy acoustic segments and textual segments containing negative sentiments.

column4: Layer-wise Multi-factor Adaptive Disentanglement for Cross-corpus Speech Depression Detection
column6: Although speaker disentanglement can improve within-corpus depression detection, cross-corpus transfer remains challenging as multi-source factor shifts are encoded and accumulated across the network hierarchy, making speaker-only and output-level constraints insufficient. To address this issue, we propose a Layer-wise Multi-factor Adaptive Disentanglement framework (LMAD) that enforces constraints at multiple key encoder layers to reduce the dependence of intermediate representations on speaker and corpus factors while preserving dependence on depression information, thereby mitigating the accumulation of nuisance information across layers. Furthermore, LMAD employs adaptive weights to modulate disentanglement strength along inter-layer and intra-layer dimensions. Experimental results shown that LMAD consistently outperforms both the baseline and speaker-only disentanglement models under bidirectional DAIC-WoZ↔Androids transfer, while maintaining competitive within-corpus performance.
column7: Minggang Wang(Nagoya Institute of Technology; University of Wollongong); Shohei Kato(Nagoya Institute of Technology); Wen Gu(Nagoya Institute of Technology); Fenghui Ren(University of Wollongong); Jun Yan(University of Wollongong)

column4: Augmenting Dysarthric Speech Severity Assessment with MOS Supervision
column6: Dysarthria is a speech disorder marked by reduced intelligibility and communicative effectiveness. Automatic utterance-level assessment of dysarthric speech can support scalable speech monitoring and therapy-related analysis. Yet training such systems is bottlenecked by the scarcity of clinically annotated dysarthric speech. This work proposes to augment dysarthric speech assessment using data from speech synthesis evaluations, specifically human-annotated utterances with Mean Opinion Score (MOS) labels from the QualiSpeech corpus. Experiments show that fine-tuning on speech synthesis assessment data consistently improves performance on both intelligibility and naturalness prediction, while joint training yields gains primarily on naturalness. These results suggest that synthesis artifacts and dysarthric speech share perceptual commonalities, and speech synthesis evaluation corpora offer a practical augmentation source that reduces reliance on scarce clinical annotations.
column7: Kaimeng Jia(Tsinghua University); Minzhu Tu(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Zengrui Jin(Tsinghua University); Siyin Wang(Tsinghua University); Chao Zhang(Tsinghua University)

column4: Clinically-Supervised Hierarchical LoRA-MoE: A Parameter-Efficient Framework for Severity-Aware Dysarthric Speech Assessment
column6: Automatic dysarthria severity assessment is crucial for clinical monitoring yet hindered by data scarcity and pronounced speech heterogeneity. While self-supervised models such as WavLM provide strong representations, adapting them to low-resource medical domains remains challenging. We propose a Clinically-Supervised Hierarchical LoRA-MoE framework that freezes the WavLM backbone and introduces shared LoRA adapters in lower layers for general acoustic modeling, together with dynamically routed expert LoRAs in deeper layers for severity-specific patterns. A clinically-supervised router selectively activates expert parameters conditioned on utterance characteristics. Experiments on the UA-Speech corpus in 2- and 5-class settings demonstrate consistent improvements over full fine-tuning, achieving F1 scores of 94.54% and 61.55%, respectively.
column7: Jiaqi Wang(Xi'an Jiaotong University); Guanghua Xu(Xi'an Jiaotong University); Hongjie Zhou(Xi'an Jiaotong University); Shuwen Bai(Xi'an Jiaotong University); Sicong Zhang(Xi'an Jiaotong University)

column4: A multilingual composite speech index to assess passage reading in Huntington’s disease
column6: Digital speech measures are a promising approach for assessing progression in Huntington's disease (HD). Reading tasks allow evaluation of both motor and cognitive dysfunction due to the high cognitive load involved. In this study, speech during passage reading was automatically detected and analyzed in 89 patients with HD and 82 matched controls in three languages (English, Polish, and Spanish). Bursts of voiced activity were identified through an adaptive thresholding method to estimate speech features. Significant differences in temporal features were observed between the HD and control groups. Features were then standardized to the language-matched controls and averaged to yield a composite temporal speech index (CTSI). Strong correlations were observed between CTSI and composite, cognitive, and motor scores from the Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale, with the highest correlation for the Symbol Digit Modality Test, which measures cognitive processing speed and attention.

column4: Vowel Nasalization in Upper Airway Diseases: An Analysis Using the CUCO Database
column6: Upper airway diseases can affect speech by altering nasal airflow and nasal-oral resonance coupling. However, most existing studies rely on general acoustic features and lack systematic analyses of vowel nasalization directly related to nasal function. Using the CUCO database, this study analyzes vowel nasalization in patients undergoing septoplasty, endoscopic sinus surgery, or tonsillectomy, and in healthy controls, at pre- and postoperative time points. Two nasalization measures, A1-P0 and A1-P1, are examined across pathology type, temporal progression, and vowel category. Results show A1-P0 is more sensitive to pathology differences, and nasalization is vowel dependent, with /u/ most sensitive to resonance changes. Only the tonsillectomy group exhibits transient early postoperative nasalization changes; no long-term differences occur in other groups. These findings support the value of vowel nasalization measures for speech analysis in upper airway diseases.

column4: What Do Deepfake Speech Detectors Actually Hear?
column6: Deepfake speech detectors often output a single score without explaining why an audio sample is flagged, where in the signal the evidence lies, or what cues drive the decision. We propose an audio-native explainability pipeline using Integrated Gradients on time-aligned self-supervised representations to localize decision evidence over time. We apply the proposed method to three WavLM-based detectors (AASIST, CA-MHFA, SLS) on ASVspoof 5 and manually annotate the highest-attribution regions to provide a semantic meaning of the most important cues. Despite similar performance, the detectors rely on different cues: AASIST emphasizes non-speech/environment cues, CA-MHFA focuses on localized phoneme artifacts, and SLS relies on word boundaries and spectral integrity. We move beyond speculative reasoning and validate our findings by causal masking of the primary detector cues. Observed performance degradation further supports the explained detector semantics.
column7: Vojtěch Staněk(Brno University of Technology); Veronika Jirmusová(Brno University of Technology); Anton Firc(Brno University of Technology); Kamil Malinka(Brno University of Technology); Jakub Reš(Brno University of Technology); Martin Perešíni(Brno University of Technology)

column4: LISE : Listenable Interpretable Speaker Embeddings
column6: Deep neural network-based automatic speaker verification (ASV) systems achieve impressive performance but their embedding representations remain opaque, lacking a structured and perceptually verifiable explanation of the vocal characteristics they encode. Existing approaches either require annotation of speaker attributes or introduce alternative representations whose interpretability is unvalidated with listeners. We propose Listenable Interpretable Speaker Embeddings (LISE), a label-free framework that decomposes pretrained speaker embeddings into a small set of components. This decomposition yields a structured representation that supports the analysis of what information has been encoded by speaker embeddings. LISE preserves ASV performance with negligible EER degradation on x-vector and ECAPA-TDNN. Crucially, the interpretability of these components for human listeners is demonstrated through listening experiments, where participants distinguished speakers with 83.9% accuracy.
column7: Xiaoliang Wu(University of Southampton); Chongxin Gan(Hong Kong PolyU); Ke Liu(University of Edinburgh); Peter Bell(University of Edinburgh); Jennifer Williams(University of Southampton)

column4: Explainable and Trustworthy Speech Emotion Recognition Using Confidence Score and Reinforcement Learning Rectified Speech Emotion Descriptors
column6: Explainable and trustworthy speech emotion recognition (SER) remains a challenging task to date, largely due to the scarcity of SER data with reliable speech emotion descriptor (SED) labels, such as prosodic features and speaker traits. This paper presents a confidence score and reinforcement learning (RL) based on-the-fly SED rectification approach for post-training SER systems on automatically annotated SED labels. Experiments on IEMOCAP and MELD suggest that explainable SER systems incorporating the proposed confidence score and RL-based SED rectification approach consistently outperform baselines without data selection or SED rectification. The best performing system, which integrates both components, surpasses the baseline without data selection and SED rectification, achieving SER gains of 2.9% and 3.3% absolute (3.7% and 5.4% relative) on IEMOCAP and MELD benchmarks, respectively.

column4: FLiP: Towards understanding and interpreting multimodal multilingual sentence embeddings
column6: This paper presents factorized linear projection (FLiP) models for understanding pretrained sentence embedding spaces. We train FLiP models to recover the lexical content from multilingual (LaBSE), multimodal (SONAR) and API-based (Gemini) sentence embedding spaces in several high- and mid-resource languages. We show that FLiP can recall more than 75% of lexical content from the embeddings, significantly outperforming existing non-factorized baselines. Using this as a diagnostic tool, we uncover the modality and language biases across the selected sentence encoders and provide practitioners with intrinsic insights about the encoders without relying on conventional downstream evaluation tasks. Our implementation is public.
column7: Santosh Kesiraju(Brno University of Technology); Bolaji Yusuf(Brno University of Technology); Šimon Sedláček(Brno University of Technology); Oldřich Plchot(Brno University of Technology); Petr Schwarz(Brno University of Technology)

column4: Inside the Latent Flow: Causal Deciphering of Attention Dynamics in Audio Separation Foundation Models
column6: Flow-matching transformers achieve strong audio separation, yet their attention dynamics are opaque. We adapt established causal-intervention principles into a deterministic, inference-time probing protocol for SAM Audio. Orthogonal probing uncovers a dual-pathway text-conditioning mechanism: additive injections control semantic identity, while cross-attention refines acoustic structure. We observe an asynchronous layerwise convergence: stable layers build temporal scaffolds early, whereas fast layers continue resolving artifacts during sampling. The model also attenuates temporal segmentation cues to maintain continuous-flow stability. Using these insights, we propose Layer-Selective Attention Caching (LSAC), a training-free acceleration method that caches attention in stable layers. Across acoustic complexities, LSAC cuts self-attention computation by ~25% with negligible quality loss and yields up to 6.7x higher quality retention than naive step reduction.
column7: Yuxuan Chen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Jilin University); Haoyuan Yu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Hunan University); Peize He(University of Electronic Science and Technology of China)

column4: Towards Interpretable Framework for Neural Audio Codecs via Sparse Autoencoders: A Case Study on Accent Information
column6: Neural Audio Codecs (NACs) are widely adopted in modern speech systems, yet how they encode linguistic and paralinguistic information remains unclear. Improving the interpretability of NAC representations is critical for understanding and deploying them in sensitive applications. Hence, we employ Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose dense NAC representations into sparse, interpretable activations. In this work, we focus on a challenging paralinguistic attribute-accent--and propose a framework to quantify NAC task-level interpretability. We evaluate four NAC models under 16 SAE configurations using a relative performance index. Our results show that DAC and SpeechTokenizer achieve the highest interpretability. We further reveal that acoustic-oriented NACs encode accent information primarily in activation magnitudes of sparse representations, whereas phonetic-oriented NACs rely more on activation positions, and that low-bitrate EnCodec variants show higher interpretability.
column7: Shih-Heng Wang(University of Southern California); Tiantian Feng(University of Southern California); Aditya Kommineni(University of Southern California); Thanathai Lertpetchpun(University of Southern California); Bowen Yi(University of Southern California); Xuan Shi(University of Southern California); Shrikanth Narayanan(University of Southern California)

column4: Spectro-Temporal Interference Confounds Phase Encoding in Spatial Audio Foundation Models
column6: Recent spatial self supervised audio models achieve high performance on localization tasks, raising questions about their encoding of microsecond interaural phase fine structures. We propose a psychoacoustic benchmark based on the binaural masking level difference to evaluate this. Using an equalization cancellation baseline and a GCC PHAT positive control we evaluate nine frozen audio models spanning binaural SSL, monaural SSL, and neural audio codecs. Four monaural negative controls yield zero BMLD confirming binaural specificity. Two general purpose binaural SSL models exhibit minimal phase sensitivity while dedicated binaural spatial SSL models achieve substantial but sub-ceiling BMLD. Progressive physical ablations show that general purpose binaural SSL models rely on spectro temporal interference textures rather than cross channel phase computation. High detection rates in speech reflect a confounding reliance on broadband envelopes rather than genuine phase encoding.
column7: Yuxuan Chen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Jilin University); Haoyuan Yu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen; Hunan University); Peize He(University of Electronic Science and Technology of China)

column4: On Optimizing Multimodal Jailbreaks for Spoken Language Models
column6: As Spoken Language Models (SLMs) integrate speech and text modalities, they inherit the safety vulnerabilities of their LLM backbone and an expanded attack surface. SLMs have previously been shown to be susceptible to jailbreaking, where adversarial prompts induce harmful responses. Yet existing attacks largely remain unimodal, optimizing either text or audio in isolation. We explore gradient-based multimodal jailbreaks and introduce JAMA (Joint Audio-text Multimodal Attack), a joint multimodal optimization framework combining Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), simultaneously perturbing both input modalities. Evaluations across four state-of-the-art SLMs and four audio types demonstrate that JAMA surpasses unimodal jailbreak rate by 1.5× to 20×. We analyze the operational dynamics of this joint attack and show that a sequential attack makes it 4× to 6× faster. Our findings suggest that unimodal safety is insufficient for robust SLMs.
column7: Aravind Krishnan(Saarland University; DFKI GmbH); Karolina Stańczak(ETH AI Center); Dietrich Klakow(Saarland University)

column4: A Unified Safety Subspace Exists in Speech Language Models
column6: Speech Language Models (SLMs) extend large language models to spoken interaction, but this multimodal integration introduces modality-specific vulnerabilities. While prior work has typically addressed speech and text safety in isolation, our work uncovers a shared safety subspace where benign, harmful, and jailbreak representations exist regardless of input modality. We identify this subspace via a PCA projection, revealing a well-defined boundary separating refusal from jailbreak compliance. Causal intervention along this boundary shifts model behavior between refusal and compliance across modalities and attack types without additional training. For example, a refusal vector derived from an audio attack reduces text jailbreak success from 76.5% to 2.2%, while a refusal vector derived from the text attack reduces audio jailbreak success from 79.0% to 3.1%. We demonstrate these results on Qwen2-Audio and GLM-4-Voice, and confirm transferability across five different attacks.
column7: Nurdaulet Mukhituly(MBZUAI); Muhammad Cendekia Airlangga(MBZUAI); Rifo Ahmad Genadi(MBZUAI); Nhi Hoai Doan(MBZUAI); Amirbek Djanibekov(MBZUAI); Samuel Munachiso Nwadike(MBZUAI); Zangir Iklassov(MBZUAI); Kentaro Inui(MBZUAI; Tohoku University; RIKEN)

column4: Do Learned Layer Weights Reflect Pretrained Information Structure in Self-Supervised Speech Models?
column6: Self-supervised speech models are commonly evaluated using learned weighted sums over frozen layers. Prior work concluded these weights are uninformative, based on weak correlation with single-layer performance. In contrast, we explore whether learned weights reflect the pretrained model's layerwise information content, measured by adjusted mutual information (AMI) between clustered layer representations and phone or word labels. Across 13 SSL models, we find significant correlations for most conditions, with strength depending on supervision amount and pretraining objective. Weights after training with 10 minutes of labeled data consistently show higher correlation with AMI than those from 1 hour. Contrastive models show strong correlation of up to 0.98, while clustering-based ones yield weaker alignment. Despite prior characterizations as unreliable, learned weights systematically reflect pretrained information structure, particularly for contrastive models under limited supervision.
column7: Yaroslav Getman(Aalto University, Finland); Tamás Grosz(Walton Institute, Ireland); Mikko Kurimo(Aalto University, Finland)

column4: XAI-Grounded Explanation Generation for Speech Deepfake Detection with Training-Free Multimodal Large Language Models
column6: Speech deepfake detection (SDD) systems require trustworthy explanations for reliable decision-making. Existing explanation ways mainly fall into two categories. Traditional explainable AI (XAI), such as gradient-based attribution, produces low-level attribution signals tightly coupled with model decisions, and harder to be understood by human than natural language explanations. Meanwhile, large language model (LLM)-based explanation generation often produces generic and ungrounded descriptions due to the lack of heuristic evidence and task-specific supervision, stemming from limited grounded explanation datasets for SDD. We therefore propose a training-free explanation framework that integrates XAI evidence with multimodal LLMs to generate grounded and specific explanations. Using the PartialSpoof dataset, we construct a grounded explanation dataset and show that methods with XAI increase inside accuracy by over 45%, verified through human evaluation and faithfulness checks.
column7: Yupei Li(Imperial College London; Technical University of Munich); Qiyang Sun(Imperial College London); Xiaoliang Wu(University of Southampton); Chenxi Wang(Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence); Berrak Sisman(Johns Hopkins University); Björn W. Schuller(Imperial College London; Technical University of Munich)

column4: Cross-Attention is Half Explanation in Speech-to-Text Models
column6: Cross-attention is widely used in speech-to-text (S2T) systems and often exploited for downstream applications such as timestamp prediction and speech-text alignment, under the assumption that it reflects input-output dependencies. While extensively debated in NLP, its explanatory role remains underexplored in the speech domain. We empirically assess the explanatory power of cross-attention in S2T models by comparing attention scores with input saliency maps from feature-attribution methods. Our analysis spans monolingual and multilingual, single-task and multi-task models at multiple scales. We find moderate alignment between attention and saliency, particularly when aggregating across heads and layers. However, cross-attention captures only about 50% of input relevance and, at best, 52-75% of the encoder saliency. These results show that cross-attention offers useful but incomplete explanatory cues and should be interpreted with caution as a proxy for model behavior in S2T systems.
column7: Sara Papi(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Dennis Fucci(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Marco Gaido(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Matteo Negri(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Luisa Bentivogli(Fondazione Bruno Kessler)

column4: Causal Tracing of Audio-Text Fusion in Large Audio Language Models
column6: Despite the strong performance of large audio language models (LALMs) in various tasks, exactly how and where they integrate acoustic features with textual context remains unclear. We adapt causal tracing to investigate the internal information flow of LALMs during audio comprehension. By conducting layer-wise and token-wise analyses across DeSTA, Qwen, and Voxtral, we evaluate the causal effects of individual hidden states. Layer-wise analysis identifies different fusion strategies, from progressive integration in DeSTA to an abrupt late-stage fusion in Qwen. Token-wise analysis shows that the final sequence token acts as an informational bottleneck where the network decisively retrieves relevant information from the audio. We also observe an attention-like query mechanism at intermediate token positions that triggers the model to pull task-relevant audio context. These findings provide a clear characterization of when and where multi-modal integration occurs within LALMs.
column7: Wei-Chih Chen(National Taiwan University); Chien-yu Huang(Carnegie Mellon University); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University; NTU Artificial Intelligence Center of Research Excellence)

column4: Disentangling Acoustic Cues in Alzheimer’s Pathology and Perception: The Roles of Language and Gender
column6: Acoustic biomarkers show promise for detecting Alzheimer's Disease (AD), yet whether the cues driving diagnostic AI align with those salient to human listeners is underexplored across languages and genders, where pathological markers and perceptual strategies differ. We train models to predict clinical AD status (pathology) and human perceptual scores across Mandarin and Greek, male and female speakers. Using SHAP for interpretability and statistical models for validation, we compare feature importance by subgroup. Results reveal a context-dependent divergence: pathological–perceptual alignment is significant for Mandarin and female speakers but disappears for Greek and male speakers, where pathology models did not exceed chance—a failure mode population-specific auditing surfaces. Global Explainable AI (XAI) explanations can mask critical demographic divergences, highlighting the need for population-specific explainability auditing for equitable deployment of clinical speech AI.
column7: Liu He(University of Science and Technology of China); Yuanchao Li(University of Edinburgh); Yin-Long Liu(University of Science and Technology of China); Rui Feng(University of Science and Technology of China); Yiming Wang(University of Science and Technology of China); Jiaxin Chen(University of Science and Technology of China); Yizhe Wang(University of Science and Technology of China); Jiahong Yuan(University of Science and Technology of China)

column4: Towards Dys-XAI: Influence-Based Explanations for Dysarthria Severity Assessment
column6: Dysarthria severity assessment is essential for therapy planning and longitudinal monitoring, yet manual perceptual rating is time-consuming and variable across clinicians. Although deep learning models achieve strong performance, their black-box nature limits clinical adoption. Existing speech explainability methods typically provide acoustic feature importance scores that are difficult for end-users to interpret. We propose an influence-based, instance-level explainability framework that explains each decision through supportive and competing training samples. Using gradient-based influence approximations, we compute per-utterance influence scores to identify supportive and competing training samples for each prediction. Controlled deletion experiments (5-20%) validate the explanations, showing that removing highly influential samples systematically shifts predictions. This approach provides auditable explanations by linking decisions to perceptible reference cases.
column7: Xiaoliang Wu(University of Southampton); Qiyang Sun(Imperial College London); Yupei Li(Imperial College London); Erfan Loweimi(University of Edinburgh); Jennifer Williams(University of Southampton); Zhengjun Yue(King's College London)

column4: What Do Neural Networks Learn for TDOA Estimation? A Cross-Architecture Probing Study
column6: Neural networks outperform classical GCC-PHAT for Time-Difference-of-Arrival (TDOA) estimation in noise and reverberation, yet their internal strategy remains unexplored. To uncover it, we turn GCC-PHAT's mathematical steps into diagnostic targets, probing hidden layers of three architectures (MLP, CNN, Transformer) and complementing with gradient attribution and causal frequency masking. We find that cross-power computation consistently emerges across all architectures and conditions, while PHAT whitening, the defining step of GCC-PHAT, fails to emerge. Instead, networks learn a magnitude-aware frequency weighting that preserves per-frequency reliability information discarded by PHAT. This makes PHAT an information bottleneck: removing it from both classical and neural GCC pipelines improves performance under additive noise. On real-world reverberant data, PHAT remains the best classical weighting, but end-to-end networks achieve lower error by learning data-adaptive weighting.
column7: Yaozhong Kang(Institute of Science Tokyo); Jiang Wang(Institute of Science Tokyo); Runwu Shi(Institute of Science Tokyo); Takeshi Ashizawa(Institute of Science Tokyo); Benjamin Yen(Institute of Science Tokyo); Kazuhiro Nakadai(Institute of Science Tokyo)

column4: TSExplorer: An interactive data annotation and exploration tool for time-series data
column6: We present TSExplorer, a cross-platform tool for interactive annotation and exploration of time-series data. The tool enables users to inspect high-dimensional datasets through multiple complementary 2D visualizations derived from high-dimensional feature representations. TSExplorer is designed as a general-purpose research tool supporting a wide range of workflows, including exploratory data analysis, annotation of unlabeled or partially-labeled datasets, comparison of feature representations, and post-hoc inspection and refinement of existing labels with interactive visual feedback.
column7: Einari Vaaras(Tampere University); Manu Airaksinen(University of Helsinki); Okko Räsänen(Tampere University)

column4: Lightweight Emotion Recognition with Disjoint Modality Fusion
column6: Modern speech emotion recognition methods typically use large-scale models and multimodal fusion, often resulting in significant computational overhead that limits real-world deployment on consumer hardware. We propose Light-DMF, a lightweight model designed to classify emotions from audio and text both independently and through a fused pathway. Our disjoint architecture supports mixed-modal data where audio or text can be present, absent, or contain conflicting emotional cues and labels. Our model has fewer than 65k trainable parameters and achieves a real-time factor below 1 in CPU-only inference. We provide open-source code and a demo to facilitate future research and offer a speech emotion recognition tool for the general public.
column7: Serkan Sulun(INESC TEC; University of Porto)

column4: SpeechBench: A Unified Speech Annotation and Analysis Tool
column6: Existing speech annotation tools do not adequately support model-assisted manual annotation workflows that use general-purpose models to pre-annotate domain-specific speech data followed by human refinement. As a result, the annotation process remains time-consuming, inefficient, and difficult to scale. We therefore present SpeechBench, an integrated tool designed to facilitate this workflow. The tool incorporates trained models for a range of speech processing tasks and provides a graphical interface for constructing multi-step, model-based pre-annotation pipelines, lowering the barrier for non-technical users. It also supports flexible deployment on private servers to meet strict data privacy requirements.
column7: Zheng Nan(University of New South Wales); Tharmakulasingam Sirojan(University of New South Wales); Mostafa Shahin(University of New South Wales); Tünde Szalay(University of Sydney); Vidhyasaharan Sethu(University of New South Wales); Beena Ahmed(University of New South Wales)

column4: corpusgen: An Open-Source Toolkit for Phoneme-Coverage-Optimized Speech Corpus Design Across Languages
column6: We present corpusgen, an open-source Python toolkit for designing speech corpora with maximal phoneme coverage across languages. The toolkit integrates grapheme-to-phoneme conversion via espeak-ng, phoneme inventories from PHOIBLE (covering 2,186 languages), and multiple corpus optimization algorithms including greedy set cover with CELF acceleration, integer linear programming, distribution-aware selection, and NSGA-II multi-objective optimization. Beyond selection from existing text, corpusgen supports targeted sentence generation through pluggable backends including LLM APIs and local transformer models with phonotactic control. A unified evaluation module reports phoneme, diphone, and triphone coverage alongside distribution quality metrics. The toolkit is pip-installable, provides both a Python API and a CLI, and is released under the Apache-2.0 license. We demonstrate its application to corpus design across typologically diverse languages, showing how coverage-optimized selection achieves near-optimal phoneme coverage with significantly fewer sentences than random baselines.
column7: Muntaser Syed(Florida Institute of Technology); Marius Silaghi(Florida Institute of Technology); Sharun Akter Khushbu(Daffodil International University); Fariha Jaigirdar(Deakin University)

column4: Speech Playground: An Interactive Tool for Speech Analysis and Comparison
column6: This paper presents Speech Playground, an interactive speech visualization and comparison tool. While existing tools such as Praat are excellent, it can be cumbersome to integrate them with modern deep learning representations and use them for comparison. Speech Playground addresses this by combining a Python backend with a web-based frontend for interactive exploration of multiple feature types, including continuous, discrete, and variable-length representations. It includes TextGrid and forced alignment support together with configurable distance and alignment settings for visual and auditory comparison. Speech Playground is intended for use in speech research, representation validation, and computer-aided pronunciation training (CAPT)-oriented experimentation.
column7: Stephen McIntosh(The University of Tokyo); Daisuke Saito(The University of Tokyo); Nobuaki Minematsu(The University of Tokyo)

column4: MER-Live: An Interactive Browser Demo of Prosody-Driven Multimodal Emotion Recognition
column6: MER-Live is a real-time multimodal emotion recognition demo in which speech is the dominant signal, supported by video and lexical cues. The acoustic branch uses a novel lightweight masked auto-encoder SER model (MSMC) on log-mel spectrograms, while the text branch acts only as an auxiliary tie-breaker rather than a keyword trigger. Users speak to the camera and watch emotion estimates update four times per second. They can hot-swap ten speaker-holdout checkpoints, record a five second utterance for IEMOCAP-style logit averaging, or upload audio files for side-by-side comparison with an open SER baseline. The 6.77M-parameter audio model, exported to TensorRT FP16, serves a batch of five in 0.24 ms on one H200, giving a 14x speed-up over PyTorch FP32. On 10-fold IEMOCAP, the deployed audio-only MSMC checkpoint used in MER-Live reaches 74.03% WA and 66.39% UA. Multimodal performance exceeds 83%.
column7: Haoyu Song(Singapore Institute of Technology); Xiaoxiao Miao(Duke Kunshan University); Pai Chet Ng(Singapore Institute of Technology); Timothy Liu(NVIDIA AI Technology Center); Aik Beng Ng(NVIDIA AI Technology Center); Ian McLoughlin(Singapore Institute of Technology)
